verses.2: This Book, free of doubt, guides those who guard against evil.
verses.3: Al-Mizan states: They believe in the unseen, keep up prayer, and spend benevolently from what We have given them.
verses.4: Al-Mizan states: They believe in what has been sent down to thee and before thee, and are sure of the hereafter.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan says that, although this chapter was revealed piecemeal and has no single theme, much of it establishes that true servitude to God requires belief in everything revealed to all His messengers, without distinguishing between revelations or messengers. It consequently admonishes the disbelievers, hypocrites, and People of the Book for dividing God’s religion and differentiating among His messengers, then lays down important laws concerning the direction of prayer, hajj, inheritance, fasting, and other matters.

The commentary postpones discussion of the opening letter-symbols to chapter 42, and discussion of the Qur’an’s being a Book and its guidance to a later place. It explains that the pious are the believers themselves: piety is not a virtue confined to one class of believers, as are good works, humility before God, or purity of intention, but a comprehensive quality found throughout every rank of true faith. Its five characteristics in these verses are belief in the unseen, prayer, benevolent spending from God’s provision, belief in revelations sent to God’s messengers, and certainty of the hereafter.

These qualities arise through God’s guidance. A first guidance makes people pious; once pious, they receive the Qur’an’s guidance, which raises their rank. Thus the five qualities of right belief and action stand between two guidances, the latter founded on the former. The disbelievers and hypocrites stand in the opposite condition, between two stages of error and blindness: their own initial straying, disbelief, hypocrisy, or disease of heart is followed by a divine sealing or increase that confirms and strengthens their error. God’s causing people to err follows their transgression and turning aside.

Because the second guidance is through the Qur’an, the first precedes it and comes through a healthy, unimpaired nature. Such a nature recognizes its own dependence, and that of all things it can perceive, imagine, or understand, on a Being beyond the chain of dependent things—unseen and imperceptible to the senses, yet the beginning and end of all else. Seeing the Creator’s care in perfecting even the smallest details of creation, it recognizes that He would not leave human beings to wander without guidance for their actions and morals. This reasoning yields belief in the One God, prophethood, and resurrection. It then produces worship and the use of every capacity—wealth, standing, knowledge, power, and other advantages—to preserve faith and convey it to others; hence prayer and benevolent spending. God thereafter grants the Qur’an’s further guidance, while the same progressive principle applies inversely to error.

The verses also indicate another life concealed behind this worldly one, by which a person lives both now and after death and resurrection. Al-Mizan defines al-Imān as the heart’s consolidation of belief, deriving from al-amn, safety: faith gives security against doubt. Faith and believers have degrees, as certainty may extend from its object to its concomitants and finally to all matters connected with it. Al-Ghayb is the opposite of what is perceived. Though it can include God, His great signs, revelation, and the hereafter, revelation and the hereafter are separately named here; therefore, in this passage the unseen must mean God alone. The three fundamentals of religion are thereby completed. The Qur’an thus directs people not to confine knowledge and belief to sensory perception, but to use sound reasoning and understanding.

The verse says that the pious are sure of the hereafter, not merely believers in it. Such certainty must remain present, because someone who merely believes may forget a belief’s demands and act against them. Certainty that every great and small deed will be accounted for prevents disobedience; forgetting the Day of Reckoning leads a person astray. Certainty and remembrance of it therefore make one guard against evil.

Finally, guidance properly belongs to God alone, and is attributed to others only metaphorically. Divine guidance expands the breast, freeing it from constraint and niggardliness; since those preserved from the niggardliness of their souls are the successful, those who are upon their Lord’s guidance are rightly described as successful.
verses.6: Al-Mizan states that those who disbelieve will not believe, whether they are warned or not.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse concerns not all disbelievers, but people whose rejection had taken deep root, so that warning could not move them from their obduracy. It probably refers to the Quraysh disbelievers who were Islam’s bitterest enemies, sought to extinguish faith, and persisted until God destroyed them at Badr and other battles. Applying the verse to every disbeliever would close the door of guidance. Its repetition in Chapter of Yā Sīn (36:10), a Meccan chapter, while the present chapter was revealed in Medina before Badr, further supports its reference to that same Meccan group.

The commentary adds that, elsewhere, “those who disbelieve” may likewise mean this group unless there is evidence otherwise. Similarly, “those who believe” refers to the first, early Muslims unless there is reason to take it differently; this designation was an honorific protocol.

On (2:7), Al-Mizan distinguishes Allah’s sealing of their hearts and hearing from the covering over their eyes, which they themselves initially placed over their souls by choosing to shut out the light of truth. After their sins and disbelief, Allah placed a further curtain or seal upon them; their disbelief and evil deeds thus lie between a self-imposed veil and a divine one. Such people face a great punishment. Disbelief, like belief, has degrees and ranks, with correspondingly varying effects.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan states that these thirteen verses concern the hypocrites, a subject it says will be discussed in detail in Chapter 63 (The Hypocrites) and elsewhere. They profess belief in Allah and the last day while lacking belief. They seek to deceive Allah and the believers, yet unknowingly deceive only themselves. The disease in their hearts is increased by Allah, and their habitual lying earns a painful chastisement. When forbidden to make mischief, they call themselves peacemakers, though they are the mischief-makers without perceiving it; when told to believe as the people believe, they call the believers fools, although they themselves are the fools without knowing it.

They tell believers that they believe, but, when alone with their satans, affirm solidarity with them and say that they were only mocking. Al-Shayṭān means evil or wickedness, which is why Iblis is called Satan. Allah repays their mockery and leaves them wandering blindly in rebellion. They have bought error in exchange for guidance, a bargain that yields neither gain nor right guidance.

The first parable compares them to a man in blinding darkness, unable to distinguish good from bad or benefit from harm. He kindles a fire and sees some distance by its light; once it has illumined what surrounds him, Allah extinguishes it by wind, rain, or a similar cause. He is left in utter darkness, pressed between the darkness of night and the darkness of his bewilderment and the nullity of his effort. Likewise, the hypocrite's declaration of Islam brings worldly benefits, since he is treated as a Muslim in such matters as marriage and inheritance. But when death approaches, when Islam's real and complete benefits should appear, Allah removes his light, nullifies his deeds, and leaves him unable to see. He is thus caught between his original darkness and the darkness added by his evil deeds: deaf, dumb, and blind, he will not return.

The second parable compares them to one caught in a rainstorm amid darkness, thunder, and lightning. Unable to see or find his bearings, he seeks to escape and find shelter, but darkness prevents him; overwhelmed by thunder and thunderbolts, he puts his fingers in his ears for fear of death, while Allah encompasses the unbelievers. Lightning nearly takes away his sight. He walks when its momentary light shines and stops when darkness returns; had Allah wished, He would have taken away his hearing and sight, for He has power over all things.

This also describes the hypocrite, who dislikes Islam but must profess himself a Muslim. His words do not reach his heart, and what he says differs from what he believes inwardly. Because of this discrepancy, his path is not properly illumined: he gropes, stumbles, advances a little, and stops. Allah thereby punishes him with disgrace; had He wished, He could have taken away his hearing and sight from the very first day.

They tell believers that they believe, but, when alone with their satans, affirm solidarity with them and say that they were only mocking. Al-Shayṭān means evil or wickedness, which is why Iblis is called Satan. Allah repays their mockery and leaves them wandering blindly in rebellion. They have bought error in exchange for guidance, a bargain that yields neither gain nor right guidance.

The first parable compares them to a man in blinding darkness, unable to distinguish good from bad or benefit from harm. He kindles a fire and sees some distance by its light; once it has illumined what surrounds him, Allah extinguishes it by wind, rain, or a similar cause. He is left in utter darkness, pressed between the darkness of night and the darkness of his bewilderment and the nullity of his effort. Likewise, the hypocrite's declaration of Islam brings worldly benefits, since he is treated as a Muslim in such matters as marriage and inheritance. But when death approaches, when Islam's real and complete benefits should appear, Allah removes his light, nullifies his deeds, and leaves him unable to see. He is thus caught between his original darkness and the darkness added by his evil deeds: deaf, dumb, and blind, he will not return.

The second parable compares them to one caught in a rainstorm amid darkness, thunder, and lightning. Unable to see or find his bearings, he seeks to escape and find shelter, but darkness prevents him; overwhelmed by thunder and thunderbolts, he puts his fingers in his ears for fear of death, while Allah encompasses the unbelievers. Lightning nearly takes away his sight. He walks when its momentary light shines and stops when darkness returns; had Allah wished, He would have taken away his hearing and sight, for He has power over all things.

This also describes the hypocrite, who dislikes Islam but must profess himself a Muslim. His words do not reach his heart, and what he says differs from what he believes inwardly. Because of this discrepancy, his path is not properly illumined: he gropes, stumbles, advances a little, and stops. Allah thereby punishes him with disgrace; had He wished, He could have taken away his hearing and sight from the very first day.

verses.21: Al-Mizan: Worship your Lord, creator of you and those before you, to guard against evil.
verses.22: Al-Mizan says that Allah made the earth a resting place and the sky a structure, and sends rain to produce fruits for sustenance; knowingly, do not set up equals to Him.
verses.23: Al-Mizan challenges doubters of what was revealed to His servant to produce a like chapter, summoning any witnesses besides Allah if they are truthful.
verses.24: Al-Mizan warns that they will never do so; therefore fear the Fire, fuelled by men and stones and prepared for the unbelievers.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan relates the call to worship to the preceding portrayal of the pious, the disbelievers, and the hypocrites. It calls all people to become God’s servants and join the pious rather than the latter two groups. Thus, the clause, ‘so that you may guard [against evil],’ primarily gives the end of worship, although it may alternatively state that God created people for that end.

The commentary explains andād as the plural of al-nidd: an alike, equal, or peer. Since ‘while you know’ is an unconditional circumstantial qualifier of the prohibition, it gives exceptional force to the command not to set up equals to Allah. Even a little knowledge should prevent one from associating partners with the God who created people and ordered the system that provides their sustenance and survival.

Al-Mizan takes the challenge in (2:23) to be one which humans and jinn can never meet. It demonstrates that the Qur’an is a divine, enduring miracle and therefore a book free of doubt. The pronoun in ‘like it’ refers to what was revealed to the servant, namely the Qur’an, and challenges opponents to produce its like in both style and meaning. But min mithlihi may also mean ‘from one like him’: if they suppose an untaught man such as the Prophet could produce it, they should bring an equivalent book from another such man. Some traditions give both explanations. The challenge extends even to the shortest sūrah. The interpretation that it asks for a chapter like The Cow is rejected as literary nonsense, because those addressed denied the whole Qur’an as forged; challenging them to match its largest chapter would not answer their doubt about its shortest ones.

The Qur’an’s claim to miraculousness contains two claims: that supernatural miracles occur, and that the Qur’an is one of them. Proving the latter proves the former. Al-Mizan therefore treats the subject in two stages: establishing the Qur’an’s miracle through its continuing challenge, and then considering how a miracle relates to the universal order of cause and effect. The challenge does not directly assert the Prophet’s prophethood; it asks about doubt concerning what was revealed to him. Once the Qur’an is established as a supernatural sign from God, his prophethood follows.

The widest challenge addresses all humanity and the jinn, so it cannot be confined to Arabic eloquence or to any isolated excellence that only specialists can assess. It challenges opponents to bring a like of the Qur’an in all its qualities together: its expression, wisdom, knowledge, moral formation, social order, legislation, politics, justice, reports of the unseen, prophecies, and freedom from discrepancy. Every person capable of understanding Qur’anic speech should compare the excellence he knows in himself or others with the Qur’an’s corresponding excellence and judge fairly whether human power could produce it. Its comprehensive knowledge, character-building, monotheistic and pious legislation, and absence of discrepancy are especially striking in a book brought by an untaught man raised among a people portrayed as marked by raiding, war, ignorance, moral abuses, and political subjection.

Likewise, a claimant to guidance for the worlds could hardly spread accurate reports of the unseen, past and future, throughout a book without a single error. Nor could a human being deliver, over twenty-three years and through changing conditions, a complete body of knowledge, laws, wisdom, admonition, parables, and histories without inconsistency or visible intellectual development. A person unable to assess this should follow natural human practice and consult those knowledgeable in the subject.

The inclusion of ordinary people in the challenge does not, in the commentary’s view, make it vulnerable to pretenders. Human understanding has degrees, as do excellences: those with sound, higher perception can recognize the finest quality, and those of lesser understanding should refer to them. A miracle meant for every individual, place, and age must be divine knowledge and spiritual reality. Material signs are confined to a particular time and place and can be witnessed only by a limited generation, whereas the Qur’an continues to confront all people in every era.

Its first particular challenge concerns its knowledge. Al-Mizan says that Islam attends to every significant and minor matter of divine knowledge, moral virtue, and religious law, including worship, transactions, social regulation, and penalties. Its details rest on monotheism, healthy human nature, and the principles flowing from them. This teaching is declared permanently valid and protected from falsehood and abrogation. Against the sociological objection that laws must change with changing social structures, the commentary answers that Qur’anic legislation grows from creation, monotheism, and excellent morality, while sociologists attend only to material development and disregard the spiritual dimension; society itself has no soul.

A second challenge lies in the recipient of revelation. The Prophet lived among his people without learning from a teacher, becoming known for scholarship, giving lectures, or composing poetry until his fortieth year; then he brought a revelation before which masters of eloquence were helpless. The suggestion that he learned from Christian monks during journeys to Syria fails because he made only two such journeys, was not left alone, and no such instruction was reported; even if it had occurred, it would not explain his monotheistic knowledge, wise laws, realities, and unmatched expression. The allegation that a Roman blacksmith taught him fails because that man’s tongue was barbarous while the Qur’an is clear Arabic. Nor could Salmān have been the source: he met the Prophet in Medina and accepted Islam after the Meccan revelations had already supplied the principles, knowledge, and narratives later repeated in Medina. The Qur’an’s accounts also differ from Biblical narratives: it clears prophets of sins ascribed to them in the Bible and confines its discourse to what benefits spiritual elevation and character.

Its third particular challenge is its prophecies and information of the unseen. Al-Mizan groups these into reports of earlier prophets and nations unknown to the Prophet and his people; predictions of future events, including events involving the Prophet, the believers, the Qur’an’s preservation, and signs before the Day of Judgment; statements of scientific realities unknown when the Qur’an was revealed and discovered only after prolonged research; and allusions to later upheavals in the Islamic community and the world. It notes that the last category is among the specialties of this work.

Another challenge is the absence of discrepancy. Material things and human intellects change and develop; a person’s later judgments correct earlier ones. Yet the Qur’an was revealed piecemeal over twenty-three years, in Mecca and Medina, travel and residence, war and peace, hardship and ease, defeat and victory, safety and danger, and it addresses every kind of subject. Still, its realities and principles contain no contradiction or contrariety; its verses explain and clarify one another. Al-Mizan quotes Imam ʿAlī’s description: ‘Its one part speaks with the other, and one portion testifies about the others.’ A book from other than God would vary between elegance and clumsiness, truth and error, and would be uneven and contradictory.

In answer to claims by non-Muslim writers that the Qur’an contains defective constructions and meanings, the commentary says that Muslim exegetical works had already raised those apparent difficulties and supplied answers showing their eloquence. The adversaries merely collected the objections and ignored the answers. Abrogation is also not a change of opinion or a contradiction: when society or circumstances change so that a rule’s underlying wisdom no longer applies, the difference lies in the subject matter. The abrogated verses themselves contain indications that their commands were temporary.

The Qur’an also challenges its opponents in eloquence, asking them to forge ten chapters or even one like it. This was directed to Arabs who had reached the height of eloquence and were intensely proud of it, yet they avoided the challenge rather than meeting it. Al-Mizan maintains that no one has matched it in the centuries since; attempted imitations, including samples attributed to Musaylamah and a later Christian writer, only exposed their authors to ridicule.

It considers two objections to a miraculous eloquence. First, if language is a human invention, how can speech exceed human ability? Second, if only one among many possible formulations of a meaning can be unsurpassable, how can the Qur’an repeat subjects in different styles and have them all be miraculous? These questions helped produce the theory of al-ṣarf, according to which God merely turned people away from imitating the Qur’an in order to protect prophethood. Al-Mizan rejects this outright. The challenge is intended to establish that the Qur’an is revelation from God’s knowledge, not a fabrication or satanic speech; its inimitability rests in its own final interpretation, known to God, and in its inherent freedom from discrepancy, not in a divine prevention of otherwise possible imitation.

Human beings devised individual words for meanings, but that does not give them the ability to arrange words so that speech perfectly reflects the intended meaning and that meaning perfectly reflects reality. Speech depends on knowledge of a language, eloquent skill, and knowledge of realities; these may occur separately, and human perception and discernment remain limited and develop over time. Thus human speech cannot be assured of freedom from factual and intellectual error or of uniform perfection even within a single discourse. A decisive speech grounded in comprehensive knowledge and free from every discrepancy cannot be the work of a mortal.

Perfect eloquence requires that words completely fit the intended meaning and that the meaning correspond to a real, permanent fact outside imagination. The order of words should accord with the natural order of the meaning and its parts. Sweet expression and fluent style are insufficient if a proposition is false; truth and comprehensive wisdom are indispensable. Truth is indivisible: one truth cannot conflict with another, whereas falsehood has many mutually opposed paths. Accordingly, the Qur’an’s verses confirm one another, and combining clear, relevant verses discloses realities not apparent from each separately. Al-Mizan regards this as a distinctive Qur’anic quality that exegetes have neglected. Hence miraculous eloquence is not based on words alone, and varied formulations of a subject can all be miraculous when their meanings accord with immutable reality and their words accord with those meanings.

The commentary affirms miracles as unusual, preternatural events displaying metaphysical authority over the material world, while denying that they violate self-evident rational truth. Attempts to reinterpret the Qur’anic accounts merely to accommodate modern physical science impose forced meanings on its language. The Qur’an confirms the general causal order: every effect has a cause, and a complete cause, with its conditions present, unfailingly produces its effect. Yet it ascribes both effects and causes ultimately to God.

Miracles are abnormal, not inherently impossible. Their effects are not alien to nature, which continually changes one form into another; the difference is that ordinary causes bring effects through a long sequence of conditions, time, and stages, whereas a miracle occurs through a prophet’s will without an apparent material cause or lapse of time. Modern unusual feats have prompted theories of unknown magnetic or electric currents that rigorous training might control; if such a theory proved complete, it would replace other explanatory causes with one pervasive natural cause. Al-Mizan does not identify any such universal cause, because that is not the Qur’an’s purpose, but accepts that every phenomenon has a natural cause by God’s permission.

God can attain His purpose even where normal avenues are closed. This may occur directly by His will without a material cause, or through an alternative natural cause unknown to us; the latter possibility appears more appropriate in light of the assertion that God has set a measure for everything. Every effect has a divinely appointed measure defining its identity and relation to all other things; the related preceding and accompanying things together form its cause, and the effect in turn becomes part of later causes. Al-Mizan accordingly concludes that God creates everything on one undeviating pattern, every material effect has a preceding cause whether normal or extraordinary, and usual causes that sometimes fail are not the real complete causes.

Although causes truly have causal power, their power is bestowed by God and they remain dependent on His permission. He is the real owner and authority; a permitted cause is like one authorized to use another’s property only within fixed limits. Thus every natural effect is truly caused by God as well as by its proximate cause.

The souls of prophets have a special power to bring signs by Allah’s permission. Magic likewise has some reality and is caused by a psychical factor in the magician, again only by Allah’s permission. Miracles, magic, extraordinary wonders of saints, and abilities gained through rigorous practice all arise from psychical factors or will-power. But the psychical source granted to messengers, prophets, and believers is divinely assisted, predominant over every opposing cause, and never overcome; unlike material things, it is not bounded by a superior material force.

A supernatural effect caused through psychical power also depends upon God’s command in addition to His permission. Human voluntary actions arise through human will, but that will and the action dependent on it are themselves dependent on God’s will and command, His word ‘Be.’ This does not mean that every human wish is God’s wish, for then no wish would remain unfulfilled. Natural and supernatural events, whether good, such as miracles, or evil, such as magic and soothsaying, require their causes together with divine permission, will, and command. In a prophet’s miracle and in an answered prayer of God’s good servant, the decisive divine command is additionally present, so that the desired effect inevitably occurs.

Al-Mizan distinguishes ordinary events, produced through normal apparent causes; evil extraordinary events such as sorcery, produced through unusual causes; good extraordinary events such as answered prayer, which make no challenge or claim; and miracles, which are good extraordinary events brought as a challenge to establish a claim. The latter two have an invincible factor because of the decisive divine command. A miracle is not miraculous merely because its cause is unknown: even if its natural cause were discovered, its distinguishing feature would remain its invincibility. Sudden healing through a believer’s prayer differs from treatment by medicine because medical treatment can be defeated by stronger factors.

Miracles are not meant to prove religious principles such as God’s oneness or resurrection, which prophets establish by reasoning. Their purpose is to authenticate the prophet’s claim that he has been sent by God and receives revelation, a claim concerning a reality beyond ordinary sense and intellect. Opponents objected that prophets were merely human like themselves; that a true messenger should not eat, work in markets, or lack an accompanying angel, treasure, or garden; that angels should descend to all people or that they should see God; and that the prophet was simply insane. The reply is that common humanity does not prevent God from granting a special favor to whomever He pleases. Earlier messengers also ate and went to markets, and an angel sent as a messenger would have to appear as a man; obstinate rejecters will see angels only at death, without joy.

The other response to prophethood was to demand a credential. Since revelation is inaccessible to anyone but the claimant and appears to defy ordinary causation, a prophet claiming contact with divine power should show another tangible supernatural effect. This is like a ruler’s envoy: explaining the wisdom of the ruler’s laws does not prove that he is the authorized envoy; he must produce the ruler’s credential. Therefore miracles are necessary for learned and unlearned alike to recognize a prophet’s claim, and revelation is a reality distinct from mental inference or merely correct thinking.

Al-Mizan rejects modern materialist reinterpretations that make a prophet an intellectual genius and social reformer, revelation his beneficial thoughts, and scripture their collection; reduce angels, the Holy Ghost, Satan, and other unseen realities to material forces or psychological traits; treat religion as a changing product of its time; and dismiss miracles as myths devised for religion’s benefit. Such prophethood would be a political device rather than a divine reality, and bears no resemblance to the scriptural and prophetic descriptions. Earlier theologians, it says, retained the lexical meanings of realities such as the Throne, Chair, Tablet, Pen, and angels, but erred in treating them as material things beyond the senses. Modern interpreters err from the outset by changing their meanings to reduce them to physical experience. The sound method is to establish meanings from language and usage, identify their referents through relevant verses, and only then compare them with science. Physical science has no authority to prove, disprove, or interpret what lies beyond matter, just as grammar cannot decide an astronomical proposition.

Returning to (2:24-25), Al-Mizan says that the universal call to worship now divides people into those who answer it, the believers, and those who do not, the disbelievers. The hypocrites are apparently omitted because outwardly they stand with the first group while inwardly they belong to the second; this perhaps explains why the earlier designation of the pious becomes ‘those who believe.’ Al-waqūd means fuel, and human beings are themselves the fuel of Hell, burning in a fire kindled and fuelled by their own selves and rising over their hearts. The stones are the idols worshipped by the disbelievers.

The parallel promise of Paradise indicates that people receive there what they prepared here: when given fruit, they recognize it as what they had been given before. The commentary cites the Prophet’s saying, ‘As you live so you will die, and as you die so you will be raised,’ to establish this correspondence. The people of Paradise differ from those of the Fire in that their Lord continually gives them increasing reward beyond what they wish. Their pure mates are free, in body and conduct, from every trait that could cause aversion or unpleasantness.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains that the gnat is among the smallest animals visible to the naked eye. These verses parallel ch. 13, verses 19-21: those who know that revelation is truth are contrasted with the blind, and the people of understanding fulfill God’s covenant and join what He has commanded to be joined. Believers recognize the parable as truth from their Lord, whereas unbelievers object to its meaning. The transgressors whom God causes to err have first chosen transgression: their consequent blindness and straying differ from the initial straying they freely chose. They break God’s covenant after confirming it, sever what He has ordered joined, spread mischief in the land, and thereby become losers.

Guidance and misguidance encompass every felicity and infelicity God gives His righteous and wicked servants. He grants the righteous a happy life, strengthens them by the spirit of faith, brings them from darkness into light, gives them a light by which to walk among people, takes them under His protection, removes fear and grief from them, answers their calls and remembers them when they remember Him, and sends angels with news of everlasting peace. The wicked undergo the opposite condition: they are led from light into darkness; their hearts, hearing, and sight are obstructed; they are made unable to see; satans become their associates, turn them from the path while they suppose themselves guided, and make their deeds appear good. God also leads them on gradually without their awareness, grants them respite while His plan remains firm, and leaves them wandering blindly in rebellion.

The commentary holds that human beings have, in this world, both a visible life and a concealed life behind it. That hidden life is good or evil according to faith and deeds, and after death, when the veil of secrecy is removed, each person will see his true form. It further appears from the Qur’anic verses that there was a spiritual life before this worldly life and that another life follows it. Thus this worldly life is the second of three lives: the third is determined by the second, and the second is governed by the first. Al-Mizan rejects the claim that the relevant verses merely present imaginary scenes as facts, or that the verses on the hereafter are allegories and metaphors; their meaning is too explicit for such explanations.

The same good and evil deeds performed in this life will be returned to a person on the Day of Requital as his own reward or punishment. The statement in 50:22, “Certainly you were heedless of it, but now We have removed from you your veil, so your sight today is sharp,” shows that the reality seen at resurrection was already present in worldly life, though hidden by a veil. Otherwise, it would not make sense to say that the person had been heedless of it or that it had been concealed from his sight. These verses are not figurative language.

The commentary distinguishes, for purposes of explanation, between recompense and the embodiment of deeds. Recompense means that paradise, hell, reward, and punishment correspond to the good and evil done in this life. Embodiment means that those deeds themselves become, or are inseparably accompanied by, their pleasant or painful requital; what is now hidden will be seen clearly at the reckoning. In reality these are not two separate facts, but the distinction brings the matter closer to the mind, just as the Qur’an uses similitudes to make people understand.

Al-Mizan relates al-fāsiqīn to al–Fisq, meaning transgression or sinfulness, a usage it says the Qur’an first employed in its prevalent sense. The word derives from fasqati ʿt-tamrah, when a date breaks out of its outer rind. This suits those who break God’s covenant, since something must first be whole in order to be broken; likewise, the transgressors are called losers because one must possess something before losing it. Qur’anic descriptions of the righteous and wicked are not decorative epithets. Each designation marks a particular stage in the human spiritual journey, with its own characteristics, effects, and consequences, just as each physical age has qualities not found before or after it.

Turning to compulsion and delegation, Al-Mizan argues first from God’s absolute ownership. Everything in heaven and earth belongs to Him, unlike a human being’s limited and socially restricted ownership of an animal or property. No creature independently owns or controls harm, profit, life, death, or resurrection. God controls every affair, may dispose of His property as He pleases, and cannot be questioned about His acts; creatures can use what is placed in their hands only by His permission and remain accountable for how they use it. God’s ownership, power, and sustaining authority are therefore real, unconditional, and unrestricted.

Yet God legislates for human beings through commands and prohibitions that seek their good in this life and the next and the perfection of society. As with human legislation, what is good and beneficial is allowed and enjoined, while what is evil and socially harmful is forbidden; obedience merits praise and reward, and violation blame and punishment. Laws arise from wisdom and benefit, recompense must correspond in quality and quantity to the act, and command, prohibition, reward, and punishment properly concern one who is free to choose. A person who, through his own prior conduct, places himself in a situation where he must violate a law may nevertheless be punished; his later helplessness does not excuse the transgression.

God therefore does not compel anyone to obey or disobey. If obedience and sin were compelled, paradise for the obedient and hell for the disobedient would be unjust: reward would be without principle, punishment would be oppression, and one person would be favored over another without cause. The compelled person would also possess a valid argument against God, contrary to the purpose that people should perish or live only by clear proof after the coming of messengers.

The commentary accordingly draws several conclusions. Divine law is not founded on compulsion: people may obey or disobey by their own choice and are fully recompensed for the good and evil they freely do. Expressions attributed to God such as causing to err, deceiving, scheming, leaving someone wandering in rebellion, or allowing Satan to overpower and accompany him cannot mean that God initially makes a person heedless, forgetful, or astray. Rather, when someone freely chooses error and sin, God leaves him in that chosen straying and increases it as a punishment for that choice. Divine decree does not cover human acts insofar as they are attributed to their doers: the acts are done by those doers, although they are not created by them. Finally, divine law is not based on delegation of power either. A master who had delegated all power to a servant could not issue authoritative commands, and such delegation would deny God’s comprehensive ownership of His possessions.

The same good and evil deeds performed in this life will be returned to a person on the Day of Requital as his own reward or punishment. The statement in 50:22, “Certainly you were heedless of it, but now We have removed from you your veil, so your sight today is sharp,” shows that the reality seen at resurrection was already present in worldly life, though hidden by a veil. Otherwise, it would not make sense to say that the person had been heedless of it or that it had been concealed from his sight. These verses are not figurative language.

The commentary distinguishes, for purposes of explanation, between recompense and the embodiment of deeds. Recompense means that paradise, hell, reward, and punishment correspond to the good and evil done in this life. Embodiment means that those deeds themselves become, or are inseparably accompanied by, their pleasant or painful requital; what is now hidden will be seen clearly at the reckoning. In reality these are not two separate facts, but the distinction brings the matter closer to the mind, just as the Qur’an uses similitudes to make people understand.

Al-Mizan relates al-fāsiqīn to al–Fisq, meaning transgression or sinfulness, a usage it says the Qur’an first employed in its prevalent sense. The word derives from fasqati ʿt-tamrah, when a date breaks out of its outer rind. This suits those who break God’s covenant, since something must first be whole in order to be broken; likewise, the transgressors are called losers because one must possess something before losing it. Qur’anic descriptions of the righteous and wicked are not decorative epithets. Each designation marks a particular stage in the human spiritual journey, with its own characteristics, effects, and consequences, just as each physical age has qualities not found before or after it.

Turning to compulsion and delegation, Al-Mizan argues first from God’s absolute ownership. Everything in heaven and earth belongs to Him, unlike a human being’s limited and socially restricted ownership of an animal or property. No creature independently owns or controls harm, profit, life, death, or resurrection. God controls every affair, may dispose of His property as He pleases, and cannot be questioned about His acts; creatures can use what is placed in their hands only by His permission and remain accountable for how they use it. God’s ownership, power, and sustaining authority are therefore real, unconditional, and unrestricted.

Yet God legislates for human beings through commands and prohibitions that seek their good in this life and the next and the perfection of society. As with human legislation, what is good and beneficial is allowed and enjoined, while what is evil and socially harmful is forbidden; obedience merits praise and reward, and violation blame and punishment. Laws arise from wisdom and benefit, recompense must correspond in quality and quantity to the act, and command, prohibition, reward, and punishment properly concern one who is free to choose. A person who, through his own prior conduct, places himself in a situation where he must violate a law may nevertheless be punished; his later helplessness does not excuse the transgression.

God therefore does not compel anyone to obey or disobey. If obedience and sin were compelled, paradise for the obedient and hell for the disobedient would be unjust: reward would be without principle, punishment would be oppression, and one person would be favored over another without cause. The compelled person would also possess a valid argument against God, contrary to the purpose that people should perish or live only by clear proof after the coming of messengers.

The commentary accordingly draws several conclusions. Divine law is not founded on compulsion: people may obey or disobey by their own choice and are fully recompensed for the good and evil they freely do. Expressions attributed to God such as causing to err, deceiving, scheming, leaving someone wandering in rebellion, or allowing Satan to overpower and accompany him cannot mean that God initially makes a person heedless, forgetful, or astray. Rather, when someone freely chooses error and sin, God leaves him in that chosen straying and increases it as a punishment for that choice. Divine decree does not cover human acts insofar as they are attributed to their doers: the acts are done by those doers, although they are not created by them. Finally, divine law is not based on delegation of power either. A master who had delegated all power to a servant could not issue authoritative commands, and such delegation would deny God’s comprehensive ownership of His possessions.
verses.28: Al-Mizan asks how people can deny Allah when He gave them life from death, will cause their death, revive them, and bring them back to Him.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains that the discourse returns to the chapter’s opening theme after first classifying mankind and then addressing all people together. The twelve verses beginning here portray the reality of man, his capacity for perfection and the breadth of his inner being, the successive stages of death and life, and his final return to God. They also enumerate God’s creative and legislative bounties: He created the earth for man, made the heaven subservient to him, appointed him His deputy on earth, commanded the angels to prostrate before him, placed the first man in the Garden, opened repentance to him, and honoured him by guiding him to worship. Thus the question, “How do you deny God,” underscores divine grace and bounty.

Al-Mizan considers (2:28) somewhat, though not exactly, similar to verse (40:11), and treats the latter as proof of al-barzakh, the intervening life between this world and the next. The first giving of death is the death that removes man from this world. Since a second giving of death presupposes a preceding life, there must be life in the intervening period before the Day of Resurrection. It calls this argument sound and says that some traditions also advance it.

It records an objection that both verses have the same meaning: the first death in (2:28) is the lifeless state before worldly life; this is followed by worldly life, death, and finally resurrection. On that reading, verse (40:11) likewise leaves no life between worldly death and Resurrection. Al-Mizan rejects the comparison. Verse (2:28) speaks of one “death,” one “causing to die,” and two givings of life, whereas (40:11) speaks of two givings of death and two givings of life. Causing someone to die requires a preceding life, while “death” may mean mere absence of life, even where no prior life existed.

Accordingly, verse (40:11) refers to death after worldly life, life in the intervening period, death after that period, and then life on the Day of Resurrection. Verse (2:28) begins with the lifeless state before this world, then worldly life, death, and the life of the intervening period. The use of thumma (then) indicates a delay before the return to God; after that intervening life, another death occurs before man is returned to his Lord.

The commentary takes these stages as showing the reality of man: he is continually changing and advancing, stage by stage, on a path of perfection. He is part of the earth, created from it and gradually developed into “another creation.” This creation proceeds along its path until the angel of death completely removes the man from the body and he returns to God. This is the course appointed for him.

Al-Mizan further says that the divine decree makes every part of the universe related to every other through continual mutual influence. Man both affects and is affected by what is in the earth and heavens. Yet his scope exceeds that of other creatures because he has been given thought and reason. By them he manages, rearranges, destroys, amends, perfects, and otherwise uses the creatures of nature; every creature falls under his domain. He obtains what he seeks by using natural forces and by producing artificial things, and the passage of time has increased his insight into nature and his ability to manipulate it. This increasingly manifests God’s declaration that what is in the heavens and earth has been made subservient to man. In this context, (2:29) means that God’s creation of all that is in the earth and His completion of the seven heavens were for man’s benefit; the verse also affirms that He knows all things.

Although man’s worldly life originates from nature and he is connected with lifeless matter at that level, the Qur’an also declares that his life emanates from God. At the level of origination, man is related to God’s command and authority, by which a thing comes to be when God says to it, “Be.” Thus man’s journey shows both his point of origin and his final destination.

As for the return, Al-Mizan distinguishes two paths. The path of happiness is the shortest way and continually raises man’s rank until he reaches divine nearness. The path of unhappiness is long and continually degrades him to the lowest of the low until he reaches the divine presence; Allah encompasses them on every side. The passage offers this only as a brief account bearing on guidance and misguidance, happiness and unhappiness, and defers discussion of the heavens to Chapter 32 (al-Sajdah), God willing.
verses.30: Al-Mizan recounts that God announced to the angels His purpose to appoint an earthly vicegerent. They asked whether He would place there one who would cause mischief and shed blood while they praised and sanctified Him; He replied that He knows what they do not.
verses.31: Al-Mizan says that God taught Adam all the names, presented them to the angels, and told them: Name these, if you are right.
verses.32: Al-Mizan reports that the angels glorified God, admitted knowing only what He taught them, and called Him the Knowing, the Wise.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan explains that the angels inferred from God’s intention to appoint a vicegerent “in the earth” that the creature would be material, endowed with desire and anger, and placed in a realm of struggle, limited resources, deterioration, and conflict. They therefore understood that God intended not merely an individual but a species whose members would need social life and cooperation, and which would consequently make mischief and shed blood. Yet vicegerency means putting one thing in another’s place, and thus requires the vicegerent to reflect its predecessor’s characteristics and capacities. How, they asked, could an earthly being marked by defects and disorder represent God, whose names and attributes are most excellent and whose essence and acts are free from defect and evil?

Their words were an inquiry, not a protest. They acknowledged God as Knowing and Wise and sought the wisdom of His decision. In effect, they said that the purpose of vicegerency was to represent God through worthy praise and sanctification; since their own nature already enabled them to do this, they were in practice fulfilling that role, whereas the earthly creature would be drawn toward wickedness. God answered both by saying, “Surely I know what you do not know,” and by teaching Adam all the names.

The commentary first concludes that Adam was appointed God’s vicegerent, not the successor of an earlier earthly creature: otherwise, teaching him the names would be irrelevant to the reply. This vicegerency extends to Adam’s descendants and hence to mankind. The knowledge taught to Adam was ingrained in human nature, continually yielding new discoveries, fresh insights, and capacities that may become actual achievements; other Qur’anic uses of the same term for human successors confirm that mankind is God’s vicegerent on earth.

God did not deny that the vicegerent would cause mischief and bloodshed, nor did He reject the angels’ praise and sanctification; His silence confirms both. Rather, He disclosed a matter that angels could not bear: a divine secret entrusted to man, whose gift outweighed the resulting mischief and bloodshed. The “unseen” which God knows is the names themselves, not simply Adam’s possession of knowledge about them. The angels were unaware even of those names’ existence. Had the issue only been whether Adam knew them, his informing the angels would have sufficed; instead, God first required the angels to name them “if you are right,” because they had implicitly claimed vicegerency, for which this knowledge was the essential qualification. Adam possessed it and they did not.

The pronoun “them” in the presentation to the angels is used for rational beings, indicating that the names, or named ones, were living, knowing beings concealed in the unseen. Adam’s knowledge was therefore not mere vocabulary. If it had been ordinary knowledge of words, the angels would have equalled Adam once they heard the names from him and could rightly have objected that they had merely been denied instruction. Nor would teaching Adam a dictionary establish his superiority over angels, who receive and communicate meanings directly without language. What the angels grasped after Adam informed them was an inferior knowledge, unlike the superior knowledge God had taught Adam. Adam merited vicegerency through that divinely given knowledge itself, not through the subsequent act of informing the angels.

Adam thus knew the realities and substantial existence of the named ones, not merely the meanings of nouns. This knowledge, intrinsically connected to vicegerency, could be learned by an earthly human being but was incomprehensible to a heavenly angel. The definite plural al-Asmāʾ, reinforced by “all of them,” denotes all names without restriction; and the rational pronoun indicates that each named reality was living, intelligent, and hidden in the unseen of the heavens and the earth.

In this setting, “the unseen of the heavens and the earth” does not mean merely their hidden regions. It means a secret hidden from all the heavens and the earth, beyond the sphere of the universe. This accords with verse 15:21: “And there is not a thing but with Us are the treasures of it and We do not send it down but in a known measure.” Every named thing has with God treasures that are everlasting, unmeasured, and unlimited; measure and limitation arise only when it is created and sent down. Their vastness is not numerical, since number itself is limited, but consists in ranks and grades. The beings presented to the angels were sublime and divinely protected realities veiled in the unseen. God sent them down with their blessings and benefactions, and created what is in the heavens and earth from their light and splendour. Though they have numerous identities, their difference is one of rank and grade, not number or person.

The commentary holds that “what you manifest and what you were hiding” probably concerns matters within the heavens and earth; together with the secrets beyond them, it encompasses all unseen things. The wording “what you were hiding,” rather than “what you hide,” shows that something had been concealed especially in relation to Adam’s vicegerency. It probably refers to Iblīs’s disbelief, hidden before his later refusal to prostrate and expressed in that refusal. On this reading, the angels’ prostration and Iblīs’s refusal occurred after God’s first statement, “Surely I know what you do not know,” but before His declaration that He knew what they manifested and had been hiding; this also explains the altered reference to the unseen of the heavens and the earth.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan holds that the wording, “he was one of the unbelievers,” shows that Iblīs did not become an unbeliever when he refused to prostrate; rather, he had long concealed his unbelief, which this event exposed. The angels’ prostration must have occurred between the declarations, “Surely I know what you do not know,” and “… I know what you manifest and what you were hiding.” Its present placement probably serves chiefly to link Adam’s creation with his placement in Paradise, since verses 28–39 concern man’s vicegerency, descent to earth, and the course determining his enduring happiness or unhappiness. This may also explain the shift from “your Lord said” to “And when We said.”

The phrase “what you were hiding” may be attributed to the whole group although Iblīs alone concealed the matter, as speech may ascribe an unidentified or anonymous individual’s act to his group. Alternatively, it may address the angels themselves: God’s announcement that He would make an earthly vicegerent apparently implied Adam’s authority even over them, as the command to prostrate confirms. They may therefore have harbored a troubling thought at the prospect that an earthly creature would be given such authority; traditions point in this direction.

The commentary says that prostration before one other than God may, in itself, be performed by God’s command as an honor to that person, as in Joseph’s story (12:100). Worship means placing oneself in the station of servitude and performing acts that manifest the master’s lordship and the servant’s lowliness. Prostration has the strongest connection with worship because one places one’s forehead on the ground.

Yet prostration and worship have distinct meanings. Worship is not a quidditative characteristic of prostration, since prostration can occur without reverence or worship, even in mockery. Thus prostration is not intrinsically reserved to God; any prohibition must come from the shariah or reason. What they forbid is assigning the prerogatives of lordship to someone besides God, not honoring a person without raising him to godhead.

Nevertheless, religious good taste, shaped by the rites of worship, strictly reserves prostration for divine worship. Islam therefore forbids prostrating before anyone other than God, even as a sign of respect. Apart from prostration, the commentary finds no proof in the Qur’an, tradition, reason, or logic against revering others than God, particularly where this forms part of love for God—for example, loving His righteous servants or honoring the graves of His friends and things connected with them.
verses.35: Al-Mizan says God let Adam and his wife dwell in the Garden and eat abundant food freely wherever they wished, but warned them not to approach a tree lest they be unjust.
verses.36: Al-Mizan says Satan caused Adam and his wife to slip and lose their state. God sent them down into mutual enmity, with an earthly abode and provision for a time.
verses.37: Al-Mizan says Adam received words from his Lord, who mercifully returned to him, being ever-returning in mercy.
verses.38: Al-Mizan states that all were sent down, but whoever follows guidance from God will know neither fear nor grief.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan treats the Qur’anic accounts of Adam in Chapters 2, 7, and 20 as one continuous narrative. Adam was created for the earth, where he was meant to live and die; the Garden was a temporary placement and test through which he and his wife were prepared for earthly life. Adam’s superiority to the angels established his fitness for vicegerency, their prostration acknowledged it, and the prohibition of the tree led, upon their eating, to their awareness of nakedness and their descent. Nakedness here means the private parts, as their covering themselves with leaves shows. Its disclosure revealed that, alongside their spiritual qualities, they possessed animal instincts and desires, and thus dependence on nourishment and growth. Their initial attachment to the spiritual world remained strong, but nakedness was only temporarily hidden and could not remain concealed in this life. Its disclosure, dependent on eating from the tree, was the last link showing their fitness for earthly existence. Iblīs sought that result.

Their not being restored to the Garden after God accepted their repentance confirms that earthly life, the eating of the tree, and the disclosure of nakedness belonged to an irrevocable divine plan. Their removal was causally connected with eating and listening to Satan, but was not undone by forgiveness because their Garden sojourn had prepared them for the world.

On the covenant which Adam forgot, the commentary rejects identifying it with the prohibition of the tree: Adam and his wife knew that prohibition when they ate, and Satan’s temptation itself referred to it. It also finds the warning about Satan less likely, because that warning addressed both Adam and his wife, whereas the covenant is presented as especially Adam’s. The covenant is therefore the general covenant made with human souls, especially the prophets, concerning God’s mastership and human servitude. Forgetting it means forgetting that God alone is Lord and Master, while man owns neither his person, qualities, acts, benefit, harm, life, death, nor resurrection. An editor notes that an earlier volume identified the prohibition of the tree as the covenant, but explains that the two statements consider it from different perspectives.

This forgetfulness absorbs a person in self and worldly attractions. The believer knows that all things and affairs belong to and proceed from God, and that what comes from Him is good and beautiful. He therefore subjects his preferences to those of his Master, does not presume to manage God’s property, and attains tranquility and a happy life free of fear and grief except toward what God disapproves. The unbeliever, cut off from the one Master, treats created things as independent powers of benefit and harm; he consequently lives in fear, grief for losses, attachment to worldly attractions, and recurring despair. Thus a straitened and unhappy worldly life springs from forgetting the covenant, while following divine guidance—expressed as neither going astray nor being unhappy, and here as having neither fear nor grief—is its opposite. It may be inferred that the tree was such that eating from it entangled one in worldly troubles and heedlessness of God. Probably Adam tried to combine its fruit with fidelity to his covenant, failed, and was then saved by repentance and divine mercy.

Al-Raghad denotes happiness, well-being, good life, and abundance. Although Adam and his wife were told not even to approach the tree for emphasis, what was actually prohibited was eating from it. Al-Ḍālimīn derives from al-Ḍulm, injustice or wrong-doing, not from al-Ḍulmah, darkness. Their wrong was against themselves: it brought the toil of earthly hunger, thirst, nakedness, and other discomforts. The prohibition was therefore advisory, directing them to what preserved their comfort, rather than an authoritative law of the shariah; their disregard was neither a sin in that legal sense nor an injustice against God. If it had been a legal offence, accepted repentance would have erased its punishment and returned them to their former position. Instead, their departure from the Garden remained the natural consequence of disregarding the advice.

An editorial note transmits in al-Tawḥīd a report from Imām Riḍā distinguishing an irrevocable will (irādah ḥatm) from a divine intent (irādah ʿazm). According to that report, God may forbid what He intends to occur and command what He intends not to occur: Adam’s eating was intended by God, just as Abraham’s sacrifice of Ishmael was not intended to occur, and no creature’s desire can overcome God’s will.

The commentary argues that Satan appeared to Adam and his wife and spoke with them face to face, rather than merely planting thoughts in their hearts. God identified him to Adam as an enemy; Satan directly offered Adam the tree of immortality and swore that he was their sincere adviser; and their Lord’s subsequent reproach presupposes that they recognized Satan. It adds that traditions describe other divinely protected prophets likewise seeing and recognizing him when he came to them. Satan visited them near the tree and entered this Garden because it was not the Garden of eternal abode. The previous command for him to get down may refer to being removed from the company of the angels or from the honor of heaven.

The plural command to get down addresses Adam, his wife, and Satan. It joins Satan’s earlier removal with a firm decree of enmity between Iblīs and Adam, his wife, and their descendants, and decrees that they will live, die, and be raised from the earth. The plural wording also extends this decree to humanity as a whole. Adam’s story may thus represent mankind’s rise, fall, and return: Adam was the representative of human vicegerency when the angels prostrated, and every person may see in his descent the soul’s movement from a lofty, spiritually near existence toward the transient world and its toil. As Adam returned by repentance, a human being may return to God and the everlasting abode of honor; one who instead follows base desire turns divine bounty into disbelief and proceeds toward the Fire.

Al-talaqqī means learning: Adam’s learning of the words from his Lord opened the way to repentance. Al-tawbah literally means return. When attributed to the servant, it is his return to God from sin; when attributed to God, it is His restoring the servant to grace, accepting the plea, and forgiving. Human repentance is enclosed by two divine acts of mercy: God first grants the help by which a servant can turn away from sin, and then accepts that return.

The commentary rejects the view that Adam’s received words were simply the plea in which Adam and his wife confessed wronging themselves, because that plea preceded the command to get down in the account of Chapter 7, whereas the received words follow the descent command in this account. There may, however, be a connection with the names God taught Adam. Since the teaching of those names was the answer to the angels’ concern that the earthly vicegerent would cause mischief and shed blood, those names must contain what rescues humanity from error and disgrace; the words of repentance were probably related to them.

Adam’s descent and accepted repentance made him know his own humility, dependence, deficiency, and servitude. Though he wronged himself by entering the world’s crossroads of happiness and misery, he attained heights of eternal bliss and spiritual perfection that would not have been possible without descending to earth through this mistake. He learned that worldly hardship, unpleasantness, and the toil of obedience bring multiplied ease, pleasure, divine satisfaction, and unlimited reward in the next life, until the servant reaches the sublime presence of his Lord. He also came to know divine attributes especially reserved for sinners: forgiveness, merciful turning, covering mistakes, compassion, and grace. This repentance made religion and the ordination of a shariah necessary, so that Adam and his descendants could know the path to the abode of bliss; the commentary accordingly notes that the Qur’an often mentions repentance before belief and righteous action.

The commands concerning descent and guidance contain the entire essence of religion first ordained for Adam and his descendants; nothing can be added to it until the Day of Resurrection. One decree, following the eating of the tree, began earthly life with its trouble and toil. The second, following repentance, dignified that life by granting divine guidance. Human life thereafter has both an earthly, material dimension and a heavenly, spiritual one. The repetition of the command to get down indicates that Adam repented between the two commands and, though he had fallen from his earlier rank, had not yet departed the Garden. The shift from speaking of this tree to that tree, and from saying to calling out, likewise indicates increased distance from his former honored place. Earthly life is tied to the earth: man is created from it, returns to it at death, and is raised from it. The commentary therefore concludes with certainty that Adam’s Garden was in heaven, although it was not the eternal Garden from which none is expelled.

Although the verses call Adam’s act injustice, disobedience, going astray, and a mistake, Al-Mizan systematically maintains that the prohibition was advisory rather than legislative. First, the stated result of eating is injustice, explained elsewhere as worldly toil—hunger, thirst, nakedness, and exposure to heat—showing that the warning protected Adam and his wife from earthly hardship, not that it imposed a legal command. Second, accepted repentance erases the effects of a legal sin, whereas it does not reverse a natural consequence: just as apologizing after disregarding advice not to put one’s hand into fire does not remove its burning, Adam’s repentance could not reverse the natural consequence of eating and descending. Third, the comprehensive shariah for Adam and his descendants was ordained only after the second command to get down, which was a creative command resulting from eating the tree, not a legislative one. No shariah had yet been promulgated for them when Adam ate. The earlier authoritative command to the angels and Iblīs to prostrate is irrelevant, because the discussion concerns Adam and his descendants.

Al-ʿIṣyān literally denotes resistance or yielding with difficulty, and can describe failure to heed advice as well as defiance of a compulsory order; its later use as a legal term for sin cannot alter its Qur’anic sense. Al-Ghawāyah means failing to look after one’s interests or manage one’s affairs properly, and does not by itself establish a sin; its force depends on whether the neglected direction was advice or an authoritative command. Similarly, repentance, forgiveness, mercy, and loss take their meaning from context. The commentary compares Adam’s case to a patient who disregards a doctor’s advice, then turns back in embarrassment and asks for treatment: the patient may need a long and difficult regimen, yet, if he perseveres, may become healthier than before. Thus Adam’s return need not imply rebellion against a legal command, while those who disbelieve in and belie God’s signs are the abiding inmates of the Fire.
verses.40: Al-Mizan commands the children of Israel to remember God’s favors, honor their covenant with Him so that He fulfills His covenant, and fear Him alone. It explains that al-ʿAhd literally denotes guarding and maintenance and, by association, may mean a covenant, oath, testament, will, encounter, or house. al-Rahbah, in fa-rhabūn, means fear and is the opposite of al-Raghbah, desire.
verses.41: Al-Mizan commands belief in the revelation sent down, which verifies what is already with them; forbids being the first to reject it or exchanging God’s signs for a mean price; and commands fear of God alone. It explains “be not the first to deny it” as being first among the People of the Book or among one’s own people, not first in an unrestricted sense, since the disbelievers of Mecca had already rejected the Message. A note states that the author does not discuss (2:42-44).

verses.44: Al-Mizan commands belief in the revelation sent down, which verifies what is already with them; forbids being the first to reject it or exchanging God’s signs for a mean price; and commands fear of God alone. It explains “be not the first to deny it” as being first among the People of the Book or among one’s own people, not first in an unrestricted sense, since the disbelievers of Mecca had already rejected the Message. A note states that the author does not discuss (2:42-44).
verses.45:
Al-Mizan explains that people seek help in matters they cannot manage and hardships they cannot overcome alone, yet God alone is the true helper. They can therefore confront all affairs through patience—courage and steadfastness—and prayer—turning toward God. Patience makes even great misfortunes seem slight, while confidence in God awakens faith and makes one realize that the cause on which one relies cannot fail to produce the desired effect.

It takes “it” in “it is a hard thing” to refer to prayer, not to seeking assistance generally: otherwise it would include patience, to which “the humble ones” is less fitting. khushūʿ is inward humility, unlike khuḍūʿ, which is displayed in the bodily limbs.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan notes that yaḍunnūn, rendered “know,” literally means “they think.” Because the context concerns belief in the hereafter, it may signify firm conviction that leaves no room for doubt, as in: and they are sure of the hereafter (2:4). Alternatively, perhaps its use shows that even an elementary idea of the hereafter can produce humility before one’s Lord.

Knowledge progresses from awareness, through doubt and an inclination to accept, to conviction when acceptance of the opposite becomes impossible. If the matter is frightening, anxiety begins at the third stage, when a person merely thinks it likely to be true. Thus, a strong supposition that one may return after death to a Lord is enough to humble a person and turn him from disobedience; firm knowledge is unnecessary for this purpose. The verse therefore resembles the command that one who hopes to meet his Lord should do good and not join anyone in His worship (18:110).

This explanation assumes that meeting the Lord means the Day of Resurrection. Al-Mizan says that if the words are interpreted otherwise, as it will describe in Chapter 7, there is no difficulty in explaining them.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan reads (2:47-48) as recalling the Children of Israel to God’s favor and distinction, while warning them of a Day on which no soul can avail another, no compensation or help can be procured, and no intercession is accepted in the sense rejected by the verse. In worldly government and judgment, punishment is sometimes set aside for extraneous reasons: pity aroused by an appeal, bribery, the influence of an intercessor, usefulness as a state witness, or support from one’s tribe or associates. Such departures arise from the changing necessities and conditions of human society.

The commentary says that ancient peoples and idolaters imagined the Hereafter as a continuation of this worldly order. They offered sacrifices and other offerings to obtain forgiveness or help, sometimes even offering human beings; they also buried possessions, arms, and sometimes companions with the dead so that these might serve them on their onward journey. Modified forms of these ideas have persisted among Muslims. The Qur’an rejects this projection of worldly material and social ties into the Hereafter: on that Day command belongs wholly to Allah, asserted ties are cut, fabricated intercessors disappear, and each soul encounters what it sent ahead. Thus, the Hereafter is severed from the natural and material connections on which such myths rely. The warning in the verse, together with verses denying bargaining, friendship, ransom, mutual aid, saviors, and the alleged intercession of idols, rejects each supposed means by which a sinner might escape judgment.

Yet Al-Mizan maintains that the Qur’an does not deny intercession absolutely. Even matters firmly decreed by God remain subject to His will and never leave His possession or control. The intercession under discussion concerns reward and punishment arising from the relationship between ruler and ruled, master and servant, not the ordinary natural means by which hunger, illness, heat, and similar conditions are addressed. A person seeks intercession when he lacks the qualification for a desired benefit or faces a punishment for disobedience without a means of protection. But it can work only for one who is otherwise fit for the benefit and has an established relation to the authority. It cannot secure an academic position for an ignorant person, nor avail a rebellious traitor who neither regrets his conduct nor submits to lawful authority. Intercession is thus a supplementary cause, not an independent cause.

An intercessor neither abolishes the master’s authority, releases the servant from servitude, abrogates the rules, nor nullifies the principle of recompense. Rather, while accepting these foundations, he appeals to grounds for pardon: the master’s nobility, generosity, and magnanimity; the servant’s misery, lowliness, and need; or the intercessor’s own honor with the master. He gives precedence to mercy and forgiveness over the particular operation of recompense, transferring the case from the jurisdiction of reward and punishment to that of pardon. God knows that a person will undergo changing conditions and wills concerning each condition accordingly.
