verses.61:
Al-Mizan recounts that the people, unable to bear one food, asked Moses to pray to his Lord for the earth’s herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions. Moses asked whether they would exchange the better for the worse and told them to enter a city, where they would have what they requested. Abasement and humiliation were brought down on them, and they returned with Allah’s wrath because they disbelieved in Allah’s signs and killed the prophets unjustly; this resulted from disobedience and exceeding the limits.

Concerning Pharaoh’s oppression, it says God delivered them from Pharaoh’s people, who imposed severe torment, killed their sons, and spared their women; this was a great trial from their Lord. The women were spared to serve their oppressors. al-Istiḥyāʾ means wishing someone to stay alive, though it may also mean treating women indecently until they lose modesty; yasūmūnakum literally means imposing upon them. The sea was parted for them, saving them and drowning Pharaoh’s followers as they watched. al-Farq contrasts with al-jamʿ, just as al-faṣl contrasts with al-waṣl; parting the sea means dividing its water. Bikum, translated as “for you,” may instead mean that it occurred soon upon their entering the sea.

God appointed Moses forty nights, after which they unjustly took the calf as a god, and gave Moses the book and the distinction so that they might walk aright. Al-Mizan compares this appointment with (7:142), which gives thirty nights completed by ten, and says the present verse states the total of the two promises, as a tradition says.

After their calf-worship, Moses tells them that they have wronged themselves, commands them to repent to their Creator and kill their people, and calls this best for them with their Creator. God turned to them mercifully, for He is the Oft-returning with mercy, the Merciful; this shows that their repentance was accepted. Al-Mizan identifies al-Bāriʾ as one of God’s beautiful names, occurring twice here and once in (59:24), and suggests that it was perhaps especially fitting here. Though close to al-Khāliq and al-Mūjid, it derives from baraʿa, yabraʿu, barʾan, to separate: God separates creation from nonexistence or man from earth. The name shows that the Creator who made them when creation was good can command a hard repentance—killing their own people—that is also good. “Your Creator” marks their special relation to Him and shows that the command is purification grounded in divine love, not revenge.

The address is to the whole Jewish nation although only some groups committed these sins, because their strong national unity meant that a group’s deed was attributed to all when the others were pleased with it; not all the Israelites worshipped the calf or killed prophets. The commentary therefore holds that “kill your people” meant killing some of them, the calf-worshippers. It adds that this may also be inferred from the reference to their calf-worship and to what was best with their Creator, apparently the final part of Moses’s speech. A tradition says their repentance was accepted and their sin forgiven after only a few had been killed. Since this acceptance came before the command’s apparent full compliance, it shows the command was a trial. The commentary compares this with Abraham’s dream and command to sacrifice Ishmael, which ended before its final stage when he was told, “O Abraham! You have indeed made the vision come true (37:104-105).” God similarly confirmed Moses’s command, treated the killing of some as its execution in full, and announced acceptance of their repentance.

The unjust changed the saying they had been given, and God sent a pestilence from heaven because they transgressed; rijz means punishment. When Moses prayed for drink, God told him to strike the rock with his staff; twelve springs gushed forth, each tribe knew its drinking place, and they were commanded to eat and drink Allah’s provisions without corrupting the land. Lā taʿthaw derives from al-ʿayth and al-ʿathy and means the greatest chaos and mischief.

For the requested foods, al-Khiyār means cucumber and al-fūm may mean garlic or wheat; Bāʾū means “they returned.” The first causal clause—that they disbelieved in the signs and killed the prophets unjustly—explains the preceding abasement, humiliation, and wrath, while the next clause, their disobedience and continual excess, explains that disbelief and killing. Thus persistent disobedience led them to reject God’s signs and kill prophets. The commentary cites (30:10), where evil-doers end by rejecting and mocking Allah’s signs, and says that one of the coming traditions explains how disobedience caused disbelief.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan explains (2:62) by distinguishing the opening phrase, “those who believe,” which refers to people who call themselves believers, from “whoever believes,” which denotes real, true imān. Allah gives no weight to such labels as believer, Jew, Christian, or Sabaean: neither reward nor deliverance from punishment follows from a good name alone, as in the claim that only Jews or Christians enter the Garden (2:111). Honor and happiness depend solely on true belief in Allah and the Last Day together with good deeds. Had the verse said, “whoever of them believes,” it would have granted these names some recognition and implied a benefit in bearing them.

The commentary holds that this Qur’anic rule is universal: true and sincere servitude, not an outward name or attribute, benefits a person, from prophets down to the lowest rank. Even prophets’ deeds would become ineffectual if they set up others with God (6:88). Likewise, the promise concerning the Prophet and his companions is restricted to “Allah has promised those among them who believe and do good, forgiveness and a great reward” (48:29); and a man given divine signs went astray when he clung to the earth and followed his low desire (7:176). Thus, standing before God rests on reality rather than appearance.

Among the narrations, Salmān al-Fārisi reports that he asked the Prophet about the people of the religion he had followed before Islam, after describing their prayers and worship, and that this verse was then revealed (al-Durr al-manthūr). Al-Mizan notes that other traditions, through different chains, likewise connect the revelation with Salmān’s people. In a report from Ibn Faḍḍāl, Imam al-Riḍā says that al-Naṣārā were named after al-Nāṣirah (Nazareth) in Syria, where Mary and Jesus settled after returning from Egypt (Maʿani al-akhbār); the commentary postpones discussion of this report until the account of Jesus in Chapter 3, God willing. The same tradition says that al-Yahūd are named for Yahūda, son of Yaʿqūb. Another report from the Imam describes the Sabaeans as neither Zoroastrians, Jews, Christians, nor Muslims, but worshippers of stars and planets (al-Tafsīr, al-Qummi). Al-Mizan characterizes this as a particular kind of idol-worship: they worshipped the idols of stars, whereas others worshipped whatever idols they chose.

For the historical question, Al-Mizan states that the extended description is taken from Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī’s al-Āthār al-bāqiyah. Al-Bīrūnī reports that the earliest known Sabaean claimant to prophethood was Yudhasaf, who appeared in India at the beginning of Tahmūrth’s reign, introduced the Persian script, and called people to the Sabaean religion. The Bishdadian kings and some Kayanis of Balkh revered the sun, moon, stars, planets, and other elements until Zoroaster appeared. Their remnants are said to have been in Ḥarrān and called Ḥarrāniyyah; alternatively, the name is linked to Hārān, son of Tārukh (Terah) and Abraham’s brother, who was allegedly one of their leaders and strongest adherents.

Al-Bīrūnī also recounts a Christian polemic by Ibn Sancala which attributes to the Sabaeans an account of Abraham: he was excluded because of a white spot on his foreskin, circumcised himself to remove it, was rebuked by an idol when he entered their temple, smashed the idols in anger, and later sought to sacrifice his son to Jupiter in repentance until a lamb was sent instead.

Al-Bīrūnī then quotes ʿAbdu al-Masīḥ b. Isḥāq al-Kindi, writing in reply to a book by ʿAbdullah b. Ismail al-Hāshimi. ʿAbdu al-Masīḥ says that people generally believe the Sabaeans practise human sacrifice, though they cannot do so openly, but that his own information portrays them as monotheists. They hold God to be free of every defect and evil, describe Him negatively rather than positively, and regard the beautiful divine names as merely allegorical because no attribute truly describes the divine reality. At the same time, they believe that the sky and heavenly bodies manage all affairs; they regard them as living beings possessing speech, hearing, and sight, and they revere light and the luminaries.

According to this report, the dome above the niche in the Umayyad mosque of Damascus had been a Sabaean prayer-house, shared at that time by Greeks and Romans in the same religion, then made into a synagogue by Jews, a church by Christians, and a mosque by Muslims. It describes their many temples and star-idols, including a sun-idol at Baʿlabak and a moon-related temple at Qirān. It also says that they claimed the Kaʿbah and its idols, and Meccan idol-worship, for their religion, identifying Lāt and ʿUzza with Saturn and Venus. Their hierarchy of prophets reportedly included Greek philosophers such as Hermes of Egypt, Agadhimun, Walles, Pythagoras, and Babaswar.

ʿAbdu al-Masīḥ further reports that some of them avoid fish as spume, poultry as always hot, garlic because it causes headache and burns blood and semen, and beans because they dull intelligence and were said first to have sprouted in a human skull. They have three obligatory prayers—eight rakʿat at sunrise, five at noon, and another at the third hour of the night—each with three prostrations, as well as optional prayers at the second and ninth hours of the day. They pray with ṭahārah and wuḍūʾ, bathe after janābah, and do not circumcise their children because they have received no command to do so. Most of their marital and penal laws resemble the shariah of Islam, while their rules concerning contact with the dead resemble those of the Torah. They sacrifice to stars, idols, and temples; priests and witch-doctors slaughter the offerings, divine the offerer’s future from them, and answer his questions. Hermes is sometimes called Idrīs, identified in the Torah with Akhnūkh, and some identify Yūdhasaf with Hermes.

Al-Bīrūnī records competing accounts of their identity. Some say the contemporary Ḥarrāniyyah are not the true Sabaeans but heathens and idolaters. On this account, the Sabaeans were Israelites who remained in Babylon when the majority returned to Jerusalem under Cyrus and Artaxerxes; favorably disposed both to Zoroastrianism and to Nebuchadnezzar’s religion, they produced a mixture of Judaism and Zoroastrianism like the Samaritans of Syria. They are said to be found in Wāsiṭ and rural Iraq, to trace their line to Enosh, son of Seth, to oppose the Ḥarrāniyyah, and to differ from them even in prayer direction, facing the North Pole while the Ḥarrāniyyah face the South Pole. Other People of the Book trace them to Sabi, another son of Methuselah. This account connects earlier eastern idol-worshippers, called Shamnān in Khurasān, with Samanian beliefs, relics in India, China, and eastern Khurasān, belief in the eternity of the universe and transmigration of souls, and the view that the sky falls through an endless vacuum and therefore moves in a circle. Some writers, however, report a group that rejects the universe’s eternity and holds that it originated one million years ago.

Al-Mizan concludes that the view attributed to some writers—that the Sabaean religion was a mixture of Judaism and Zoroastrianism with elements of Ḥarrāniyyah belief—seems more suited to this verse, since the verse plainly enumerates groups that followed divinely inspired religions.
verses.63: Al-Mizan says God took their covenant, raised the mountain over them, and commanded them to hold firmly to what He gave and remember it, so that they might guard against evil.
verses.64: Al-Mizan says that after they turned back, only Allah’s grace and mercy saved them from being losers.
verses.65: Al-Mizan says they knew those among them who exceeded the Sabbath’s limits, and Allah said to them, “Be apes, despised and hated.”
verses.66: Al-Mizan says it became an example to witnesses and later people, and an admonition to those who guard against evil.
verses.67: Al-Mizan recounts Moses’ command from Allah that his people sacrifice a cow; when they asked whether he ridiculed them, he sought Allah’s protection from being among the ignorant.
verses.68: Al-Mizan says they asked Moses to have his Lord identify the cow. He replied that it was neither old nor young but middle-aged, and told them to do what they were commanded.
verses.69: Al-Mizan says, asked to clarify the cow’s color, Moses replied that it was intensely yellow and delighted those who saw it.
verses.70: Al-Mizan says they asked Moses to have his Lord identify the cow, for all cows seemed alike to them; if Allah pleased, they would be guided.
verses.71: Al-Mizan says Moses described a sound, unblemished cow not used for ploughing or irrigation. They said he had now brought the truth and sacrificed it, though unwillingly.
verses.72: Al-Mizan says they killed a man and disputed the matter, while Allah was to bring out what they concealed.
verses.73: Al-Mizan says: “Strike the dead body with part of the sacrificed cow.” Thus Allah gives life to the dead and shows His signs so that they may understand.
verses.74:
The commentary reads the lifting of the mountain literally. It glosses al-Ṭūr as “mountain,” notes its substitution by al-jabal elsewhere, and gives al-Natq the sense of pulling out. Within the covenant account, the mountain was raised to frighten the Israelites into firmly holding to and remembering what they had received, not to compel them; had God intended compulsion, taking a covenant would have been needless. The objection that such a miracle would coerce faith and obedience is therefore baseless: threat and fear do not force either, or Moses’s miracles generally would count as coercion. Reducing the event to a natural convulsion whose summit merely appeared to loom overhead stems from rejecting miracles and would make language vulnerable to arbitrary distortion. Laʿalla, rendered “so that,” expresses hope or uncertainty with respect to the hearer or situation, never with respect to God, who cannot be uncertain; hence its Qur’anic rendering as “so that” or “in order that.”

The Sabbath-breakers were made apes, despised and humiliated; khāsiʾīn means despised or humiliated. Their fate was a nakāl, an exemplary punishment intended to make witnesses and later people desist from such transgression, and thus an admonition to those who guard against evil.

The commentary calls this the story of the cow, from which the chapter takes its name. Its arrangement is dramatic rather than chronological: verses 67-71 give the middle of the story, verse 72 its beginning, and verse 73 its conclusion. The direct second-person address to the Israelites through verse 66 changes to third-person reference to them before the Prophet in verses 67-71, then returns to the second person. The command to sacrifice the cow and its specifications form a parenthetic prologue to the murder and resurrection, initially creating suspense because the relation between sacrifice and finding the murderer remains concealed. The story is absent from the current Torah, which may explain the indirect address; nevertheless, its rule concerning an unknown slain person and an unworked heifer implies that something of this kind occurred.

The prologue is not a mere narrative. The Israelites’ accusation that Moses was ridiculing them imputed aimless, ignorant speech to their prophet. Their repeated phrase, “your Lord,” treated God as though He were Moses’s Lord rather than theirs; and their claim that all cows were alike did not merely express difficulty identifying one cow, but treated cows as inherently indistinguishable and demanded enough details to locate a supposedly efficacious individual. Yet the original command was unrestricted: any cow would have sufficed, because the result came from the divine will, not from some inherent quality of a particular cow. Their repeated demands were therefore arrogance and disobedience.

The commentary sees in this conduct their refusal to obey without knowing every reason, their aversion to belief in the unseen, and their wish for independence even where it did not belong to them. Their demands to see God and for a visible deity illustrate the same attempt to reduce the unseen to the seen. Requiring proof is itself correct, but they wrongly supposed that a general divine command was insufficient until its full rationale was known. Moses’s appeal for God’s protection, rather than a bare assertion that he was not ignorant, showed his reliance on divine protection, which cannot fail.

Their needless questions progressively restricted the command. God first described the cow as neither advanced in age nor too young, but al-ʿAwān, a female of middle child-bearing age, and mercifully told them to do what they had been commanded rather than pursue more questions. They then asked about its color and were told that it was intensely yellow, pleasing to beholders. Although its age and color had now been given, they again claimed that cows were all alike. The final description excluded a cow used for ploughing or irrigation and required it to be sound and without blemish. Their declaration, “Now you have brought the truth,” implied that the earlier divine and prophetic statements had not been true. They sacrificed only after they could find no further excuse, while still shifting blame for their prior refusal onto Moses and, by implication, God.

Verse 72 begins the principal episode. The disagreement over the slain man was mutual repulsion: every group disowned responsibility and charged another with the killing, while God was about to disclose what they hid. The two pronouns in the next verse refer respectively to the dead body and the cow. The commentary records and rejects an alternative that treats the passage as merely a legal rule like that in Deuteronomy, where bringing the dead to life would mean identifying the killer through retaliation. The wording about striking the corpse with part of the cow and Allah’s bringing the dead to life leaves no room for denying an actual miracle and resurrection.

Regarding hardened hearts, the commentary explains qaswah as sternness or hardness of heart, while aw, “or,” here means bal, “rather”: their hearts were not merely like rocks but worse. Rocks, despite their hardness, may release bursting streams or split so that water emerges; water is a sign of softness, whereas these hearts let no truth issue from them. Some rocks also fall down from fear of Allah. Though cracking, earthquakes, ice, snow, and melting water are natural causes, all such causes return to the First Cause. Rocks obey the divine decree that places them under secondary causes, with an understanding created in their nature. Since fear rests on perception, as do glorification and obedience, their falling may truly be described as fear of God; Qur’anic descriptions of thunder glorifying God and shadows prostrating belong to the same kind. Thus rocks fear God while the Jews’ hearts lack fear of His wrath, and the closing warning affirms that Allah is not heedless of what they do.
verses.75: Al-Mizan asks why their belief should be hoped for when some among them knowingly altered Allah’s word after understanding it.
verses.76: Al-Mizan says that they profess belief when meeting believers, but privately rebuke one another for disclosing what Allah revealed, lest the believers use it against them before their Lord.
verses.77: Al-Mizan asks: Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and proclaim?
verses.78: Al-Mizan says that illiterates among them know only lies about the Book and merely conjecture.
verses.79: Al-Mizan pronounces woe on those who write the book with their own hands, claim it is from Allah, and sell it for a small price; woe is due for both their writing and their gain.
verses.80: Al-Mizan challenges the claim that the Fire will touch them only a few days: either Allah promised it—and never fails His promise—or they speak of Him without knowledge.
verses.81: Al-Mizan states that whoever earns evil and is beset on every side by his sins will abide in the Fire.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan explains that unbelievers, especially in Medina, expected the Jews to recognize and support the Messenger of God. Aws and Khazraj knew the Medinan Jews as followers of a divine religion and a revealed Book, so they seemed likely to accept the latest divine religion and its prophet, assist its cause, and spread truth. Yet, once the Prophet migrated to Medina, the Jews showed their latent hostility. The rebuke asking whether their belief should be hoped for is thus fitting: concealing truth and altering divine words had long been their pattern, so their reversal of what they had said before Islam should not surprise.

The commentary says that the shift to addressing the Prophet and believers while referring to the Jews in the third person continues the style used in the preceding story of the Cow, whose event the Jews had omitted from the Torah. It exposes their practice of altering and manipulating the divine Book.

The two clauses about meeting believers and being alone with one another are not contrasting clauses, but describe two separate forms of transgression and ignorance. First, they hypocritically profess acceptance of Islam in order to escape trouble, ridicule, and even death. Second, they seek to deceive God, forgetting that He knows both the seen and the unseen. The commentary infers that Jewish laypeople in Medina sometimes told believers of foretellings about the Prophet in the Torah, or of information proving the truth of Islam and its prophet. Their leaders forbade this disclosure, calling it something revealed to them which should be concealed lest believers argue against the Jews before their Lord. This treats God as though He would not know unless the believers brought an argument before Him, and therefore as though His knowledge were confined to what is apparent. The verse refutes this: human knowledge is limited because perception depends on bodily organs, senses, space, time, and material causes; God’s knowledge is not so limited.

Al-Mizan sees this as evidence of the Israelites’ materialistic outlook: they applied human limitations to God, conceiving Him as present and active within matter and as controlling it according to the principles by which a material cause produces and governs its effect. It says that this error is not confined to Jews, but is also held by Muslims who accept the fundamentals of matter and give God’s life, knowledge, power, choice, will, decree, order, and management the same meanings as their human counterparts. It calls this an incurable disease for people who do not understand, and says that such views have made Islam an object of ridicule to those without access to true faith and correct Islamic knowledge. The commentary reports detractors’ taunt that, although Muslims ascribe to their Prophet the saying, “God created Adam in His likeness,” some followers have made a god in Adam’s likeness.

One group ascribes to God the qualities of matter. Another regards the divine meanings of shared names and attributes as wholly inaccessible and, consequently, reduces them to negatives: that God is not non-existent, unaware, powerless, or lifeless. Al-Mizan holds that this leaves them believing in, worshipping, and inviting others to what neither they nor anyone else knows. True religion avoids both extremes: God is neither like His creatures nor merely a collection of negative propositions. Common people should believe that God is a thing unlike other things; that His knowledge and power are unlike ours; that His will is not produced by contemplation; and that He speaks without a mouth and hears without ears. Those of higher understanding must reflect on His signs and gain deeper knowledge of religion; their greater knowledge also entails responsibilities different from those of ordinary people.

Regarding the illiterates, the commentary explains that ummiyyūn are those who cannot read or write, while amāniyy is the plural of al-umniyyah, meaning a lie. Some Jews could read and write the Book but altered it; the others knew nothing of it except the lies transmitted by that former group and therefore only conjectured.

The verse threatening woe condemns those who write the book themselves, attribute it to Allah, and sell it for a small price. Its pronouns may refer either to all Jews or only to the interpolators; on the former reading, the illiterates also share in the woe and condemnation.

Al-Khaṭīʾah, rendered “sins,” denotes the psychic condition produced by evil-doing. Thus the verse first mentions earning evil and then the resulting condition of sins enclosing a person on every side. Such total enclosure leaves no opening through which guidance can reach him, leading to everlasting residence in Hell. Were there even an iota of faith or a good trait such as justice, guidance could still penetrate. Complete enclosure includes cases of polytheism, as well as disbelief and denial of the divine signs, and broadly covers whatever makes a person abide in Hell forever.

The verses on the Fire and the Garden, like the earlier verse concerning believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabaeans, establish that salvation and eternal happiness rest on true belief and good deeds. The earlier verse denies value to merely adopting labels such as Muslim or Jew; these verses deny value to merely claiming salvation.
verses.83: Al-Mizan recounts that the Children of Israel covenanted to worship only Allah; do good to parents, kin, orphans, and the needy; speak good words to people; maintain prayer; and pay zakāt. Yet, apart from a few, they turned away and continue to turn aside.
verses.84: Al-Mizan states that they witnessed and pledged a covenant neither to shed blood nor to expel their people from their cities.
verses.85: Al-Mizan reproaches them for killing their people and expelling some from their homes while helping one another in wrongdoing and transgression. Yet when those expelled came as captives, they ransomed them, although expelling them was forbidden. They thus accepted the Book’s rule of ransom while rejecting its prohibition of expulsion. Their recompense is disgrace in this world and the most grievous chastisement on the Day of Resurrection; Allah is not heedless of what they do.
verses.86: Al-Mizan says that they chose the life of this world at the cost of the hereafter; their chastisement will not be lightened, nor will they be helped.
verses.87: Al-Mizan states that Allah gave Moses the Book, sent messengers successively after him, and gave Jesus, the son of Mary, clear evidence and the support of the holy spirit. Yet whenever a messenger brought what they disliked, they acted insolently, calling some liars and killing others.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan explains that (2:83) begins by referring to the Children of Israel in the third person but shifts to the second person when it quotes their verbal covenant. The Israelite narrative had initially used direct address for admonition and reprimand, then changed to the third person for reasons of eloquence in the story of the Cow; the quoted covenant restores the earlier address. This also connects the covenant’s final commands, to maintain prayer and pay zakāt, with the renewed admonition that they turned away.

The prohibition of worshipping anything but Allah is expressed as information, a form which gives the ban utmost force, as though compliance were beyond doubt and the servants would not dare approach idolatry. The same form continues in the command to do good, which may also be translated imperatively. Beneficence is ranked by priority: parents, who are the root of one’s existence and nearest to one; then kin; then, beyond relatives, orphans, who in childhood have lost their father—their guardian, protector, and bread-earner; and then other needy persons. For humans, al-yatīm denotes one whose father has died, not one whose mother has died; in animals, it is said of one whose mother has died.

Ḥusnan is an infinitive used adjectivally for emphasis, while some recite it ḥasanan. The command to speak good words requires gracious social conduct toward people, whether believers or unbelievers. It is not abrogated by the verse of fighting, because social contact and fighting have different times and settings; stern words used to correct a child do not negate good social relations.

The covenant in (2:84) likewise conveys its prohibition in an informative form: they must not shed blood or expel their people from their cities. In (2:85), al-taẓāhur means helping one another. The pronoun in the literal wording, “while it was unlawful for you their very turning out,” begins a sentence and has no antecedent. The verse exposes their inconsistency: they observe the rule of ransoming captives while disobeying the ban on expelling them, though both commands are in the same Book.

Qafiaynā means sending one after another; the discussion of the clear evidence given to Jesus is deferred to Chapter 3, (The Family of ʿImrān). Finally, ghulf is the plural of al-aghlaf, derived from ghilāf, a cover. Their claim that their hearts are shielded by covers and veils, so the call cannot reach them, is answered by the statement that Allah has cursed them because of their unbelief, and that little is their belief.
verses.89: Al-Mizan states that a Book from Allah confirming what they possess came to them; although they had formerly sought victory over disbelievers and recognized him when he came, they disbelieved in him, so Allah’s curse is on the unbelievers.
verses.90: Al-Mizan condemns them for selling their souls by denying Allah’s revelation out of envy that He should bestow His grace on whomever He pleases among His servants. They returned with wrath upon wrath and face a disgraceful punishment as unbelievers.
verses.91: Al-Mizan relates that, when called to believe in Allah’s revelations, they profess belief only in what was revealed to them while rejecting what lies beyond it, though it is truth confirming what they possess. It challenges this claim: if they were believers, why had they killed Allah’s prophets?
verses.92: Al-Mizan states that Moses brought them clear evidence, yet in his absence they took the calf for a god and were unjust.
verses.93:
Al-Mizan identifies the Book in (2:89) as the Qur’an. It reads “they used to” as indicating that, apparently, whenever Arabian pagans clashed with the Jews, the latter sought victory by the right of the Prophet and by his prophethood and emigration; this had become so habitual that even the pagans knew of it. The Jews recognized Muḥammad as the awaited prophet because every attribute and detail in their books fitted him perfectly, yet they denied him, incurring the curse pronounced on unbelievers.

The commentary explains that baghyan, “out of envy,” is accusative because it gives the reason for their disbelief in Muḥammad despite recognizing him: they envied Allah’s bestowal of grace on whichever servant He pleased. “They returned with wrath upon wrath” may mean that they returned doubly enraged, or that they incurred divine wrath twice—first for disbelieving in the Torah and then for disbelieving in the Qur’an. It therefore portrays them as partisans of the Prophet long before his birth, who prayed for victory by his name and his Book. When he was sent and the Qur’an revealed, they recognized the very prophet they had awaited, but envy and arrogance led them to deny him and abandon what they had formerly said. Their previous disbelief in the Torah shows this was disbelief upon disbelief.

Their claim in (2:91) to believe only in what was revealed to them refers to the Torah, but Al-Mizan says they did not truly believe even in that. The conjunction “then” connects the question about their killing of the prophets directly to their profession of faith: were it true, why had they killed Allah’s prophets, disbelieved in Moses by taking the calf for a god, and said, “We hear and disobey,” when the covenant was made and the mountain raised over them?

Verses (2:92-93) recall Moses’ clear evidence, their worship of the calf in his absence, the command to hold firmly to what they had been given and listen, and their response of disobedience. The word ushribū, from al-Ishrāb, “to make to imbibe” or “to make to drink,” says that they imbibed the calf rather than merely its love, emphatically depicting them as though they had drunk the calf itself into their hearts. It contains two metaphors: the calf stands for love of the calf, and imbibing into hearts stands for loving. The final question is derisive: it ridicules their killings of the prophets, their disbelief in Moses, and their repeated, arrogant sins while they claimed to be true believers.

A narration from Imam al-Ṣādiq explains (2:89) by saying that Jews found in their books that Muḥammad, the Messenger of God, would migrate and settle between ʿAyr and Uḥud. They searched for this place and dispersed around Taymāʿ, Fadak, and Khaybar; when travelers reached Medina between ʿAyr and Uḥud, they recognized the land they sought. The Jews acquired property there, and Tubbaʿ later attacked and besieged them. When they told him that it was the migration-place of a prophet and that none might settle there before his coming, he left Aws and Khazraj there so that they would assist the prophet. After those tribes increased and seized Jewish property, the Jews threatened that they would expel them when Muḥammad came. Yet when he was sent, the Helpers—Aws and Khazraj—believed in him, while the Jews denied him.

Two reports from Ibn ʿAbbās similarly state that the Jews sought victory over Aws and Khazraj by the right of the Messenger of God before his mission, but rejected him when God raised him from the Arabs, despite the descriptions they had given. One report recounts that, when reminded of those earlier invocations and descriptions, Salām b. Mushkim of Banu al-Naḍīr denied that Muḥammad had brought anything familiar or was the prophet they had foretold; it says the verse was then sent down. Another report says that Banu Qurayzah and Banu al-Naḍīr invoked God by the right of the untaught prophet and were granted victory, but denied Muḥammad when he came although they had no doubt about him. The author notes that similar traditions occur through other chains.

Al-Mizan then answers a commentator who calls these reports weak in transmission, incompatible with other reports, and anomalous in meaning because praying by the person or right of the Prophet supposedly violates the shariah: no one, he argues, has a right over God. The commentary replies that this objection misunderstands both oath and right. An oath joins a statement, command, request, or exclamation to something noble, placing the honor of that thing at stake if the assertion proves false, the promised act is not done, or the request is disregarded. Thus oath is the strongest form of emphasis, and its object must be more honorable than the matter emphasized. The Qur’an records oaths by Allah’s name and attributes, and Allah swears by His Prophet, angels, books, and created things. Their suitability for such oaths shows that each has a God-given dignity, reflecting a divine attribute or an activity related to divine sublimity; all honor ultimately comes from God.

Accordingly, the commentary sees no objection to a supplicant’s entreating God by something to which He has given dignity. Excluding the Messenger alone from this form of honor would be an affront to him, especially when God Himself swears by the Prophet: “By your life! they were blindly wandering on in their intoxication (15:72).”

Right, in contrast to wrong, means what is real and established rather than imagined; social rights, including monetary and familial rights, fall under this heading when firmly established. The Qur’an nullifies humanly claimed rights except those established and confirmed by God, whether in creation or legislation. No one can impose a right on God or compel Him to do or give anything. Yet God may, in the legislative sphere, make something incumbent upon Himself, thereby establishing a right for its beneficiary. The commentary cites “even so [now] it is a right on Us [that] We deliver the believers (10:103)” and “And certainly Our word has already gone forth in respect of Our servants, the messengers: Most surely they shall be assisted ones, and most surely Our host alone shall be the victorious ones (37:171-173).” The promised assistance is general and unconditional; deliverance is thereby a right of believers and assistance a right of messengers, established by God Himself and enhancing their dignity.

It follows, in Al-Mizan’s view, that one may entreat God by His Messenger, by the right of His messengers, or likewise by His friends and their right, since God has established their right to His assistance in the path of happiness. The assertion that no one has any right on God is rejected as nonsense if it denies rights God has established for Himself: a supplicant invokes not a right forced upon God by a creature, but His own pledged and unbroken promise.

The passage closes with Appendix A, a biographical index of authors referred to in this and other volumes of al-Mizan, generally giving their names, dates, scholarly affiliations, and fields. It directs readers to Appendix B for works associated with those authors. Appendix B is a bibliography of works cited in these volumes, identifying and cross-referencing tafsīr, ḥadīth, history, law, theology, lexicography, and other writings with their authors.
verses.94: Al-Mizan challenges them: if the future abode with Allah is exclusively theirs, they must invoke death if truthful.
verses.95: Al-Mizan says they will never invoke it because of what their hands have sent before; Allah knows the unjust.
verses.96: Al-Mizan says they are the greediest of men for life—even greedier than polytheists—and each desires a life of a thousand years; yet long life will not avert chastisement, and Allah sees what they do.
verses.97: Al-Mizan says to whoever is an enemy of Gabriel: by Allah’s Command, he revealed it to your heart, verifying what was before it and as guidance and good news for believers.
verses.98: Al-Mizan says that whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel and Michael faces Allah, the enemy of the unbelievers.
verses.99:
Al-Mizan says that clear signs have been revealed and that disbelief in them is confined to transgressors, because their transgression causes their disbelief. Alternatively, the definite article in “the transgressors” may identify the group earlier described as breaking Allah’s covenant after its confirmation.

The commentary explains the challenge of (2:94) as answering Jewish claims that the Fire would touch them only for a few days and that they accepted only what had been revealed to them. These claims implied exclusive salvation and happiness in the next world. The future abode denotes that abode’s felicity; its being “with Allah” means firmly established by His order and permission, while its being “purely” theirs means unmixed with punishment or humiliation. Their claim to it to the exclusion of others rests on their assumption that all other religions are false. God challenges this self-delusion by requiring them, if truthful, to invoke death.

The argument is held to be self-evident: anyone, even an animal with limited perception, freely chooses comfort over distress and seeks a pure life rather than one troubled by harm. If prevented from it, he continues to desire and seek it. Therefore, if the Jews truly believed that pure otherworldly happiness belonged exclusively to them, they would yearn for it in heart, speech, and action.

Their refusal to invoke it is due to what their hands have sent ahead: deeds such as killing prophets, disbelieving in Moses, and breaking covenants. “What their hands have sent before” figuratively attributes all deeds to the hands and the sending of deeds to them, though it is the person who sends them ahead. A person’s actions, especially habitual ones, disclose his unconscious and subconscious character. Evil deeds reveal an evil nature that does not wish to meet its Lord or dwell in the abode of His friends; Allah knows the unjust.

Verse (2:96) explains this refusal by their extreme greed for the insignificant life of this world, which turns them away from the happy life of the next abode. They are greedier for life even than the polytheists, although the latter’s denial of the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment should make their attachment to worldly life unparalleled. Each wants the longest possible life, expressed as a thousand years. Apparently, the conjunction means that they are greedier than even the polytheists. One syntactic reading takes the pronoun as that of shaʾn or qiṣṣah and makes being granted a long life the subject; another may refer it to their love of such a life. In either case, neither long life nor the desire for it can ward off Divine Chastisement, because every life is limited and ends. The ending invokes al-Baṣīr: although Allah has neither body nor eye, He fully cognizes all that is perceived by the eyes; this is a facet of al-ʾAlīm (the Knowing).

The commentary apparently treats (2:97) as a response to Jews who arrogantly rejected the revelation brought to the Messenger on the pretext of being enemies of Gabriel; traditions concerning the occasion confirm this background. The two verses give four replies: Gabriel brought the Qur’an by Allah’s Command, not by his own will; the Qur’an verifies the earlier Divine Book in their possession; it guides those who believe in it; and it gives believers good news. A sensible person has no reason to turn away from guidance and good news merely because their bearer is regarded as an enemy.

Gabriel, Michael, and the other angels are honored servants who have no authority except to obey the Divine Command, and the messengers likewise have authority only by and from Allah. Enmity toward them is therefore enmity toward Allah. Calling Allah “the enemy of the unbelievers,” rather than simply their enemy, also gives the reason: Allah is their enemy because they are unbelievers, and He is the enemy of the unbelievers.

The use of “your heart,” rather than the expected “my heart,” emphasizes that neither Gabriel nor the Messenger has independent choice in revelation: Gabriel faithfully carries out the Command, while the Messenger’s heart is the receptacle of revelation, over which he has no control, and which he must convey to his people. The repeated movement between addressing the Jews directly and referring to them in the third person indicates that, after prolonged admonition and condemnation, they no longer deserve the honor of direct address. Yet the divine Speaker does not leave them without pronouncing judgment upon their heedlessness and depravity. Further explanation of Gabriel’s bringing revelation to the Messenger’s heart, and of Michael and the other angels, is deferred, God willing.
verses.100: Al-Mizan explains al-Nabdh as throwing away or renouncing. “A messenger” refers definitively to Muḥammad, not to recurring messengers, since “when there came” denotes a single event. The verses expose the Jews’ hostility to truth: immersed in falsehood, they cast aside their covenants, concealed the Torah’s foretelling of the prophet of Islam, and rejected the Qur’an although it verified what they possessed.

verses.102:
Al-Mizan notes that this verse has produced an almost unparalleled range of exegetical disagreement. Commentators differ over whom “they” denotes; whether tatlū means reciting, lying, faking, or following; whether the satans are jinn, human beings, or both; and how ʿalā relates their activity to Solomon’s kingdom. They also dispute the cause of the satans’ disbelief, the manner in which they taught sorcery, whether mā means “what” or “not,” how the conjunction functions, the meaning of “sent down,” the identity of Hārūt and Mārūt, Babylon’s location, the nature of their teaching and warning, and the way sorcery separated spouses. Some even question whether the account is historical or parabolic. Yet, despite these proliferating readings, the Qur’an retains its eloquence, coherent meaning, and beauty.

It appears from the context that the verse concerns the Jews’ widespread practice of sorcery, founded on popular stories. Al-Mizan holds that their transmitted stories cannot be relied on, because they altered, interpolated, and omitted material from their divine books and records; nevertheless, the Qur’anic admonition proceeds from beliefs which they themselves related. They attributed Solomon’s kingdom, his subjugation of jinn, human beings, animals, and birds, and his extraordinary acts to sorcery, claiming that some enchantments came from him and the rest from Hārūt and Mārūt.

The Qur’an refutes this attribution. Solomon, an innocent and sinless prophet whose high rank, knowledge, wisdom, and unique kingdom are established elsewhere in the Qur’an, could not have practised sorcery, which is disbelief in God. The story was invented by the satans and conveyed to their human allies; the satans disbelieved by misleading people through teaching sorcery.

Al-Mizan explains that the Jews after Solomon, each generation handing this legacy to the next, followed what the satans from among the jinn faked and lied about his kingdom. Tatlū has this sense because the accompanying ʿalā changes its semantic value. The satans are identified as jinn by reading together the satans who worked for Solomon in (21:82) and the jinn who learned of his death in (34:14). The conjunction in “and Solomon was not an unbeliever, but the satans disbelieved” means “while”: Solomon did not disbelieve through sorcery; rather, the satans did so by teaching it.

The commentary takes mā in “what was sent down” as relative, not negative: the Jews also followed what was sent through inspiration to the two angels at Babylon, Hārūt and Mārūt. These angels were given sorcery as a trial for human beings, just as human nature has been taught ways of evil in order to be tested. Before teaching anyone, they warned that they were only a trial and that practising sorcery for wrongful purposes would make the learner a disbeliever. It could be used only to nullify witchcraft, expose sorcerers’ vile practices, and similar purposes. Yet people learned from them what destroyed domestic peace, turning the love between husband and wife into hatred and separation, and thus learned what harmed rather than profited them.

The qualification that sorcery cannot harm anyone except with Allah’s permission prevents the supposition that sorcerers can upset the divinely ordained order or undo the Divine Decree. Sorcery has whatever effect it has only within the system designed by God. This parenthetic qualification follows the clause about separating spouses because that clause describes sorcery’s effect; the following clause concerns instead its harm and lack of profit.

Those who bought sorcery knew, through reason and through Moses’ teaching that “the magician shall not be successful wheresoever he may come from” (20:69), that it was a most wicked source of social disorder and that it deprived its purchaser of all good in the hereafter. They nevertheless sold their souls for it. Since they did not act on what they knew, their knowledge was as ignorance: knowledge that does not lead its possessor to the straight path is not truly knowledge. The passage also declares that belief and guarding oneself against evil would have brought a better reward from Allah.
verses.103: Al-Mizan explains that, had the Jews followed belief and piety rather than the satans’ tales and the practice of sorcery, they would have received Allah’s reward. Sorcery constitutes disbelief in the sphere of action, like withholding zakāt, not disbelief in the sphere of faith. Had it been disbelief in faith, the verse would have said only, “And if they believed,” without adding, “and guarded themselves [against evil].” The Jews did believe, but their failure to avoid what Allah forbade rendered that belief valueless, and they were therefore called disbelievers. Allah’s reward would have been better than the gains and profits they sought through sorcery and disbelief.
verses.104:
Al-Mizan holds that this is the Qur’an’s first address beginning, “O you who believe!” The address, and the description “those who believe,” are marks of honour peculiar to the Muslim community, whereas earlier communities are called such things as a people, dwellers, or children. Yet “those who believe” appears, on reflection, to have a more particular import than “the believers.”

The commentary argues from the prayer of the bearers of the throne for “those who believe” in (40:7-8). Those for whom forgiveness is sought are then described as those who return to God and follow His way, while their righteous fathers, wives, and offspring are mentioned separately as being joined to them in the gardens. Had “those who believe” meant everyone who professed belief in the Messenger regardless of its quality, there would have been no need to distinguish those righteous relatives. Likewise, (52:21) speaks of the offspring who follow believers in faith being united with them without diminishing the believers’ works. This would be pointless if all believers and their descendants were already one undifferentiated rank; rather, the wording shows that the earlier believers have a superiority and that their offspring are raised to their rank as an honour to them.

Accordingly, “those who believe” in these contexts denotes a particular honoured group: the foremost and first of the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed the Messenger in the hour of straitness. The distinct expressions in (59:8-10), referring both to those who had precedence in faith and to “those who believe,” indicate that each has its own significance, and (48:29) also supports this conclusion. Most probably, the contrasting phrase “those who disbelieve” similarly refers to the foremost disbelievers in the Messenger, including the polytheists of Mecca, as in (2:6).

This does not restrict the laws stated in verses addressed to “O you who believe!” to that select group. The distinction between whom a speech honours by addressing and whom a law binds is essential: every command and prohibition in such verses applies generally to all believers. The same is true whether a law is addressed to the believers, to the Prophet or Messenger personally, or revealed without a direct address. Nevertheless, the special sense should not be imposed on every occurrence; context decides, and “those who believe” in (4:137) and (11:129) plainly cannot denote that early distinguished group.

The command concerning rāʿinā requires believers to say “Wait for us,” that is, unẓurnā, and to listen, instead of saying “Have regard for us.” Failure to obey this rule is treated as disbelief, for which there is painful chastisement. The prohibition is emphatic because Jews used rāʿinā as a distorted, taunting expression akin to “Hear, may you not be made to hear!” as described in (4:46). A tradition cited by the commentary reports that Muslims had used Rāʿinā when speaking to the Prophet to ask him to wait so that they could understand him properly; but the word carried an abusive connotation in the Jews’ language. Jews exploited this ambiguity, seeming to address the Prophet respectfully while intending abuse. The Qur’an therefore directed believers to use unẓurnā instead. This is one instance in which disobedience to a religious law is termed disbelief.

The commentary initially reads “the People of the Book” here as the Jews, since the preceding discussion concerns them. Having previously received a Book, they disliked the Qur’an’s descent upon Muslims because it removed their distinction as the People of the Book. Their resentment was avarice over a favour they did not possess and opposition to God’s bestowal of mercy and grace on His servants, though Allah chooses whom He pleases for His mercy and is the Lord of mighty grace. Alternatively, the phrase may include both Jews and Christians, widening the admonition after its particular reference; their shared characteristics, especially enmity toward Islam, support this broader reading, as do the ensuing statements in (2:111) and (2:113).

verses.106:
Al-Mizan defines juridical abrogation as the disclosure that the period of a command has ended: the command is no longer valid or in force. Lexically, al-Naskh means removal or annulment, and can also denote copying, as though writing were removed and transferred; the Qur’an similarly uses al-tabdīl, changing one sign for another, in (16:101).

Abrogation does not make a Qur’anic verse non-existent. It cancels the command that the verse promulgated. Since a verse is called a sign because it points to a Divine Command, abrogation removes its quality as a sign of that command: the verse remains, but no longer indicates a binding order. By contrast, al-insāʾ means causing forgetfulness, erasing something from memory or knowledge. The juxtaposition of the two expressions therefore shows that abrogation erases a verse’s effect, whereas al-insāʾ eradicates the verse itself from memory.

The commentary takes “sign” in a broad sense. Qur’anic verses are signs through their inimitability; Divine laws are signs through producing piety and nearness to God; created things point by their existence to their Creator and by their qualities to His names and attributes; and prophets and the friends of God call humanity to God by word and deed. Signs consequently differ in strength, scope, and aspects of symbolism. A sign with only one aspect may be wholly removed, while a sign with several aspects may lose one alone. Thus a Qur’anic verse may be abrogated as law while remaining a Divine sign through its eloquence and miraculous character.

Al-Mizan derives this general conception from the reasoning of the next verse, which declares that Allah possesses the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. It identifies two objections to abrogation. The first says that every Divine sign has a real benefit unavailable elsewhere; replacing it would destroy that benefit and would imply that God changed a command because new circumstances taught Him what He had not known. Such change is possible for creatures with incomplete knowledge, not for God. The commentary says that this objection ultimately assumes that Divine power is not comprehensive and unrestricted. The second objection concedes unlimited power before an act is done, but claims that once something is created it lies beyond that power and cannot be changed. This rejects God’s all-encompassing ownership, supposing that once He has arranged something in one way He cannot arrange it otherwise; it is the belief portrayed in: “And the Jews say: The hand of Allah is tied up (5:64).”

The question, “Do you not know that Allah has power over all things?”, answers the first objection: God can replace a sign with one equal or better in benefit. The question concerning His kingdom answers the second: as Owner of the heavens and earth, He may manage His property as He wills. No other being owns anything in a way that could restrict His authority. When God grants someone possession, His own ownership is neither transferred, ended, nor diminished, unlike a human owner who transfers property to another; He remains its real Owner and Controller, with unrestricted ownership and management.

If people view what is in their hands as possession without independent authority, God is their Guardian. If they fix their eyes on their apparent independence, they must still recognize that they cannot manage their affairs or attain their desired results without His help; He is their Helper. Thus, from either perspective, His power and ownership remain unchallenged. The two questions are not joined by a conjunction because each answers a separate objection. The use of “Allah,” rather than “Him,” in the final clause shows that “besides Allah you have no guardian or helper” is an independent declaration reinforcing the preceding replies, rather than an integral part of them.

The commentary draws several conclusions. Abrogation occurs not only in religious law but also in creation. It requires an abrogated thing and an abrogating thing, and the latter contains all the benefit and perfection found in the former. Although the two differ in form, they share benefit and perfection. The succession of one prophet by another, as well as the replacement of life, death, sustenance, and similar factors, conforms to the natural order and to changing requirements of social welfare and human perfection. Likewise, an abrogating law can lead individuals and society to spiritual and temporal well-being just as the former law did; each is perfectly suited to its own time and more beneficial in its own context. Thus forgiveness was commanded when Muslims lacked numbers and arms, while fighting was commanded after Islam had gained strength and its opponents feared the Muslims.

Abrogated verses, Al-Mizan says, are seldom without language indicating that their command is temporary. It cites: “But pardon and forgive [them] until Allah should bring about His command (2:109),” said to have been abrogated by the verse of fighting, “and … confine them until death takes them away or Allah makes some way for them (4:15),” which was itself abrogated by the verse of flogging. The phrases “until Allah should bring about His command” and “or Allah makes some way for them” signal a transitory order awaiting abrogation.

The relation of abrogation is distinct from that between a general statement and a particular one, an unconditional clause and a conditional one, or an unspecified proposition and a specified one. The apparent conflict between an abrogating and an abrogated ruling is resolved by the welfare and benefit shared by both rulings. In the other cases, the apparent conflict is removed because the particular, conditional, or specified expression manifests the speaker’s real intention more strongly and clearly; the general is read through the particular, the unconditional through the conditional, and the unspecified through the specified. The commentary says the same principle applies to decisive and ambiguous verses.

Nunsihā derives from al-insāʾ and is general and unconditional. Al-Mizan holds that it is neither restricted to the Messenger of God nor inclusive of him, because God had already promised him: “We will make you recite so you shall not forget, except what Allah pleases (87:6-7).” Since that is a Meccan verse and the verse of abrogation is Medinan, the Messenger could not forget after this promise. The objection that “except what Allah pleases” permits his actual forgetfulness is rejected: such exceptions emphasize God’s power without entailing that the excepted event will occur. Similarly, “except as your Lord pleases” in the description of the Garden (11:108) establishes God’s power to alter the arrangement, although all Muslims agree that the people of Paradise will never be removed from it. Moreover, if the Prophet could actually forget what God taught him whenever God willed, the promise would add no new grace, since all humans and animals remember and forget only by God’s will. The promise must therefore mean that he would never forget, while God still retained full power to make him forget.

Some people recite the word as nansaʾahā, from al-nasʾ, delay. On that reading, the verse means that whatever sign God nullifies or postpones by delaying its appearance, He brings one better or like it. Advancing or delaying a matter in Divine management does not lessen its perfection or benefit. “We bring one better than it or like it” shows that the abrogated rule was good and that its replacement is at least equally good; goodness arises from a thing’s perfection or a rule’s benefit. Every Divine management is therefore the ideal of goodness, perfection, and benefit.

It cites: “But pardon and forgive [them] until Allah should bring about His command (2:109),” said to have been abrogated by the verse of fighting, “and … confine them until death takes them away or Allah makes some way for them (4:15),” which was itself abrogated by the verse of flogging. The phrases “until Allah should bring about His command” and “or Allah makes some way for them” signal a transitory order awaiting abrogation.

The relation of abrogation is distinct from that between a general statement and a particular one, an unconditional clause and a conditional one, or an unspecified proposition and a specified one. The apparent conflict between an abrogating and an abrogated ruling is resolved by the welfare and benefit shared by both rulings. In the other cases, the apparent conflict is removed because the particular, conditional, or specified expression manifests the speaker’s real intention more strongly and clearly; the general is read through the particular, the unconditional through the conditional, and the unspecified through the specified. The commentary says the same principle applies to decisive and ambiguous verses.

Nunsihā derives from al-insāʾ and is general and unconditional. Al-Mizan holds that it is neither restricted to the Messenger of God nor inclusive of him, because God had already promised him: “We will make you recite so you shall not forget, except what Allah pleases (87:6-7).” Since that is a Meccan verse and the verse of abrogation is Medinan, the Messenger could not forget after this promise. The objection that “except what Allah pleases” permits his actual forgetfulness is rejected: such exceptions emphasize God’s power without entailing that the excepted event will occur. Similarly, “except as your Lord pleases” in the description of the Garden (11:108) establishes God’s power to alter the arrangement, although all Muslims agree that the people of Paradise will never be removed from it. Moreover, if the Prophet could actually forget what God taught him whenever God willed, the promise would add no new grace, since all humans and animals remember and forget only by God’s will. The promise must therefore mean that he would never forget, while God still retained full power to make him forget.

Some people recite the word as nansaʾahā, from al-nasʾ, delay. On that reading, the verse means that whatever sign God nullifies or postpones by delaying its appearance, He brings one better or like it. Advancing or delaying a matter in Divine management does not lessen its perfection or benefit. “We bring one better than it or like it” shows that the abrogated rule was good and that its replacement is at least equally good; goodness arises from a thing’s perfection or a rule’s benefit. Every Divine management is therefore the ideal of goodness, perfection, and benefit.
verses.108: Al-Mizan warns against questioning the Messenger as Moses was questioned; whoever exchanges faith for unbelief has lost the straight way.
verses.109: Al-Mizan says that, from envy after the truth became manifest to them, many People of the Book wish to turn believers back to unbelief. Believers are to pardon and forgive them until Allah brings His command, for He has power over all things.
verses.110: Al-Mizan says: Maintain prayer, pay zakāt, and find with Allah every good you send ahead for yourselves; He sees what you do.
verses.111: Al-Mizan calls the claim that only a Jew or Christian enters the garden a vain desire, and tells its claimants to provide proof if truthful.
verses.112: Al-Mizan states that whoever wholly submits himself to Allah and does good will have his reward with his Lord, and will neither fear nor grieve.
verses.113: Al-Mizan recounts that Jews deny Christians any good and Christians deny Jews any good, though both recite the Book. Those without knowledge speak similarly, and Allah will judge their differences on the Day of Resurrection.
verses.114: Al-Mizan calls most unjust those who prevent people from Allah’s mosques so that His name is not remembered and who strive to ruin them. They should enter them only in fear, and will have disgrace in this world and great chastisement in the hereafter.
verses.115:
Al-Mizan says it appears that (2:108) addresses some Muslims who, despite believing in the Prophet, asked him questions like those the Jews put to Moses. They are consequently admonished alongside the Jews, and tradition supports this reading. To adopt unbelief instead of faith is to lose the straight path.

Regarding (2:109), the commentary says that many People of the Book, envious although the truth had become manifest to them, wished to turn believers back to unbelief. It reports that the passage refers to Ḥuyayy b. al-Akhṭab and other Jews with him. According to the exegetes, the command to pardon and forgive was abrogated by the verse of fighting. The command Allah was to bring is understood as a directive about the Jews that would be revealed before long, just as “except in fear” had hinted at the later ban on idolaters approaching the Sacred Mosque. The commentary reserves fuller explanation of al-amr (command) for its treatment of (17:85).

On (2:111), Al-Mizan dismisses the claim that only Jews or Christians enter the garden as a vain desire requiring proof. Its explicit conjunction of Christians with Jews signals that the sins and crimes of both will henceforth be enumerated together. On (2:112), it calls the verse a third reiteration that spiritual felicity does not depend on names or nomenclature: honor with God belongs only through true faith and complete surrender to Him. Whoever so submits and does good has reward with his Lord, without fear or grief. Comparison with the preceding declarations shows that true belief entails complete submission to God, and that al-iḥsān, to do good, is synonymous with good deeds.

For (2:113), “while they recite the Book” means while they follow the Book revealed to them. Since it clearly shows them the truth, Jews and Christians should not dismiss one another as following nothing good. The next sentence supports this meaning: “those who have no knowledge” are the unbelievers other than the People of the Book and the polytheists of Arabia, who used to say that either the Muslims or the People of the Book followed nothing good. Allah will judge between the disputants on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Mizan says that (2:114) apparently refers to the unbelievers and polytheists of Mecca, and that these two verses were revealed not long after the Messenger of God emigrated to Medina. Its past-tense “was” describes a past event and fits the pagans of Mecca and their misdeeds. Traditions identify “he who prevents” as the Meccan unbelievers who barred Muslims from praying in the Sacred Mosque, Masjid al-Ḥarām, and in other mosques within the precinct of the Kaʿbah. They are the most unjust because they prevent Allah’s name from being remembered in His mosques and seek their ruin; they should enter them only in fear, and face worldly disgrace and great chastisement in the hereafter.

The commentary explains (2:115) through Allah’s true mastership. Unlike human possession, which covers benefits and effects rather than the thing itself, Allah’s ownership cannot be altered or transferred and permeates both things and their benefits and effects. Since a possession cannot exist independently of its owner, all directions exist through God, who preserves, manages, and encompasses them; whoever turns in any direction truly turns to Him.

East and west are relative terms covering every direction except the two imaginary points of true north and true south. Since any direction one faces is east or west, the unconditional wording “whither you turn” implies that all directions belong to God. East and west are singled out because people determine directions through the rising and setting of the sun and other heavenly bodies.

Al-Mizan treats “therefore, whither you turn, thither is Allah’s face” as putting the cause in place of the effect: one may turn to whichever direction because Allah’s face is there too. The editor’s note identifies “face” as metaphorical. The conclusion, “surely God is Ample-giving, Knowing,” confirms this: al-Wāsiʿ, rendered “ample-giving,” signifies what is extensive, abounding, and far-reaching, so Allah’s ownership embraces every direction. Being all-knowing, He knows one’s aim and intention regardless of direction and is not confined to a direction as creatures are when they look at something. Thus the verse gives latitude concerning the direction of the qiblah, but not its location, because it speaks only of directions.
verses.116:
Al-Mizan identifies “they” as the Jews, who called Ezra (ʿUzayr) God’s son, and the Christians, who said the same of Jesus Christ. The People of the Book had first used “son of God” honorifically for prophets, just as they called themselves God’s sons and chosen people; the metaphorical usage gradually became a belief in real sonship.

The verses refute this belief with two proofs. First, begetting belongs to physical beings: one separates part of oneself, develops it, and produces another member of one’s species similar to oneself. Nothing can resemble God or belong to His species. Everything in the heavens and earth is His possession, exists and is governed through Him, and is naturally subject and obedient to Him; therefore none can be His like or son.

Second, God is al-Badīʿ, the Originator: the one who produces without a prior model or blueprint. God alone is Originator in this true sense. He creates without imitation, gradual development, or the aid of secondary causes; when He decrees a thing, He says, “Be,” and it is. Since begetting entails gradual development, it cannot be ascribed to such an Originator. Originating also means that what is created is unlike every other thing.

The commentary further concludes that obedience and worship of God bind everything in the heavens and earth, and that God’s acts are not gradual. Hence whatever comes to be gradually has another, non-gradual existence emanating from the Divine Command: His command, when He intends anything, is only that He says to it, Be, and it is (36:82); And Our command is but one, as the twinkling of an eye (54:50).

It explains subḥān as an accusative infinitive synonymous with al-tasbīḥ (glorification of God), used with God’s name or a pronoun referring to Him in place of an omitted verb, originally sabbaḥtuhu tasbīḥan. It teaches believers to declare God’s glory when something unworthy is attributed to Him. al-Qunūt means worship and self-abasement. Grammatically, “and it is” follows from “Be,” rather than forming a conditional clause; consequently, its verb is not apocopate.

verses.118:
Al-Mizan explains that “those who have no knowledge” are the polytheists and other unbelievers apart from the People of the Book. As verse 113 joined the People of the Book to the Arabian polytheists and unbelievers, this verse joins the latter to the People of the Book: including the Jews, who disputed with Moses and demanded what these pagans demand. Their shared manner of thought shows that their hearts are alike.

The demand for God to speak to them or send a sign is refuted because the signs they seek have already been made clear. Only those who are sure can benefit from them; these ignorant people cannot, because their hearts are immersed in ignorance and afflicted by prejudice and envy. This explains why they are called those without knowledge.

Having exposed their demand as false, God assures the Messenger that He has sent him with the truth, as a bearer of good news and a warner. The statement comforts him by showing that these opponents are people of the Fire who will not follow guidance, much like those described in: Surely those who disbelieve alike is to them whether you warn them or do not warn them, they will not believe (2:6).

verses.120: Al-Mizan states that the Jews and Christians will not be pleased until the Prophet follows their religion. Allah’s guidance alone is true guidance; if he follows their desires after knowledge has come to him, he will have from Allah neither guardian nor helper.
verses.121: Al-Mizan says that those given the Book who read it as it ought to be read are the ones who believe in it, while whoever disbelieves in it are the losers.
verses.122: Al-Mizan calls the Children of Israel to remember His bounty and their distinction above nations.
verses.123:
Al-Mizan explains that, after the preceding admonitions, the address returns to the Jews and Christians and sums up the discussion: they will not be satisfied until the Prophet follows a religion they have fashioned from desire and opinion. “Surely God’s guidance, that is the [true] guidance” identifies God’s guidance with the revealed Qur’an and confines real guidance to it; consequently, their religion has no guidance and is only desire presented as religion. The Prophet possesses knowledge while they possess ignorance; thus, if he followed their desires after the knowledge given him, he would have from God neither guardian nor helper.

The commentary takes “These [it is who] believe in it” as answering the implicit question whether inviting Jews and Christians is futile if they will not believe. Its main explanation understands those given “the Book” as a truth-seeking group among Jews and Christians, and the Book as the Torah and Gospel: because they read it as it ought to be read, they truly believe in their Book and will believe in the Prophet. This may also mean that belief in a revealed book entails belief in every book revealed by God, or specifically in the Qur’an; on these readings, “it” may refer successively to more than one noun. Alternatively, “the Book” may be the Qur’an and those given it the believers; then those who read it properly, rather than Jews and Christians following desire, believe in it, and the restriction forms a converted proposition.

Finally, the commentary says that (2:122-123) close the address to the Children of Israel by joining its end to its opening. They are called to remember Allah’s bounty and preference over the nations, and warned of a day when no soul can benefit another, no compensation is accepted, no intercession profits, and none are helped.
verses.124:
Al-Mizan explains that the Abrahamic passages beginning with (2:124) prepare for the change of al-qiblah and the rules of ḥajj, while setting out the pure Islamic religion in its beliefs, morals, and laws. They show Abraham’s imamate, his building of the Kaʿbah, and his prayer for a messenger from among his descendants.

The bestowal of imamate occurred at the end of Abraham’s life, after Ishmael and Isaac had been born and after Ishmael and his mother had been settled in Mecca. Abraham’s request, “And of my offspring?” presupposes that he knew he had descendants. Before the angels’ annunciation of Ishmael and Isaac, however, both he and his wife had apparently abandoned hope of children, as their response to the annunciation shows (15:51-55) and (11:71-73). Had he made this request before receiving children or their promised birth, he would have needed to qualify it. His imamate was therefore granted after the good news and after the trials of his life. The clearest and hardest of these was the commanded sacrifice of Ishmael, called “a manifest trial” (37:102-106), and it too occurred in Abraham’s old age, since Ishmael and Isaac were given to him then (14:39).

Al-ibtilāʾ and al-balāʾ mean testing: commanding someone or placing him in hardship so that his hidden qualities—such as obedience, courage, generosity, chastity, knowledge, and faithfulness, or their opposites—are made manifest through action. Words may lie, but action discloses what a person is. The “certain words” by which God tried Abraham are words insofar as they convey divine information, commands, and prohibitions and thus issue in action. Although “word” can exceptionally designate a corporeal being, as Jesus is called a Word from God because he was created by God’s word, God’s attributed “words” ordinarily mean His speech. A word is described as accomplished or fulfilled when what it conveys is implemented.

God’s word and action are one in reality, yet “word” may still be used according to its communicative function: whatever reality God discloses or command He imposes is His speech because it conveys information or obligation. Likewise, “word” can designate a firm intention or deed when it carries the import of a word. Thus the “certain words” are the difficult situations and divine covenants Abraham encountered—his dispute with his people over the stars and idols, the fire, emigration, the sacrifice of his son, and the like. The Qur’an does not specify them because their individual identification is not the verse’s concern; what is certain is that, because imamate followed their fulfilment, they proved Abraham’s capacity for it. If “he fulfilled them” refers to Abraham, it means that he obediently completed what was required; but the commentary takes the pronoun as referring obviously to the Lord, meaning that God enabled Abraham to do what was required. It rejects the view that the “words” are the sentences, “Surely I am going to make you an imam for men” through “My covenant will not include the unjust,” because the Qur’an does not use “words” to mean “sentences.”

An imam is a leader whose followers conform their words and deeds to his. Al-Mizan rejects the common identification of imamate here with prophethood. Grammatically, “Surely I am going to make you an imam” promises a future status Abraham did not then possess, whereas the very revelation addressed to him proves that he was already a prophet. Historically, he had already been a prophet and messenger when he received the annunciation of Isaac and Ishmael and was granted imamate. Imamate is therefore distinct from both prophethood and messengership.

Nor does it mean mere precedence, obligatory obedience, al-khilāfah, al-wiṣāyah, or temporal and spiritual headship. Prophethood is receiving divine news; messengership is conveying it; and authority, succession to a prophet, and religious or political headship all concern matters that already accompany prophethood or messengership. A divine status is not an empty new title. Imamate has its own reality: an intrinsic quality by which people ought faithfully to follow a person and make their words and actions conform to his. It would be meaningless to promise Abraham, already a prophet whose obedience was obligatory, that he would newly become a prophet, be newly obeyed, become a successor, or rule people by God’s command.

The Qur’an explains imamate as guidance “by Our command” (21:72-73) and (32:24), not simply any guidance.
