The Divine Command, also called the Kingdom, is the sublime Godward aspect of created things: free of time, space, change, and variation, and identical with a thing’s actual existence under the divine “Be.” It contrasts with al-khalq, the created aspect subject to change, growth, deterioration, time, and space. Thus an imam guides through a Divine Command closely associated with him. In its esoteric sense, imamate is al-wilāyah—guardianship and authority over people in their deeds and activities—and its guidance conveys them to their final destination by God’s command. This differs from guidance that merely shows the way, whether offered by prophets, messengers, or other believers through explanation, exhortation, and warning.

The qualifications for imamate stated in connection with this guidance are unconditional patience in every divine test and the highest certainty concerning God’s signs. Abraham’s vision of the kingdom was the prelude to this certainty (6:75). Those near to God are not veiled by the rust of sin, ignorance, and doubt; they possess absolute certainty and see the ʿilliyyīn as they see hell. An imam must therefore have such certainty and see the kingdom, the esoteric side of the universe and the sphere of the Divine Command.

Because imams guide by God’s command, the inner reality of what they guide—the hearts and deeds of people—is constantly before them. Hearts and deeds, like all things, have both the side of command and the side of creation. Hence the realities of human good and evil deeds are under the imam’s observation, and he has authority over both the way of felicity and the way of wretchedness. Since every people will be called with its imam (17:71), the imam leads people to God when hidden things are tested on the Day of Resurrection just as he leads them in the outward and inward life of this world. The verse also indicates that no period can be without an imam, since it speaks of every people. An editor’s note adds that, on the author’s explanation of 17:71, “imam” there is general and may include leaders of disbelief.

Imamate cannot belong to one touched by injustice or sin, however slight, because such a person needs another to guide him. The contrast in “Is he then who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or he who himself does not go right unless he is guided?” (10:35) means that the one who truly guides to the truth is rightly guided in himself, whereas one who requires another’s guidance cannot be that guide. The imam must consequently be al-maʿṣūm, protected from error and sin. The wording that God revealed to the imams “the doing of good [deeds] and the establishing of prayer and the giving of zakāt” (21:73) establishes not merely a command to do good but that their deeds actually were good, through divine inspiration and help. Conversely, one who is not maʿṣūm can never be an imam who guides to the truth.

“My covenant will not include the unjust” includes anyone who committed injustice—polytheism, idol worship, or any other sin—at any point in life, even if he later repented and became righteous. The commentary reports a teacher’s fourfold argument: people are either unjust throughout life, never unjust, unjust first and just later, or just first and unjust later. Abraham would not have sought imamate for those unjust throughout or unjust at the end; among the two remaining groups, God excludes those unjust at first and righteous later. Only those never unjust at any time remain, namely the maʿṣūm. The verse thus indicates that imamate is a divinely appointed station; that the imam is protected by divine ʿiṣmah; that the earth never lacks a rightful imam while humans remain; that the imam receives divine support; that people’s deeds are not hidden from him; that he knows what they need for their worldly and otherworldly good; and that no one can surpass him in any virtue.

The objection that every prophet should then be an imam confuses a necessary condition with its converse. Guidance to God by His command requires that the guide be rightly guided by God rather than by another person, but it does not follow that everyone whom God guides is thereby a guide to God. The Qur’an names many prophets as guided while not stating that they guided others to the truth in this special sense (6:86-90); prophethood and imamate are therefore not synonymous.

This guidance by command is described as a firm divine decree continuing in Abraham’s posterity: after Abraham had reached guidance through reflection and reasoning and declared himself free from his people’s worship, he expected the further guidance of God, and God made it “a word to continue” in his descendants (43:26-28). Here “word” designates the guidance itself, not speech. The commentary concludes that this divine guidance continues in the ummah after the Messenger of God and is confined to Abraham’s progeny. Abraham’s request concerning his offspring was not for every descendant; God’s answer excludes only the unjust and thereby grants imamate to a selected righteous group among them. By calling it “My covenant,” the verse emphasizes that the unjust are far removed from the divine covenant; its wording also shows that attaining imamate is exclusively God’s act, not a status humans can reach by themselves.
verses.125: Al-Mizan recalls that God made the House a place to which people return and a sanctuary of safety, commanded prayer at Abraham’s standing-place, and charged Abraham and Ishmael to purify it for circumambulation, devotion, bowing, and prostration.
verses.126: Al-Mizan recounts Abraham’s prayer that the town be secure and its believing people sustained with fruits. God grants even the unbeliever brief enjoyment, then drives him to the Fire, an evil destination.
verses.127: Al-Mizan recalls Abraham and Ishmael raising the House’s foundations and praying that God accept their work, for He hears and knows.
verses.128: Al-Mizan recounts Abraham and Ishmael praying for complete submission to God, a submissive group from their offspring, insight into their devotional ways, and God’s merciful turning toward them.
verses.129:
Al-Mizan explains that the House’s being a rendezvous, al-Mathābah, refers to its role in the legislation of the ḥajj and the sanctuary it provides: it is a place to which people repeatedly return. The command to take a place of prayer at Abraham’s standing-place is joined by “and” to the preceding statement, so that the preceding statement also has the force of an order: return to and perform the ḥajj of the House, and take there a place for prayer and invocation. Alternatively, some exegetes supply “We said.” The wording does not simply command prayer at the standing-place; rather, it prescribes taking a place of prayer there, while the preceding statement introduces the reason for that prescription.

The injunction to Abraham and Ishmael to purify God’s House may mean keeping it exclusively for the worship of those who circumambulate, remain there in devotion, and pray; or it may mean maintaining its physical cleanliness against the carelessness of visitors. Those who bow and prostrate are the worshippers who pray.

Abraham’s prayer for security and fruits for Mecca’s inhabitants was granted. The commentary argues that God would not quote an unaccepted prayer without indicating its rejection, since that would be vain mockery, incompatible with the truthfulness and dignity of His speech. Abraham’s many recorded prayers disclose his hopes, striving in God’s way, spiritual virtues, rank, and nearness to God.

When Abraham qualified his request for sustenance with “such of them as believe,” he knew that the town’s inhabitants would include unbelievers, that his request in its general form covered them too, and that he had dissociated himself from God’s enemies, even his own father. Although he also knew that the worldly order could not normally restrict provision to believers alone, he added the qualification. God granted the prayer for believers and extended provision to unbelievers, because withholding livelihood from the latter would unnecessarily disrupt the established order of this world.

Abraham did not merely ask that the believers of the town receive fruits, because he sought an attraction and honor for the town centered on the Sacred House. Since the House stood in a barren valley, it required food and fruits if people were to settle there. The two readings of “I will grant him enjoyment” have the same meaning. God’s response further honors the House and pleases Abraham: provision for unbelievers is not a sign of their honor before God, but an extension of Abraham’s accepted prayer and an honor for the town. Their enjoyment is brief, and they will then be driven to the Fire.

The commentary takes “raising the foundations” as an allegorical expression: the walls, raised upon the foundations, are counted as part of them, and the rising is attributed to the foundations although it is the walls that are raised. The direct appearance of Abraham and Ishmael’s prayer, without “they said” or a similar introduction, dramatically presents the scene as though their voices are heard while they build. This is a Qur’anic narrative style that brings an event before the senses more effectively than ordinary reporting. Their failure to specify the work they ask God to accept expresses humility: they regard their construction as an insignificant deed, unworthy of their Lord, while affirming that He hears their prayer and knows their intention.

The islām for which Abraham and Ishmael pray is not the elementary submission that distinguishes an outward convert from an open rejecter and consists in professing faith and performing required deeds, whether sincerely or hypocritically. As prophets, Abraham and Ishmael already possessed that grade; Abraham was even commanded to become Muslim when he was already Muslim (2:131). Nor is it fitting to ask God for what lies simply within human power, except under a special condition requiring Divine intervention. Islām therefore has grades, and the islām sought here is total servitude and unconditional surrender of everything a servant possesses to his Master.

A person may prepare for this sublime islām, yet the average person cannot attain it amid the ordinary conditions of heart and mind, because the necessary conditions are beyond him. Like lofty stages of al-wilāyah and other perfections, it may thus be regarded as a Divine gift for which one may rightly pray. Moreover, while voluntary acts are attributed to a human being, enduring qualities and traits formed in the soul through repeated acts are beyond his power and should especially be attributed to God when they are virtuous. This accords with the Qur’anic manner of asking God to establish prayer, join one with the good, grant gratitude and good deeds, and make one submissive.

Likewise, “show us our ways of devotion” does not mean teach them duties or assist them in acts they have yet to perform. Al-manāsik denotes acts of worship that they were performing or had performed; “show us” means strengthening them by disclosing the realities of those acts. Their request thus concerns a sublime islām and insight into worship, not their ordinary meanings. Their request that God “turn to us mercifully” is also not a plea for forgiveness of sin: Abraham and Ishmael, as prophets protected by God from error and sin, did not require the pardon needed by sinners.

The commentary considers the objection that their offspring might have been intended to receive only the elementary grade of islām. Such a reading might seem plausible because the offspring are mentioned separately, and outward islām has legal and social effects: one who professes the two testimonies is treated as Muslim, with life protected and the rules of marriage and inheritance applied. On this view, the prophets would seek the highest islām for themselves and the elementary grade for a community containing hypocrites, weak believers, and firm believers.

Al-Mizan rejects this distinction. The plane of legislation differs from that of invocation. In legislation, the Prophet set a minimum outward standard to enlarge the circle of islām and preserve the religious order; manifest islām protects its inner reality as a shell protects its kernel. Prayer, however, seeks reality, truth, and nearness to God, where appearances have no value. Abraham’s prayer for his progeny was not worldly attachment: otherwise he would have prayed first for his father and would not have repudiated him once he knew him to be God’s enemy. Thus, when Abraham asks for a group from his offspring “submitting to Thee,” he seeks the reality rather than the outward appearance of islām. The addition “to Thee” confirms this, for it would be unnecessary if mere formal submission were meant.

Finally, the prayer for a messenger from within that group—one who recites God’s communications, teaches the Book and wisdom, and purifies them—was a prayer for the Prophet. The Prophet himself used to say: “I am the prayer of Abraham.”
verses.130: Al-Mizan states that only one who makes himself foolish turns away from Abraham’s religion; God chose Abraham in this world, and he will be among the good ones in the hereafter.
verses.131: Al-Mizan says he submitted to the Lord of the worlds when his Lord said, ‘Submit.’
verses.132: Al-Mizan states that Abraham and Jacob enjoined their sons to remain Muslims until death, because Allah had chosen this faith for them.
verses.133: Al-Mizan recounts that, as Jacob neared death, he asked his sons whom they would worship. They pledged to worship his God and the God of Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac: one God, to Whom they submitted.
verses.134:
Al-Mizan first states that the community which has passed away is accountable for what it earned, while later people are accountable for their own deeds and not for its deeds.

It explains that al-raghbah with ʿan means turning away or disliking, while with f it means inclining toward or desiring. Whether safiha is read transitively, with nafsahu as its object, or intransitively, with it as a specification, the result is the same: one who abandons Abraham’s religion is foolish, unable to distinguish his benefit from his harm. This accords with the tradition that wisdom is that by which the Beneficent is worshipped.

Al-Iṣṭifāʾ, God’s choosing, means selecting the best part from what is mixed. In relation to al-wilāyah, it corresponds to the sincerity of servitude: the chosen person is wholly surrendered to his Lord in all affairs and gladly accepts His decision. Thus selection is not distinct from islām, total surrender, and verse (2:131) explains Abraham’s being chosen: he was chosen when commanded to submit and answered, “I submit myself to the Lord of the worlds.”

The shift from “We chose him” to “his Lord said to him,” rather than “We said,” indicates a confidential conversation between God and Abraham at a station from which others were excluded. Abraham, despite this exclusive grace, did not address God with familiarity or regard himself as worthy of such nearness. In humility, as a powerless servant sustained by his Master’s grace, he submitted to the Lord before Whom all worlds surrender.

Al-Islām, al-taslīm, and al-istislām all mean submission that does not disobey or oppose. Surrender to God entails accepting both His creative measures and decrees and His legislative commands and prohibitions; consequently, islām differs in degree. The first stage is outward acceptance of the commandments through the al-shahādatayn, whether or not faith has entered the heart. The first stage of al-īmān is sincere belief in those testimonies, accompanied by faithful obedience to most of the shariah’s rules.

The second islām is sincere, detailed acceptance of all true beliefs, necessarily accompanied by good deeds, though occasional slips remain possible. It is followed by a second īmān: detailed and reasoned belief in the realities of religion, free from doubt and joined to striving with wealth and life in God’s way. From this arises the third islām, in which intellect and spirituality subdue the animal faculties, worldly desires are controlled, worship is performed as though God were seen, and nothing inward resists His commands or resents His decree. The third īmān follows it, marked by such qualities as humility in prayer and avoidance of vain matters. This is the stage meant by Abraham’s answer of submission; its concomitants include contentment with the Divine Decree, obedience, patience and forbearance for God’s sake, self-denial, piety, and loving and hating for His sake. Sometimes the second and third stages are counted as one.

The fourth islām comes when Divine grace unveils the reality that the Kingdom belongs wholly to God: nothing possesses independent existence, attributes, or acts, except as God bestows something upon it. This is a Divine gift, not an attainment available through personal will or effort. It is probably the islām for which Abraham and Ishmael prayed in (2:128). By contrast, the command to Abraham in (2:131) was legislative: received early in his life, it was answered by his free choice and obedience. His later prayer sought either what was beyond his power or steadfastness in it.

The fourth īmān follows this gift when its reality permeates every condition and act. It is certainty that nothing is independent of God and that no cause acts except by His permission; therefore its possessors neither grieve at calamity nor fear impending danger.

Al-Ṣalāḥ literally denotes capability or fitness. Regarding deeds, a good deed is fit for God’s honour, His pleasure and reward, and for raising good words to Him. Regarding persons, “the good ones” are a selected group among the pious, admitted into an exclusive mercy distinct from the general mercy encompassing all things and from the mercy specially ordained for the pious. Their goodness is also not merely the general honour of al-wilāyah, which prophets, truthful ones, and martyrs share. Its distinctive feature is that God takes the good one into His special mercy and grants comprehensive security from chastisement.

Because God Himself attributes this goodness to persons, and recompense ordinarily corresponds to deeds, personal goodness is a special honour that cannot be earned by deeds or attained by one’s own choice. “They have therein what they wish and with Us is more yet” may distinguish the reward of deeds from an additional gift of pure Divine mercy. Goodness has ranks. Although Abraham was already among the good ones in this world, his prayer to be joined to the good ones shows that a group had preceded him; his request was granted in the hereafter. Al-Mizan concludes that this group was Muḥammad and his purified progeny: Muḥammad already claimed this goodness and its wilāyah, whereas Abraham prayed to be joined to those who possessed it.

Abraham’s and Jacob’s injunction in (2:132) concerns the same religion. Since death itself lies beyond human control, “die not unless you are Muslims” means: remain Muslims continually, so that whenever death arrives you are Muslim. It also indicates that religion is Islām.

On (2:133), Al-Mizan notes that “father” is correctly used for a grandfather, an uncle, and a biological father; it therefore supports calling an uncle “father.” “One Allah only” removes the possible notion, held by idol-worshippers, that Jacob’s God differed from the God of his fathers or that there were multiple gods. The sons’ submission concerns their worship: they will worship God wholly in accordance with Islām. Their reply shows that Abraham’s religion, inherited by Isaac, Jacob, Ishmael, and their descendants among the Children of Israel and Ishmael, was Islām alone; no one was entitled to turn away from it or summon people to another religion.
verses.135: Al-Mizan rejects the call to become Jews or Christians and affirms adherence to Abraham’s upright religion, free of polytheism.
verses.136: Al-Mizan professes belief in Allah; in what was revealed to the Muslims and to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes; in what was given to Moses, Jesus, and all prophets; and in submission to Allah without distinguishing among them.
verses.137: Al-Mizan says that those who believe in like of what the believers believe are rightly guided, while those who turn away are in great dissension; Allah will suffice the believers against them, for He is Hearing and Knowing. This faith is the dyeing of Allah—the finest dyeing—and entails worshipping Him alone.
verses.138: Al-Mizan says that those who believe in like of what the believers believe are rightly guided, while those who turn away are in great dissension; Allah will suffice the believers against them, for He is Hearing and Knowing. This faith is the dyeing of Allah—the finest dyeing—and entails worshipping Him alone.
verses.139: Al-Mizan challenges their dispute concerning Allah, who is Lord of both parties: each has its own deeds, while the believers are sincere to Him.
verses.140: Al-Mizan challenges the claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Jacob, and the tribes were Jews or Christians: Allah knows better, and none is more unjust than one who conceals testimony received from Allah. Allah is not heedless of what they do.
verses.141:
Al-Mizan explains that the religion of Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and their descendants was Islam: the one religion of divine unity. Jewish and Christian sectarian divisions arose from their adherents’ desires, biases, and ambitions, which dyed God’s religion with innovations. Religion is one as its worshipped God is one, and Muslims must hold to Abraham’s original religion rather than the dissensions of the People of the Book.

The commentary holds that worldly change often corrupts religious life: extraneous matters are inserted, essential elements rejected, and worldly aims replace divine ones. Religion then acquires national or tribal coloring, innovations displace its original purpose, and what is evil is defended as virtue while virtue is abandoned. The Jews’ call to Judaism and the Christians’ call to Christianity are thus divergent claims arising from their own differences. The answer is adherence to Abraham’s upright religion, followed by all their prophets after him. Had Abraham’s religion contained later sectarian additions, he would have been a polytheist, because what is not from God cannot call to God but calls to something other than Him. Abraham’s religion contains nothing not from God.

Al-Mizan identifies the truth of (2:136) as belief in the one God and in all that the prophets brought, without distinction among them; this is Islam. Belief in the Creator is mentioned separately because it is a natural instinct and does not depend on prophetic proofs. The verse then affirms what was revealed to the Muslims—the Qur’an or its knowledge—what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, and Jacob, what was given to Moses and Jesus, and what was given to all prophets. Moses and Jesus are singled out because the address concerns Jews and Christians, who respectively call only to them; the final reference to the prophets prepares for the declaration that no distinction is made among any of them.

The difference between saying that revelation was “revealed” to the Muslims and the named patriarchs and “given” to Moses, Jesus, and the other prophets is significant. “Giving” can convey the basic idea but does not necessarily make revelation explicit. Since Jews and Christians claimed Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes for their respective religions, calling what they received merely “given” could have allowed the claim that they only followed what Moses or Jesus later received. Saying it was revealed to them establishes that they themselves brought a divinely revealed religion. No comparable misunderstanding arose concerning prophets before Abraham, whose religion neither group claimed, so their religion is described as having been “given.”

Al-Asbāṭ, like al-qabāʾil among the Ishmaelites, means tribes descended from one forefather. Israel had twelve tribes, each descending from one of Jacob’s twelve sons. “The tribes” may refer metaphorically to the groups, because prophets who received revelation came from them, or to the prophets as individuals; it does not include Joseph’s brothers, who were not prophets.

Al-Mizan says that “If then they believe in like of what you believe in” means that belief in what the Muslims believe brings right guidance. The word “like” is added to cut off dispute: an invitation simply to believe what Muslims believe could be met by the objection that they believed only what had been revealed to them. The formulation instead calls them to the same unadulterated truth and leaves no opening for obstinate argument, exposing that their own position is not pristine truth. Their refusal is al-Shiqāq—hypocrisy, disputation, and dissension. Allah’s sufficing the Messenger against them is a promise of help that was fulfilled; the same favour will be completed for the Muslim nation when God wills. The verse is parenthetic between the surrounding verses.

The “dyeing of Allah” is the divine colour of this belief, superior to the dyes of Judaism and Christianity that arise when religious dissension leads people off the right path. “And Him do we worship” grammatically states the condition and supplies the reason for this divine dyeing.

The commentary treats (2:139) as a rebuke of the People of the Book’s dispute with Muslims. Disputes between followers about a leader ordinarily arise because they follow different leaders; because each claims exclusive closeness to the same leader; or because one party alleges that the other’s bad conduct disqualifies it from following him. None applies here: both worship the same God; each party has its own deeds, so their deeds do not conflict; and Muslims are sincere in devotion to God. Their dispute therefore has no basis.

Regarding the claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Jacob, and the tribes were Jews or Christians, Al-Mizan says that God has informed both parties that Moses and Jesus and their books came after Abraham and these prophets. Concealing this testimony is especially unjust. The preferred meaning is concealing the known fact that the laws of Judaism and Christianity were sent after Abraham and the other named prophets. It is also possible that the testimony means God’s witness that those prophets had died long before the Torah and Gospel were revealed, but the first meaning better fits the context.

Finally, the dead community has what it earned, and later people have what they earn; disputing over the group to which others belonged brings no benefit, nor does silence about it bring harm. People should occupy themselves with what they will be questioned about. The verse is repeated because Jews and Christians excessively disputed this matter despite knowing that Abraham lived long before Judaism and Christianity existed. Discussion of prophets is nevertheless beneficial when it seeks their teachings and spiritual virtues, which is why the Qur’an recounts their histories and calls people to reflect on them.
verses.142: Al-Mizan says the foolish will ask why Muslims left their qiblah. East and West belong to Allah, who guides whom He likes to a straight path.
verses.143: Al-Mizan states that Allah made the community a medium nation, so that it might witness for the people and the Messenger might witness for it. The former qiblah distinguished followers of the Messenger from those who turned back; though difficult except for the rightly guided, it did not render their faith fruitless, for Allah is Affectionate and Merciful.
verses.144: Al-Mizan states that Allah saw the Messenger turn his face heavenward and directed him to a qiblah pleasing to him: the Sacred Mosque. All Muslims must face it wherever they are. Those given the Book know this command is truth from their Lord, and Allah is not heedless of what they do.
verses.145: Al-Mizan states that, even before every sign, those given the Book will not follow the Muslims’ qiblah; nor can the Messenger follow theirs, and they do not follow one another’s qiblah. Following their desires after knowledge has come would make one of the unjust.
verses.146: Al-Mizan states that those given the Book recognize him as readily as they recognize their sons, yet a party of them knowingly conceal the truth.
verses.147: The truth comes from the Lord, so one should not doubt it.
verses.148: Al-Mizan states that each has a direction to which he turns; people should therefore hasten to good works. Wherever they are, Allah will gather them all, for He has power over all things.
verses.149: Al-Mizan states that, from whatever place one comes forth, one must face the Sacred Mosque. This command is truth from the Lord, who is not heedless of what people do.
verses.150: Al-Mizan states that Muslims must face the Sacred Mosque wherever they are. This leaves people no argument except the unjust; Muslims must fear Allah rather than them. By it, Allah completes His favor and guides them on the right course.
verses.151:
Al-Mizan treats these verses as a single connected discourse on appointing the Kaʿbah as the Muslims’ qiblah. It rejects reports alleging a disorder in their sequence or mutual abrogation, because they conflict with the verses’ evident sense.

The anticipated objection to the change of qiblah comes from the Jews, attached to Bayt al-Maqdis and their former precedence in this religious symbol, and from the Meccan polytheists, ready to object to any new command. The preceding account of Abraham and Ishmael—their building and cleansing of the House, and their prayers for Mecca, the Prophet, and the Muslim community—prepared minds for the change. The change was a major post-hijrah command: it unified Muslims physically in worship and spiritually against divergent opinion. Al-Mizan characterizes the Jews, in particular, as resenting commands with a concrete material aspect while not caring to dispute merely spiritual rules.

Their implied challenge was whether replacing a qiblah prescribed for earlier prophets could be God’s command: either God would be abrogating His own law, which the Jews denied was possible, or the Muslims would have abandoned divine guidance. The answer is that no building, stone, object, or direction inherently possesses the right to be qiblah. All belong to Allah, who may command as, when, and how He wills, solely for human guidance, perfection, and welfare. The “fools” are the Jews and Arabian polytheists, called so for their unsound conception of divine law. The former qiblah is Bayt al-Maqdis, which the Prophet and Muslims had faced in Mecca and for a period after arriving in Medina; attributing it to the Muslims makes their departure from it seem more striking. East and West stand for all directions, which are fixed relative to celestial rising and setting. The indefinite ṣirāt indicates that nations differ in the paths by which their differing capacities attain perfection and happiness.

Al-Mizan reads the making of a “medium nation” in connection with the impending change of qiblah and guidance. It rejects an explanation of “medium” as a balance between materialist peoples devoted to bodily life and ascetic peoples devoted only to spirit. Though a religion balancing body and soul is true in itself, it does not explain witnessing: being a criterion between extremes neither gives a community knowledge of them nor explains why the Messenger witnesses over that community.

The Qur’anic witnessing in question is rather testimony on the Day of Judgment concerning people’s deeds and whether messengers conveyed their message. Such testimony presupposes seeing, in this life, realities that ordinary senses cannot grasp: not merely outward acts, but belief and unbelief, felicity and wretchedness, acceptance and rejection, submission and arrogance. Since people will be judged for what their hearts have earned, this witnessing belongs only to those whose affairs Allah directly manages and whom He enables to perceive hidden realities. The witnesses will testify for or against people, alongside other things connected with deeds—such as angels, time, place, religion, the Book, limbs, organs, senses, and hearts. Al-Mizan infers that these realities have a mode of life and perception appropriate to them, by which the particulars of deeds are impressed upon them; life need not resemble human life.

This rank cannot belong to every member of the ummah, nor even to all just and pious believers. It belongs to the pure friends of Allah, who are under His guardianship, receive His favor, and proceed on the straight path. Thus, calling the ummah witnesses means that witnesses arise within it, just as excellence attributed to the Children of Israel may belong to outstanding persons among them rather than every individual. The objection that all believers are called witnesses near their Lord is answered by the phrase “near their Lord”: it concerns a rank conferred on the Day of Resurrection and is general to believers of all nations, not a statement that every Muslim already possesses this witnessing in the world.

The community is “medium” because it stands between the Messenger and the people: connected to him on one side and to the people on the other. This position follows its being chosen, relieved of hardship in religion, and made Muslim in fulfillment of Abraham’s prayer. As those who submit without disobedience or arrogance, its members do not find divine rules burdensome. The Messenger precedes them because he guides, teaches, and purifies them; through this, Abraham’s prayer for a messenger who would recite the communications, teach the Book and wisdom, and purify his people is fulfilled. The community’s position between Messenger and people therefore directly grounds both kinds of witnessing; it is not a middle point between bodily and spiritual extremes.

The former qiblah was instituted to distinguish the follower of the Messenger from one who turns back upon his heels, an expression for evasion or dissension. “That We might know” may mean that the Messenger might know, in the plural idiom by which a superior speaks for himself and his subordinates; or it may refer to God’s knowledge accompanying a thing’s actual existence rather than His prior knowledge of all things. Mentioning “the Messenger,” rather than saying “you,” stresses that obedience to his messengership is what effects the separation. The qiblah “which you had” is Bayt al-Maqdis, not the Kaʿbah; the contrary reading would needlessly make each qiblah prescribed twice.

Divine legislation trains and perfects people by separating obedient submission from arrogance. The first qiblah accordingly served this test, even though the Kaʿbah was to become the final qiblah. Prayers made toward Bayt al-Maqdis remain valid: when Allah abrogates a rule, its validity ends from abrogation, not from its original institution. This is entailed by the assurance that faith would not be fruitless and manifests divine affection and mercy. Al-raʾfah denotes pity for an afflicted person, while al-raḥmah is more general mercy.

The Messenger’s turning of his face toward heaven shows that he awaited or hoped for a command concerning the qiblah and desired a qiblah specially prescribed for him; it does not imply dissatisfaction with Bayt al-Maqdis. Traditions on the occasion report that Jewish taunts over the Muslims’ facing the Jewish qiblah saddened him and led him to await revelation at night. Had revelation maintained the former direction, it would still have proved that he followed Allah’s command rather than Jewish imitation; there is never shame in obeying the Master. Yet the new command both answered the taunts and pleased the Messenger.

“Towards the Sacred Mosque” renders al-Shaṭr, literally “part of”; the intended part is the Kaʿbah. The expression parallels the previous orientation toward a part of the Remote Mosque, its known Rock, and preserves details lost by simply saying the Kaʿbah or Sacred House. The command first addresses the Messenger personally and then all Muslims, supporting reports that it came while he led a prayer and turned during it. The People of the Book know the command’s truth either through prophecies of Muḥammad’s prophethood or of the true Prophet facing the Sacred Mosque; Allah knows their concealment of this knowledge.

Their refusal to follow the new qiblah is not caused by ignorance or insufficient proof but by obstinacy, hatred of the religion, and desire. The Messenger, possessing clear proof from his Lord, cannot follow theirs; the wording may also be a prohibition expressed as a proposition. Jews face Bayt al-Maqdis and Christians the East, and neither follows the other because each follows its own desire. The singular warning against following their desires is addressed to the Prophet but intended for his ummah, and it identifies their recalcitrance as injustice. The People of the Book recognize the Messenger—not their Book—as unmistakably as their sons, through the prophecies in their scriptures, though some knowingly hide the truth. The shift from directly addressing the Prophet to referring to him in the third person emphasizes how manifest his truth is to them; the ensuing prohibition of doubt, though similarly singular, is likewise meant for the ummah.

Every nation has a qiblah prescribed according to its circumstances and needs; no direction possesses qiblah-status inherently or immutably. Rather than dispute this, people should hasten to and compete in good works, since Allah will gather all wherever they are and has power over all things. Al-Mizan adds that the statement may also extend to divine measure and decree in creative affairs and their corresponding legislation.

The command to face the Sacred Mosque applies firmly in Mecca and every other place. Although “from whatsoever place you come forth” has been read either as leaving any location and arriving at another, or as leaving a town—possibly Mecca—the decisive point is the universal obligation. Its verbatim repetition emphasizes observance in every condition, not merely in a list of locations.

The command has three stated benefits. First, because Jewish scripture indicated that the promised Prophet would turn from Bayt al-Maqdis toward the Kaʿbah, the change removes any valid Jewish argument that he was not the foretold Prophet. The unjust will nevertheless persist in arguing from desire, so Muslims must not fear them but fear Allah. Second, obedience contributes to completing divine favor through perfecting religion. Third, it offers hope of guidance to the straight path.

Al-Mizan records and rejects another exegete’s view that the promise to complete favor predicted the conquest of Mecca, the cleansing of the idol-filled Kaʿbah, and exclusive Muslim custody of it. The resemblance to wording concerning victory does not establish this: both passages use language of final purpose and promise future completion, neither announces its fulfillment; moreover, the qiblah verse addresses all Muslims whereas the other uses singular address to the Prophet and belongs to a different context. Fulfillment, if indicated by a verse, belongs instead to the declaration that religion was perfected and favor completed. Other verses likewise promise, rather than announce, completion of favor.

The sending of a messenger from among the community is a divine favor parallel to appointing the Kaʿbah as qiblah, and both answer Abraham and Ishmael’s prayer. The addressees can be understood at three levels: esoterically, the earlier submissive group entrusted with religion and its followers; literally, the Muslims among Ishmael’s descendants, identified as the Arabs of Mudar; and legislatively, all Muslims, Arab and non-Arab. The communications recited are the Qur’an’s words, not merely their meanings. Purification removes false beliefs such as polytheism and denial of true faith, base traits such as pride and avarice, and immoral actions such as murder, fornication, and intoxicants. Teaching the Book, wisdom, and what was previously unknown encompasses primary and secondary religious knowledge.

In a report of al-Qummi from Imam al-Ṣādiq, the Prophet faced Bayt al-Maqdis for thirteen years in Mecca and seven months after emigrating, then, while leading ẓuhr in the mosque of Banu Salim, Gabriel turned him toward the Kaʿbah after two rakʿahs; the remaining two were prayed toward it, occasioning the objection about the former qiblah. Al-Mizan notes numerous Sunni and Shiʿa reports of this kind, differing over timing, and judges the prevalent date—Rajab in the second hijrah, seventeen months after the migration—more likely correct.

Sunni reports say that, on the Day of Judgment, nations will deny that prophets conveyed their messages; Muḥammad’s ummah will testify for the prophets on the basis of Qur’anic information, and the Prophet will then testify to his ummah’s purity, justice, and probity. Al-Mizan accepts this only if the latter testimony is restricted to a selected group; it rejects an all-inclusive sense as self-evidently incompatible with the Qur’an and sunnah, given the oppression and tyranny within the ummah, and also rejects testimony founded on hearsay. A report from Imam al-Bāqir states that only imams and messengers are witnesses over people, since many in the general ummah could not be accepted as witnesses even in a trivial worldly case. Imam al-Ṣādiq similarly denies that all people of qiblah are meant; he identifies the witnesses as the ummah in which Abraham’s prayer was granted, the best and medium ummah. Another report from him, through his father from the Prophet, says Allah favored this ummah with the quality formerly given only to a prophet, namely witnessing over creatures; Al-Mizan finds it compatible when “ummah” is understood as that submissive group. A report of Imam ʿAlī calls the Messenger the witness of the witnesses and identifies the witnesses as the messengers.

Abu Baṣīr reports from the fifth or sixth Imam that Allah did command the Prophet to pray toward Bayt al-Maqdis; Al-Mizan takes this as confirming that the former qiblah was Bayt al-Maqdis. It cites a report from Imam al-ʿAskarī that the Meccans’ attachment to the Kaʿbah and the Medinans’ inclination to Bayt al-Maqdis made the respective contrary commands tests of who followed Muḥammad even against personal preference. These reports refute the interpretation that makes the Kaʿbah, rather than Bayt al-Maqdis, the qiblah “which you had.”

In a report of al-Zubayrī from Imam al-Ṣādiq, faith is wholly deed, with utterance itself one such deed; when Muslims asked about prayers toward Bayt al-Maqdis and those who had died praying so, Allah called prayer “faith” and assured its acceptance. The Imam concludes that guarding one’s limbs and fulfilling their obligations brings perfect faith, while falsehood or transgression concerning them leaves faith incomplete. Al-Mizan notes that, although the report places the assurance after the change, it does not conflict with the commentary. Another report in al-Faqīh, with a different nineteen-month dating, describes Gabriel turning the Prophet during ẓuhr and another Medina congregation turning during ʿaṣr, giving rise to the name Mosque of the Two Qiblahs; al-Qummi gives a similar account with the Banu Sālim location. A report from Imam al-Bāqir makes facing the qiblah in obligatory prayer necessary, such that turning away invalidates it; Al-Mizan says many widespread reports likewise connect the command to obligatory prayer.

Imam al-Ṣādiq, in al-Qummi’s report, explains that Jews and Christians recognized the Messenger through descriptions of Muḥammad, his companions, and his migration in the Torah, Gospel, and Psalms, but rejected him when he came. Al-Mizan notes a similar report in al-Kāfī from Imam ʿAlī. Many Shiʿa reports apply Allah’s gathering of people wherever they are to the companions of al-Qāʾim, some under the principle of the Qur’an’s “flow.” Two Sunni reports respectively interpret completion of favor as dying in Islam and entering the Garden.

Al-Mizan’s academic and historical discussion explains that the recurring need to face qiblah in prayer, slaughter, and other acts first led to rough estimation and then to geographical, astronomical, and trigonometric calculations based on longitude and latitude. The Indian Circle established a location’s meridian and its inclination from Mecca; later, the compass offered an easier method once that inclination was known. Both had defects. Early longitude estimates were less accurate than latitude estimates, because latitude could be measured by the North Pole’s altitude whereas longitude depended on timing shared celestial events across distant places with inadequate instruments and communication.

The discussion credits Shaykh Ḥaydar Qulī Sardār Kābulī’s Tuḥfat al-ajillah fī maʿrifat al-qiblah with modern recalculations and charts. It presents his finding that Medina lies at 24°57’ latitude and 39°59’ longitude, with an inclination toward Mecca of 0°45’, as showing that the niche of the Prophet’s Mosque exactly follows the original direction and thereby as a miracle of the Prophet. It also credits ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Baghāʾirī with charts for more than 1,500 towns. A compass does not exactly show qiblah because the magnetic and geographical poles differ, magnetic poles shift, and the magnetic North Pole lies about a thousand miles from the geographical North Pole. The discussion credits Ḥusayn ʿAlī Razm Ārā with calculating magnetic-geographical differences and qiblah inclinations for roughly one thousand towns, and inventing a compass intended to determine them accurately.

Finally, Al-Mizan explains qiblah sociologically. Human society arises from a divinely bestowed natural awareness that survival and development depend on collective effort. Its laws, values, leadership, ownership, customs, and traditions are outward symbols of inward ideas and ideals. Since Allah is free of matter and cannot be sensed physically, inner devotion must be expressed by material acts: prostration signifies abasement, bowing glorification, circumambulation self-sacrifice, standing in prayer divine greatness, and wuḍūʾ and ritual bathing spiritual cleansing for divine presence. Undivided attention to Allah is worship’s soul, and these representations sustain and perfect it.

Idolaters face their material objects of worship, but divine religions reject this as a path that diverts attention from Allah and risks polytheism, even if its original aim—embodying undivided attention—accords with human nature. Islam appoints the Kaʿbah as the universal direction of prayer, with further duties or encouragements to face it and prohibitions on facing it or turning one’s back to it in certain circumstances. Thus the Muslim is continually mindful of the House of Allah. Socially, one qiblah joins Muslims across places and times around a single point, displaying unity of belief, social connection, and Islamic brotherhood. Were this spirit to permeate their material and intellectual life, it would perfect society; the qiblah has preserved religious unity even amid the community’s divisions into groups, sects, and divergent ideologies.
verses.152:
Al-Mizan explains that this command follows three immeasurable favors bestowed on the Muslims: God sent them a prophet from among themselves, guided them to the straight path and highest perfection, and assigned them their own qiblah. The qiblah set their religion on its course toward perfection, unified their worship, and strengthened their religious and social virtues. They are therefore commanded to remember God through devotion and obedience, so that He remembers them through His favor, and to thank Him rather than be ungrateful, so that He increases His bounty and grace. This accords with: and remember your Lord when you forget and say: May be my Lord will guide me to a nearer course to the right than this (18:24); If you are grateful, I would certainly give you more; and if you are ungrateful, My chastisement is truly severe (14:7). Both verses preceded the qiblah verse.

Al-dhikr (remembrance) may oppose al-ghafiah, inattention or heedlessness. Inattention is not knowing what one already knows while the original knowledge remains in memory; remembrance, accordingly, is knowing what one knows. It may also oppose al-nisyān, forgetfulness, which is the cessation of knowledge from the mind; in this sense remembrance is the presence of knowledge in the mind. The latter is intended in and remember your Lord when you forget … (18:24).

Remembrance and forgetfulness also have distinctive effects for which the terms may be applied even without their actual mental states. One who fails to help a friend whose need he knows may be said to have forgotten him, despite remembering him. Verbal remembrance, such as reciting God's names, apparently belongs to this extended usage, since speech presupposes mental remembrance; if it is a real meaning, it is a lower degree of remembrance.

The commentary holds that remembrance has many degrees. The intensity in such commands as then remember Allah as you remember your fathers, rather a more intense remembrance (2:200) belongs to thought or feeling, not words. In (18:24), the command to say, “May be my Lord will guide me …,” directs the servant who has fallen to a lower rank through forgetting what he knew to remember his Lord and hope for a rank nearer the right course. Thus heartfelt remembrance has degrees, as does the presence of an idea in the mind.

Finally, “Remember Me” concerns God Himself. If remembrance is knowledge of knowledge, and ordinary knowledge is the attainment in the knower's mind of a thing's form and idea, it confines the known within the knower's mind. God cannot be known or remembered in that manner: He transcends describers and is not comprehended in knowledge. If the command uses remembrance literally rather than metaphorically, then human beings possess, or can possess, a kind of knowledge defined differently from ordinary knowledge.
verses.153: Al-Mizan urges believers to seek help through patience and prayer, affirming that Allah is with the patient.
verses.154: Al-Mizan says that those slain in Allah’s way are alive, although people do not perceive their life.
verses.155: Al-Mizan says that believers will be tested by fear, hunger, and losses of property, lives, and fruits. The patient are those who, when misfortune comes, say: “Surely we are Allah’s and to Him we shall surely return”; they are given good news.
verses.156: Al-Mizan says that believers will be tested by fear, hunger, and losses of property, lives, and fruits. The patient are those who, when misfortune comes, say: “Surely we are Allah’s and to Him we shall surely return”; they are given good news.
verses.157:
Al-Mizan reads these five verses as a single, harmoniously ordered revelation, apparently sent shortly before al-jihād was legislated. They prepare believers for recurrent, community-wide trials arising from their own monotheistic faith, rather than ordinary private hardships. Individual affliction permits one to draw upon the steadiness of others, but a calamity that overtakes a whole community can overwhelm collective judgment, courage, and social life. The envisaged trial is a conflict in which enemies seek to extinguish God’s light and the call of truth, while believers can spread true religion and just rule, and uproot falsehood, only through fighting. The verses therefore encourage fighting for Islam: martyrdom is not extinction but a desirable life, and patience and prayer enable believers to bear the coming burdens. Patience checks fear and disruption; prayer directs them to their Lord and places their affairs before the One to whom all power belongs.

The commentary calls patience one of the Qur’an’s most highly praised virtues and prayer one of its greatest acts of worship, repeatedly placed foremost among good deeds. Although both are means of assistance, this verse particularly singles out patience because its setting is hardship and struggle against enemies. Allah’s being “with” the patient is not merely the universal companionship by which He encompasses and governs all affairs; it is a special proximity of help and aid. Patience is thus the means of relief from distress.

Al-Mizan rejects the interpretation that martyrs are “alive” only through enduring fame and grateful remembrance. Such fame is not real life and cannot be the intended Divine truth. This reading reflects the materialist denial of life after death: having made death the end of perception, materialists must invent posthumous reputation as an imagined reward to persuade people to sacrifice themselves for country or other ideals. But if the person has perished, there is no one left to enjoy this alleged noble life. The phrase “but you do not perceive” also does not suit a meaning as publicly observable as fame. Moreover, the related description of martyrs as receiving sustenance from their Lord, rejoicing in His grace, and rejoicing for believers yet to join them depicts a real life.

It is possible that some Muslims knew of Resurrection while remaining uncertain about al-barzakh, the period between death and the Day of Resurrection; the verse could therefore affirm the martyrs’ life in al-barzakh. It speaks of true life rather than extinction: the life of bliss belongs to believers, whereas posthumous existence for unbelievers is described as perdition. Bodily senses perceive only the material side of worldly life and thus foster the common delusion that death is annihilation. The verse corrects this sensory judgment and consoles believers, so that death in God’s way—whether their own or that of those dear to them—does not shake their hearts. The separation is temporary in comparison with the martyr’s enduring grace and God’s pleasure.

The commentary takes the verse as clear proof that human beings remain alive in al-barzakh, where the dead are rewarded or punished until Resurrection. It reports and rejects the claim that the verse concerns only the martyrs of Badr. If death truly annihilated a person, preserving those martyrs alive would not be a miracle but an impossibility; and if their apparently slain and disintegrated bodies were merely a sensory delusion, no confidence could remain in sense-perception. It likewise criticizes the view of some scholars of traditions that unseen beings such as angels and believing souls are material but exceptional ethereal bodies, able to penetrate solid bodies and exempt from ordinary physical change solely by a special Divine will. By severing such things from cause and effect, that account would undermine intellectual principles and even the reality it seeks to preserve.

Other Qur’anic descriptions support al-barzakh: martyrs’ joy includes other believers, not only a limited group; the dead face a barrier until they are raised; angels are seen at death before the distinct Day of Resurrection; the confession of having undergone two deaths and two lives requires an intermediate life and death; and Pharaoh’s people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening before the Day of Resurrection, which has no morning or evening.

Al-Mizan further holds that this intermediate survival establishes the immateriality of the soul. The human being is not identical with the body: the body disintegrates, but the person continues in bliss or punishment according to traits, tendencies, and deeds acquired in worldly life, not according to bodily or social attainments. Qur’anic language of God taking souls completely at death and sleep, withholding some and sending others back, shows that the soul is distinct from the body. Likewise, when the angel of death takes a person completely, what is lost in the earth is the body, not the reality designated as “you.”

The soul is from God’s command, expressed by the instantaneous “Be,” and so is not bound by the gradual processes, time, and space that govern material things. Human bodily formation proceeds through material stages, but then becomes “another creation,” endowed with perception, will, thought, and effective action—activities that cannot arise from matter as such. The soul begins in connection with the body, as a fruit with its tree or a flame with its oil, though these comparisons are imperfect; at death it becomes wholly separate and independent of it.

The announced trials of fear, hunger, and loss explain why believers were told to seek help through patience and prayer and why martyrdom was described as life. Al-Mizan takes the immediate context to concern fighting in God’s way: al-jihād brings believers to the summit of virtue, strengthens upright religion, and requires patience, prayer, and confidence that sacrifice of wealth and life is neither forfeited nor fruitless. If believers prevail, they remain alive while their enemies’ unjust rule is destroyed; if they are killed, they remain alive and safe from that rule. In either event they attain one of two excellent outcomes. “Fruits” apparently means children or progeny, whose loss in fighting is especially grievous, although some exegetes interpret it as dates and “property” as other possessions.

The patient receive glad tidings whose greatness is initially left unspecified because it is guaranteed by God. They are defined not by merely uttering, or even merely understanding, the words, “Surely we are Allah’s and to Him we shall surely return,” but by penetrating their reality. al-Muṣībah is any event that befalls a person, though it is normally used for a distressing one. Genuine patience rests on knowing that God possesses the human being in a real sense: existence, faculties, actions, and every condition depend wholly upon Him, while the servant has no independent authority. Human ownership of self, children, possessions, faculties, and acts is only an apparent attribution permitted by God. Ultimately all such attribution returns to its original state, in which ownership belongs only to God. One who grasps this ceases to regard anything as independently his and therefore has no ground for fear, anguish, or grief at its loss; God may administer His own property as He wills.

Al-Mizan then explains that moral traits are formed through repeated corresponding acts until their knowledge becomes fixed in the soul. Courage, for example, is acquired by repeatedly facing danger, so that boldness becomes a settled disposition. It identifies two recognized systems of ethical training. The first pursues socially praised worldly qualities—honour, public esteem, security, prestige, or a lasting good name. Classical moralists, including Greek philosophers, followed this system. The Qur’an does not endorse it, because its standard is public approval and disapproval; even verses that appear to cite social consequences ultimately refer to reward or punishment beyond this world.

The second system directs attention to otherworldly reward and punishment, Divine measure and decree, and God’s names and attributes. It teaches that misfortune and prosperity occur by God’s permission, so a believer should not indulge in vain grief or joy over what could not have been averted or obtained otherwise. This does not abolish free will or make striving useless. A person’s voluntary acts are parts of the causes through which effects occur: hunger is not satisfied without eating, and it is foolish to expect effects while omitting their causes. Human power is neither irrelevant nor the sole sufficient cause, for innumerable causes, foremost among them the Divine will, affect events. Forgetting this produces conceit, pride, miserliness, excessive joy, sorrow, and grief. The Qur’an does not attribute indecency to Divine decree, since that would annul responsibility; but it attributes possessions and events to God where this prevents a person from imagining that his own power is independent and complete. This is the ethical system used by the prophets.

A third system, according to Al-Mizan, belongs exclusively to the Qur’an. It does not merely repel low traits; it removes every motive other than God. Since all might, power, and dominion belong to Allah, one who truly knows this has no reason to act for others’ notice, fear, hope, or reliance. Firm awareness that every being and attribute belongs to God leaves nothing independent of Him; it produces reliance, fear of God, strength, self-respect, self-sufficiency, and pure servitude, and turns the servant away from all other than the Eternal Truth. This knowledge is the import of the verses on patient believers’ return to Allah.

The commentary therefore distinguishes social ethics, which seek a lower sociological reality, from prophetic ethics, which seek real perfection and everlasting felicity, and from Islam’s training in the Absolute Reality—God Himself through uncompromising monotheism. It rejects a western orientalist’s assertion that Islam’s religious teachings are merely moral precepts shared by all religions: different knowledge and aims necessarily produce different results. This Islamic system has produced a distinguished social structure and many righteous servants, divine scholars, and friends of God. Because it rests on love of the Lord and preference for His will, its results may at times go beyond what social wisdom or the ordinary rational basis of general religious commandments approves; love has rules distinct from reason.

Finally, Al-Mizan distinguishes “blessings” from “mercy.” The plural blessings are a special form of mercy: God’s blessing is His merciful turning toward the servant; angels’ blessing is their turning toward a person as mediators of that mercy; and human blessing is turning humbly to the Lord in supplication. Mercy is the comprehensive Divine gift and bounty encompassing all things, while al-salāh is one particular mercy, which probably explains the plural “blessings” and singular “mercy.” Blessings stand to mercy as preliminaries to a result, as a glance to seeing, or as casting into fire to burning.

Their being “followers of the right course” is the result of the blessings and mercy, not simply another name for guidance. Mercy guides them to God; blessings are the preliminaries of that guidance; and following the right course is their subsequent acceptance and progress upon it. Though distinct in this sequence, all three are Divine mercy from another perspective. Like a host who receives a guest, guides him along the road, tends to every need, and finally brings him home, God’s comprehensive hospitality resembles mercy, its particular attentions resemble blessings, and the guest’s arrival resembles following the right course. The emphatic grammatical construction of the verse further indicates the lofty prestige and rank of these believers.
verses.158:
Al-Mizan explains that the Ṣafā and the Marwah are the two Meccan hills between which pilgrims perform al-saʿy, walking quickly seven consecutive times during ḥajj or ʿumrah. The Qur’an calls them “among the signs of Allah” not merely in the general sense in which all created things indicate their Creator, but because God has appointed them as places of worship and prescribed particular rites there. They therefore lead people to and remind them of God.

The clause, “so whoever makes a pilgrimage to the House or performs ʿumrah thereof, there is no blame on him to go round them both,” follows from their being Divine signs. Its purpose is to legislate al-saʿy as part of the Islamic shariah, not to declare it voluntary or non-obligatory. Since the hills are places appointed for God’s worship, worshipping Him there causes no blame. The Qur’an may enact an obligation through wording that does not, in isolation, explicitly express obligation, as in its descriptions of jihād, fasting, and shortening the prayer while travelling. Had the aim here been only to recommend al-saʿy, the verse would more suitably have expressed God’s approval of going between the two hills.

The wording for “go round them both” is used here for the journey between the hills, not necessarily for circumambulation around an object. Likewise, al-taṭawwuʿ, “doing good on one’s own accord,” is not linguistically confined to voluntary, non-obligatory deeds. Its root denotes acting willingly, the opposite of acting under dislike or compulsion; willingness is compatible with an obligatory act. The form signifies taking upon oneself the willing performance of good, though common usage may restrict it to supererogatory good deeds.

Al-Mizan presents three possible connections for the final clause, “and whoever on his own accord does good, then surely Allah is Grateful, All-knowing.” First, it may continue “whoever makes a pilgrimage,” supplying a general reason for legislating the walk after the particular reason that the hills are God’s signs; then voluntary good means obedience in general, not a non-obligatory deed. Second, it may begin a new sentence connected with the verse’s opening and refer specifically to going between the hills; then it indicates the desirability of al-saʿy. Third, it may refer to ḥajj and ʿumrah themselves, indicating the desirability of those two acts of worship.

“Grateful” and “All-knowing” are among God’s beautiful names. Gratitude ordinarily means that a beneficiary responds to a benefactor’s favor by praise or by using the gift in a pleasing way. God is the eternal Beneficent and the source of every beneficence, so no one can place Him under an obligation. Yet in His benevolence He treats His creatures’ good deeds as though they had done Him a favor, although those deeds are themselves His benefaction to them. He repays them with gratitude and further beneficence—a double beneficence. Thus “Grateful,” when applied to God, is used in its real, not allegorical, sense.
verses.159: Al-Mizan states that those who conceal the clear proofs and guidance revealed and made clear in the Book are cursed by Allah and by those who curse. But Allah turns mercifully to those who repent, amend their conduct, and make the truth manifest.
verses.160: Al-Mizan states that those who die in disbelief are under the curse of Allah, the angels, and all men.
verses.161:
Al-Mizan states that the cursed abide in it, without any lightening or postponement of their chastisement.

The commentary explains that “the guidance” is the religious knowledge and shariah that lead to eternal bliss, while “the clear proofs” are the revealed verses, signs, and arguments attesting to that guidance. Concealing them may consist either in withholding the verses themselves or in concealing their real meaning through misinterpretation and misapplication, as Jewish leaders did with verses foretelling the Prophet: what they did not know they hid, and what they knew they diverted from him.

That the truth was made clear “for men” means for all mankind, not the Jews alone. Since a general message cannot be individually delivered to everyone, those who know it are links by which it reaches the ignorant. A learned person who fulfills the pledge to explain revelation makes the truth clear to people; one who hides knowledge keeps it concealed. Such concealment causes religious disagreement and deviation. Religion accords with human nature and the discerning mind accepts it when it is clearly presented; lack of knowledge is therefore paired with religion’s naturalness in (30:30). The latter mode of clarification ultimately depends on the former, the purity of heart found in the prophets.

The commentary reads (2:213) as showing that disagreement over the Book arose through the revolt of those scholars who possessed its knowledge. Their concealment, alteration, and misinterpretation of revealed truth, and their injustice, bring religious deviation; this is the injustice described as hindering people from Allah’s way and seeking to make it crooked in (7:44-5). The present verse thus follows from (2:213) and announces the recompense of that revolt.

Allah’s curse is His removal of them from mercy and bliss, whereas the curse of those who curse is their prayer that Allah remove them from mercy and bliss. Because neither curse nor “those who curse” is restricted, every curse is directed to the revolters who conceal the Divine Proof and Guidance. True happiness is religious happiness, which Allah has fully explained and which nature accepts; only one who knows it and knowingly rejects and denies it can be deprived of it. One to whom it has not been clarified is not included. Learned people are pledged to disseminate the divine proofs and guidance they receive; concealing them effectively amounts to rejecting them. The following statement concerning those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers apparently either supplies the reason for, or intensifies, this same judgment.

Repentance is accepted only when accompanied by amendment and manifesting the truth. The former concealer must publicly announce both the truth formerly hidden and his previous concealment of it; otherwise, he still hides that concealment and is as though he has not repented.

Those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers are those who persist obstinately and arrogantly in belying Allah’s signs and guidance, including those who conceal what He revealed. A person who has not accepted true religion because it was never made clear to him is not truly a disbeliever, but is al-mustaḍʿaf: one without true faith who is not hostile to it, whose judgment rests with God. The frequent coupling of disbelief with belying, including in (2:39-40), supports this distinction.

Allah has decreed that every curse from angels or men attaches exclusively to these obstinate concealers. Like Satan, to whom God said, “And surely on you is curse until the Day of Judgment (15:35),” learned people who conceal their knowledge share in a general, unrestricted curse. The verse’s tone and meaning are therefore especially severe.
verses.162:
Al-Mizan explains that the change from “curse” to “chastisement” shows that the curse will become their chastisement on that Day.

The shifts between first-person divine speech and the name “God” match the verse’s purposes. “We revealed” and “We made it clear” become “God does curse” to display intense displeasure with maximum force, since no name is greater than God’s. The speech then returns to “I turn (mercifully)” to express the highest mercy and benevolence: God Himself turns mercifully to the repentant, an immediacy not conveyed by saying that God or their Lord turns to them. The following reference to “the curse of God” again uses the Divine Name for the same reason: to intensify the force of displeasure.
verses.163: Al-Mizan declares that Allah alone is God, the Beneficent, the Merciful.
verses.164: Al-Mizan presents the heavens and earth, night and day, beneficial ships, life-giving rain, animals, changing winds, and subservient clouds as signs for those who understand.
verses.165: Al-Mizan says that some take equals besides Allah and love them as they love Him, while believers love Allah more strongly. When the unjust see the chastisement, they will know that all power belongs to Allah and that His chastisement is severe.
verses.166: Al-Mizan says that, when chastisement is seen, those who were followed will repudiate their followers and all their ties will be severed.
verses.167:
Al-Mizan treats these verses as one connected discourse: they establish monotheism, provide its proofs, condemn polytheism, and describe its final result.

The statement that “your God is one God” reserves divinity exclusively for God in a manner fitting His sublime status. A thing may be called one in respect of an attribute while remaining multiple in other respects; but God is one in His divinity, knowledge, power, and life. His attributes are distinct only in verbal meaning, not in reality: they are His very person and are not separate or multiple as created attributes are. The commentary distinguishes this from the oneness of person denoted by al-aḥad, which means an essence that admits neither division nor multiplication.

The wording “your God is one God” is deliberate. To say merely that God is “one God” would not establish monotheism, since polytheists also counted each deity as one god; nor would “your God is one” exclude the possibility that He was one member of a species of gods. By making “one God,” in contrast to two or more gods, the predicate of “your God,” the verse restricts godhead to Him alone.

“There is no god but He” further removes every misinterpretation. Al-Mizan understands it to mean that no real, actual god other than God exists. It repudiates the supposed deities that exist only in their worshippers’ imaginations; it is not primarily an argument refuting other gods in order to prove God’s existence. The Qur’an treats God’s existence as self-evident and argues rather for such attributes as His oneness, creatorship, knowledge, and power. Nor is there room for a merely possible, transient being to be the ultimate cause of all things; alternatively, the implied predicate may be understood as “true” or “actual.” The names “the Beneficent, the Merciful” complete the meaning of Lordship: His Beneficence bestows every general bounty, and His Mercy grants the special favours of guidance and the bliss of the next world.

Verse (2:164) supplies the rational proof of the preceding declaration. The heavens and earth, the alternation of night and day, ships, rain, living creatures, winds, and clouds show that each of these phenomena has a God; that all belong to one God; that this God is also man’s God; and that He is the Beneficent giver of general bounty and the Merciful giver of ultimate happiness. Its purpose is not simply to combine all phenomena into a single sign of God’s existence or unity. Rather, the several phenomena are signs establishing these connected truths for people who understand.

First, the heavens, earth, and their regular changes necessarily require a Creator. Second, despite the vast diversity of the cosmos, from the greatest bodies to the smallest constituents, all things stand within an interrelated and uniform system governed by inviolable law. The same ordered design appears throughout the universe; there is no exception or chance in its comprehensive arrangement. Thus the universe has one Creator and Manager. Third, man is an earthly creature whose life and continuance depend upon this very unified system: celestial light and heat, the earth, day and night, winds, clouds, rain, and goods conveyed from place to place. The God who creates and manages the universe therefore creates and manages man. Since the next world is the destination of this abode, the One who manages an affair also manages its end, granting each thing what it needs for worldly happiness and, where it is qualified, for the bliss of the next world. This is the proof conveyed by the names the Beneficent and the Merciful.

The creation of the heavens and earth includes their bodies, forms, transformations, conjunctions, separations, and all that the earth produces. The alternation of night and day arises through the earth’s rotation and its revolution with its tilted axis; the differing lengths and intensities of daylight produce diverse earthly conditions from which people benefit. Ships carry beneficial cargoes and food between regions. Although made through human will and power, they too are ultimately God’s handiwork: man is not a sufficient cause and remains dependent on God’s will and permission, just as natural causes do. The human maker and a natural cause both receive their strength and capacity from divine creation; nothing is independent of God either in its existence or activity.

Al-Mizan therefore rejects the claim that humanly manufactured things cannot be attributed to God. Materialists argue that belief in a Creator arose from ignorance of natural and psychological causes, and will vanish as science discovers or produces them. The commentary replies that theists have always affirmed a creative cause for the whole universe, including phenomena with known natural causes. The universe, as a complete network of causes and effects, depends on a Cause above and encompassing it; this does not deny the operation of particular natural causes or place the Supreme Cause merely at the top of their chain. Materialists are consequently rejecting something other than the theistic claim, and contradict themselves when they hold all events, including human actions, to be compelled by causes but exempt a man’s creation of another man from ultimately depending on the Cause of the universe.

Likewise, philosophers first establish the all-pervasive causal order and then show that transient, possible causes must terminate in an essential, self-existent Cause; they do not invoke God merely where a natural cause is unknown. The Qur’an affirms both particular causes and human voluntary acts, yet ascribes without exception all things and happenings to God. God creates human beings and what they make, while human acts remain truly attributable to their agents. His measuring of everything means that He has set things within the limits of material causes, time, and space. The error of assigning unknown effects directly to God, while making voluntary actions independent of Him, is attributed to imprecise religious argument. Some Muslim traditionalists and theologians similarly deny that sinful human products can be ascribed to God. Al-Mizan answers that voluntary acts and their products may be attributed to God in a manner befitting Him. An idol, considered as a shaped stone or metal, is God’s creation; considered as an object worshipped besides Him, it is attributed to Satan or man. The same distinction applies to other human products.

Rain is part of a regulated system in which water rises, condenses or freezes, returns to the earth, and is stored or flows in streams and rivers. Since water is the source of life and the growth of plants and animals depends on it, rain both points to a Creator and shows that the God of rain is the God of man. Winds, produced through natural factors especially the sun’s heating of air, aid pollination, cleanse the atmosphere, and carry rain clouds; they likewise indicate a Creator, the unity of the universal Creator, and His lordship over human life. Clouds are condensed vapour made subservient in their movement and rain through winds, temperature, and other factors by God’s permission. Together, day and night, rain, winds, and subservient clouds form the principal terrestrial phenomena underlying the life of plants, animals, and human beings. The “understanding” required here is al-ʿaql: perfect comprehension by which man distinguishes good from evil, truth from falsehood, and fact from fiction. It is the perceiving person himself, not merely one faculty of the soul.

Those who take “equals” besides Allah violate the exclusive divinity already established, knowingly following base desire rather than reason. The term includes not idols alone, but angels, human beings worshipped besides God, and everyone obeyed without divine authority; the following verse’s reference to leaders and followers confirms this scope. The verse also establishes that love of God is real, not merely a metaphor for obedience. Love varies in strength, and believers are stronger in their love for Allah; if love meant only obedience, no comparison could be made with the supposed obedience given to false gods, which is no obedience before God.
