The condemnation, however, is not of love as such or simply of loving God less. It concerns the following that results from love. The polytheists follow their false objects of worship because they imagine them to possess power to obtain desired things or repel harm; they thereby abandon the truth wholly or in part, and one who follows God only in some matters is not truly His follower. A person must not give God a partner in this love. Stronger love of God means exclusively obeying His commands and not following another independently of Him.

Love for one whose obedience is itself obedience to God is not censured. Thus love of the Messenger, whom God commands people to obey, is one with love of God. The same applies to the Prophet and his progeny, divinely guided scholars, the Book of God, the traditions of His Prophet, and every sincere means that brings one to God’s remembrance. Loving and following them draws one nearer to God, and honouring divinely approved signs that remind one of Him is part of piety. Yet none of these signs may be regarded as independent of God or as possessing independent control over benefit, harm, life, death, or resurrection; such a belief turns them from God’s signs into equals of God and becomes al-shirk.

The wish that the unjust could see means that they would see, in this world, the day on which they witness the chastisement and realize that all power belongs wholly to Allah. They will then recognize the grave error of assigning power to their false deities and the severity of God’s punishment for their polytheism and wrongdoing. Those who followed will receive none of the benefit they expected from their leaders. The leaders will renounce them, their ties will be cut off, and no power or effect will remain besides God. The followers will wish to return to the world so that they might renounce those whom they had taken as equals and followed, just as those leaders have renounced them. God will show them their deeds—their love and obedience toward these leaders—as intense regret, and they will not emerge from the Fire. Al-Mizan takes this last statement as evidence against those who maintain that the chastisement of the Fire will eventually end.
verses.168: Al-Mizan commands all people to eat the lawful and good things of the earth and not follow Satan’s footsteps, for he is their open enemy.
verses.169: Al-Mizan says that Satan enjoins only evil, indecency, and speaking against Allah without knowledge.
verses.170: Al-Mizan rebukes those who, when called to follow Allah’s revelation, unconditionally follow what they found their fathers doing, even if their fathers had neither understanding nor right guidance.
verses.171:
Al-Mizan explains that al-ḥalāl denotes freedom from prohibition, while al-ṭayyib denotes what is agreeable, as opposed to what is bad or evil. Satan’s “footsteps” are the ways leading to his aim of misleading people through polytheism and taking them away from God; he enjoins through insinuations and temptations. Evil and indecency concern actions, whereas speaking against Allah without knowledge concerns speech.

The command is addressed to all people. It rejects the self-imposed food taboos of polytheists, who falsely attributed them to God, and cautions that inherited myths and superstitions may persist even among believers if remnants of an old system are allowed to mix with the new one. “Eating” may include the general use and usufruct of earthly bounties. The verse therefore grants a general, unrestricted permission to use what is lawful and good in the earth, except what other proofs exclude. Such use must have no impediment in the thing itself or in human nature; something acquired unlawfully, for example, is rejected by one’s nature.

The prohibition against Satan’s footsteps covers both abstaining from food and consuming it on Satanic grounds. One may abstain only where God approves the abstinence, and may use things only by God’s permission; this verse and similar ones provide that general permission, while one must ascertain that a particular thing has not been forbidden. To abstain from what God has made lawful without proof is to legislate for oneself against God’s law. Following Satan’s footsteps is thus worshipping God by a manner He has neither allowed nor approved. Although the stated rationale implies that one should neither act nor refrain without knowledge, the commentary says that this is not the precise point of the verse, since it is following Satan rather than following his footsteps.

The appeal to ancestral practice in (2:170) confirms this explanation. It is irrational because it is an unconditional commitment to follow forefathers without considering whether they possessed knowledge or right guidance. There would be no blame in following forefathers in matters in which they were known to have knowledge and guidance. The verse does not hyperbolically deny that the fathers knew anything at all; rather, it exposes the absurd consequence of the unconditional claim by presenting a case in which no one would permit such following.

For (2:171), Al-Mizan says that the Prophet’s call to unbelievers resembles a shepherd calling animals that hear only a sound and do not understand its meaning. They are deaf to beneficial speech, dumb in not uttering sensible words, and blind to what is worthwhile; their means of understanding are closed. It appears that the parable contains a reversal: though ascribed to the disbelievers, it initially describes the caller to guidance, that is, the Prophet. Yet it is appropriately assigned to the disbelievers because “deaf, dumb [and] blind, so they do not understand” describes them, not the caller.
verses.172: Al-Mizan says: Believers should eat Allah’s good provision and thank Him alone, for they worship Him alone.
verses.173: Al-Mizan says that only what dies of itself and what has been invoked in the name of other than Allah are forbidden. One compelled to eat them without revolt or excess incurs no sin, for Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
verses.174: Al-Mizan says that those who conceal Allah’s revealed Book for a small price eat only fire; on the Day of Resurrection Allah will neither speak to nor purify them, and they will suffer a painful chastisement.
verses.175: Al-Mizan says: They have bought error for guidance and chastisement for forgiveness; how bold they are to endure fire.
verses.176:
Al-Mizan states that Allah revealed the Book with the truth, and that those who differ concerning it stand in great opposition.

The commentary says that the address now turns from people generally to the believers, who are expected to hear and accept God’s call. It appears as though God turns away from an intractable, self-opinioned group impervious to reason and addresses those who believe in Him. Accordingly, “the good things that We have provided you with” is a more loving expression than the earlier impersonal command to people generally to eat the lawful and good things of the earth. By speaking directly of what He has provided, God is shown as known and near to believers, affectionate and compassionate toward them; this prepares the command to thank God alone as monotheists.

Apparently, the construction of “the good things that We have provided you with” means that God’s provision is all good. It does not distinguish good provisions from bad ones, since the point is to remove prohibition and prevent believers from abstaining from any provision God has given them. Such abstention would be self-imposed, unauthorized legislation and speech without knowledge. Similarly, the wording “give thanks to Allah,” rather than “give thanks to Us,” suits the theme of monotheism, while “if Him it is that you worship” confines worship to God alone.

Invoking a name other than God’s means slaughtering for something other than Him, such as sacrificing for idols. The concession for one forced by emergency to eat forbidden things applies when he is neither unjust nor exceeding the limit and does not wish to oppose God’s law. If his own revolt or excess caused the necessity, he may not eat them. Allah’s being Forgiving and Merciful shows that this is a concession to believers, while the basis of prohibition remains even in such a case.

The commentary identifies those who conceal the Book for a small price with the People of the Book, whose elders and leaders arbitrarily prohibited many good and lawful things despite the Book’s containing no such prohibition. They concealed this in order to preserve their status and prestige and to retain the gifts, wealth, and property flowing to them through their authority.

Al-Mizan holds that the verse unambiguously proves that deeds are embodied, take bodily form, and emerge as their own results. Concealing revelation for a price is described as eating fire; it is then portrayed as buying error for guidance, bartering chastisement for forgiveness, and finally as boldness in enduring fire. Thus, their misdeed itself is transformed into the fire.
verses.177:
Al-Mizan relates that this verse was revealed amid the public controversy following the change of qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Kaʿbah. It rejects the idea that righteousness lies in merely facing East or West. Rather than defining righteousness abstractly, the Qur’an describes the righteous themselves, showing that ideals have value in Islam only when embodied in a person’s character. Its description proceeds through belief, deeds, and morals: belief begins with faith in Allah, the last day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets; the righteous are then called true; and finally they are called pious.

The faith intended is complete faith in all the true gnosis God requires. Such faith necessarily produces its effect: the believer is not overtaken by doubt or confusion, does not resent what befalls him, and is protected in morals and action from adverse influences. The unrestricted statement, “these are they who are true,” means that they are genuine believers in every respect, like those who submit without inward constraint to the Prophet’s judgment (4:65). Thus, they belong to the fourth stage of belief, exemplified in: When his Lord said to him, Submit [yourself], he said: I submit myself to the Lord of the worlds (2:131).

Their deeds include giving wealth, out of love for Him, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the stranded wayfarer, beggars, and for freeing captives; keeping up prayer; and paying zakāt. Prayer concerns Divine worship, while zakāt is a financial obligation established for the economic good of society. Voluntary spending precedes the mention of zakāt because it broadens beneficence so that the poor’s needs may be met and their condition improved. The needy, al-masākīn, are in worse circumstances than the poor, al-faqīr; ibn al-sabil is one stranded on a journey; and al-riqāb refers to slaves. Distress denotes hardship or poverty, affliction includes such losses as illness, injury, or loss of property or child, and conflict denotes the intensity of war.

The moral qualities named are fulfilment of promises and patience in distress, affliction, and conflict. “Their promise” includes every commitment a person undertakes—statements, transactions, and social and family dealings—but does not mean faith itself or the consequent duty to follow the shariah. The qualifying words “when they make a promise” show this, since accepting true faith and submitting to its requirements are unconditional obligations, not dependent on a person’s voluntary undertaking. Patience is steadfastness before overwhelming misfortunes and formidable enemies. Although these two qualities do not enumerate every virtue, the commentary holds that the others invariably accompany them: patience is passive endurance, while fulfilling a promise is active; together they mean that people carry out what they say and do not retreat even under hardship.

Truth is a comprehensive virtue encompassing knowledge and action, inseparable from the basic virtues of continence, bravery, wisdom, justice, and their branches. Human life consists of belief, speech, and action; in the truthful person, action conforms to speech and speech to belief. Since man inwardly accepts right and truth, truthful belief in the right perfects faith, character, and deeds. The restrictive expression “these are they who are true” therefore identifies the righteous as the true ones. Likewise, “these are they who are the pious” concerns perfection: complete piety is impossible until righteousness and truth are complete.

Al-Mizan finds the same attributes and destination in other Qur’anic descriptions of the righteous: they believe in God and the last day, spend for His sake, fulfil vows, and endure patiently (76:5-12); they are in bliss and among those drawn near to Allah (83:18-28). They are God’s servants, over whom Satan has no authority (15:42), and the foremost drawn near to Allah in the gardens of bliss (56:10-12). Consequently, the righteous are foremost in drawing near to God in this world and foremost in receiving the garden’s bounties in the next. They stand at the highest, fourth stage of belief, among those who do not mix faith with iniquity and thus have security and guidance (6:82).

Finally, the accusative form of “the patient,” unlike the indicative forms of the other attributes, is taken as a deliberate indication of patience’s excellence and importance. It has also been said that Arabic may alter case in a long succession of adjectives to break its monotony.
verses.178:
Al-Mizan explains that the command concerning retaliation is addressed to believers and thus legislates for Muslims; the verse is silent concerning non-Muslims, whether protected by an Islamic state or otherwise. Its specification of the free, slave, and female does not abrogate verse 5:45 (life is for life), but explains its text. al-Qiṣāṣ means retaliation because it follows the offender’s act with a corresponding punishment.

Remission is granted to the murderer when the slain person’s heir or heirs waive their right of retaliation. The word “anything” includes full or partial remission: if only some among several heirs remit, retaliation no longer applies and blood-money is due. Calling the aggrieved heir the murderer’s “brother” is intended to stir love and kindness and indicates that God highly prefers forgiveness. After remission, the heir must seek the blood-money according to usage, while the murderer must pay it well and without vexing delay. This commutation is a merciful alleviation from God, but once made cannot be revoked: an heir who later retaliates has exceeded the limit and incurs painful chastisement.

Al-Mizan holds that remission and blood-money are merciful concessions, but that public welfare and social peace depend on retaliation itself; it alone guarantees life and guards people against murder. Retaliation, rather than killing as such, produces life, since unjust killings negate life. It also includes reprisals for injuries and other offenses, and its very name indicates that the punishment answers an unjust act.

The commentary further reports that scholars regard “and there is life for you in the retaliation” as exceptionally concise, clear, eloquent, and forceful, surpassing pre-Islamic sayings such as “Killing stamps out killing.” By using the definite “the retaliation” and the common noun “life,” it shows that the resulting good is broader than the prescribed punishment. It states plainly both the purpose—life—and the means—retaliation; exhorts people to claim the life reserved for them; and, by saying “for you,” makes clear that the Lawgiver seeks only their interest and gains no benefit thereby.
