verses.180: Al-Mizan: When a person who leaves wealth nears death, he must make a customary bequest for parents and near relatives—a duty upon those who guard against evil.
verses.181: Al-Mizan: Whoever alters a bequest after hearing it bears the sin; surely Allah is Hearing, Knowing.
verses.182:
Al-Mizan explains that the wording of (2:180) indicates an obligatory rule: al-kitābah, rendered “prescribed,” is used in the Qur’an for definitely obligatory laws, and “a duty” likewise denotes a compulsory order. Yet its qualification, “upon those who guard (against evil),” somewhat weakens this force; if it were simply obligatory, “upon the believers” would have been more fitting. It is said that the inheritance verse later abrogated this ruling; if so, only its obligation was abrogated, while its recommended character remained. Perhaps the qualifying phrase was used for this purpose. al-Khayr means wealth, probably substantial rather than insignificant wealth, and al-Maʿrūf denotes what is known or customary in good and favour.

For (2:181), “the sin of it” refers to alteration, while the other pronouns refer to the bequest made according to usage. Because bequest is a maṣdar that may be masculine or feminine, the masculine pronouns are used. By saying that sin rests “upon those who alter it,” rather than simply “upon them,” the verse identifies the particular sin as altering a will and prepares for the following exception.

Al-Mizan takes al-Janaf in (2:182) to mean deviation or inclination towards sin and disobedience, as shown by its pairing with “an act of disobedience.” The verse qualifies the preceding one: the sin belongs to one who alters a bequest made according to usage. But, God knows best, if someone fears that a testator’s bequest is or will become disobedient or deviate toward a wrong course, and reconciles the parties without error or sin, he incurs no blame. He has not altered a sound bequest; he has altered only the wrong and sin within it.
verses.183: Al-Mizan states that fasting, prescribed as it was for earlier peoples, is meant to foster guarding against evil. It is required for a limited number of days; the sick and those on a journey must make up an equal number later, while those able only with difficulty must feed a poor person as redemption. Willing performance of good is better, and fasting is for the believers’ benefit.
verses.184: Al-Mizan states that fasting, prescribed as it was for earlier peoples, is meant to foster guarding against evil. It is required for a limited number of days; the sick and those on a journey must make up an equal number later, while those able only with difficulty must feed a poor person as redemption. Willing performance of good is better, and fasting is for the believers’ benefit.
verses.185:
Al-Mizan maintains that the three verses form one connected revelation whose single purpose is to legislate the fast of Ramaḍān. Grammatically, “the month of Ramaḍān” explains the “counted number of days,” whether it is treated as the predicate of an understood subject, the subject of an understood predicate, or an alternative to “fasting.” The first two verses are not the original promulgation of the law but a deliberate preparation for the final command, “so whosoever of you witnesses the month, he shall fast therein.” They calm resistance to a naturally burdensome duty by recalling that earlier peoples also fasted, promising piety, stressing that the days are few, and setting out concessions. Unlike retaliation and bequest, which accord with powerful natural feelings, fasting denies food, drink, and sex and therefore requires such preparation if people are to receive it willingly.

The address “O you who believe” recalls the believers’ faith so that they will accept divine commands despite desire and habit. Kitābah, literally writing, here denotes prescription, enjoinment, and an irrevocable decision. Siyām and ṣawm originally mean abstention from an act; in religious usage fasting chiefly means abstaining, with intention (niyyah), from specified things between dawn and sunset. “Those before you” denotes adherents of preceding revealed religions, not necessarily every prior community or every detail of their fasting. The comparison concerns only the principle of abstention, not its duration, rules, or particulars. Although the present Old and New Testaments praise rather than explicitly make fasting obligatory, Jews and Christians have observed various fasts; the Qur’an also relates the abstention from speech of Zachariah and Mary. Fasting was likewise found in unrevealed religions, which apparently reflects a natural human recognition that it draws one near the Creator. Restricting “those before you” to Jews and Christians, or to prophets alone, rests on weak traditions.

The purpose, “so that you may guard yourselves,” is piety, not a bargain with God. Idolaters fasted to placate deities, avert their anger, or obtain requests; but God has no need, emotion, or deficiency. The good or evil of worship and sin returns to human beings themselves. Piety requires restraining material desires and worldly attachment so that one is not drawn away from the Lord. Abstaining even from lawful desires—food, drink, and sex—especially trains ordinary people to abstain from unlawful things, obey God, and approach Him.

“Counted days” both makes the duty appear light and indicates that the prescribed number is integral to it; the days are the month of Ramaḍān. Al-Mizan rejects the claim that the phrase originally meant three days each month plus ʿĀshūrāʾ and was later abrogated by the Ramaḍān fast. A communal practice of that kind would have been securely recorded, whereas the traditions offered are mutually contradictory. It further calls the alleged obligation or desirability of fasting ʿĀshūrāʾ an Umayyad innovation: after Karbalāʾ, the Umayyads made the day auspicious, treated it as an ʿīd, and fabricated its supposed virtues and antiquity, though it has neither an appropriate national, historical, nor religious basis. Contextually, the third verse clarifies the first two and cannot have descended separately to abrogate them; even if it were an independent sentence, no contradiction would exist to permit abrogation. The further claim that “counted days” itself abrogated the original prescription is still more untenable, since the second verse plainly continues and completes the first.

For sickness or journey, the fast of Ramaḍān is waived but the same number must be fasted afterward. The wording “on a journey,” rather than “a traveller,” requires present travel, not travel completed or merely intended. Against the predominant Sunni view that the sick person or traveller may choose whether to fast, Al-Mizan holds that they must break the fast and make it up later; this is also narrated from the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt and reported from some Companions. The proposed unstated qualification, “and did not fast,” is neither demanded by the context nor sufficient to establish a mere option: in a legal enactment, permission to break the fast may signify obligation, recommendation, or allowance, and the Lawgiver would not leave an essential legal aspect unstated.

Those who can fast only by exhausting themselves are under an obligatory fidyah: feeding a poor person with food sufficient to satisfy hunger and of the normal kind eaten by the giver. Iṭāqah implies performing the task with hardship and overstrain, while fidyah is a material substitute. The phrase “on them” establishes obligation, not choice. Al-Mizan rejects the view that able people were initially free either to fast or feed a poor person and that this was later abrogated, leaving the rule for the elderly, pregnant women, and nursing women. It says this fragments a unified discourse, creates clashes between its statements, and requires the same word, yuṭīqūnahu, first to mean those able to fast and then those unable to fast. It would also make successive parts of the passage abrogate one another without warrant, while the supposedly abrogated clause never concerned those unable to fast.

Taṭawwuʿ means doing a deed willingly and gladly, without reluctance, whether obligatory or otherwise; its later specialized use for supererogatory works should not govern this verse. Thus the verse urges believers to undertake the prescribed fast willingly, because the law has been made beneficial and easy for them. “Whosoever on his own accord performs good” metaphorically states the cause in place of its effect: voluntary fasting is better than reluctant fasting. It does not mean merely adding a second feeding or feeding an additional poor person, for that interpretation wrongly limits taṭawwuʿ to non-obligatory acts, deprives the connective particle of force, and confuses voluntary addition with willing performance. Fasting willingly is good in two respects: fasting is good, and willingly doing good is itself good.

Likewise, “that you fast is better for you” is not addressed only to those excused from fasting and does not mean that they may preferably fast in Ramaḍān instead of making it up later. There is no evidence for this restriction; the syntax differs from that of the sick and traveller clause; those persons are not given a choice to omit fasting; and even on the contrary supposition, their choice would concern the time of fasting, not fasting versus non-fasting. The phrase does not enact an optional law but affirms that God’s command is beneficial to those addressed.

Ramaḍān is the ninth lunar month, between Shaʿbān and Shawwāl, and is the only month named in the Qur’an. Nuzūl means coming down; inzāl means bringing down all at once, whereas tanzīl means bringing down gradually. The Qur’an is so called because it is recited, and the name applies both to the whole Book and to portions of it. The statement that it was sent down in Ramaḍān appears to conflict with the statement that it was revealed gradually throughout the roughly twenty-three years of the Call. One response says that the entire Qur’an descended to the lowest heaven in Ramaḍān and was later sent to the Messenger in portions. Yet the description of the Qur’an as guidance and discrimination raises the question of how it could guide while remaining there; the proposed answer, that it possessed only latent guiding power, is inadequate for verses that are addresses tied to their occasions or for abrogating and abrogated verses, which cannot sensibly be revealed together before their occasions.

Nor does “sent down in Ramaḍān” merely mean that the first verses descended then. This lacks contextual support and conflicts with the account that the Call began on the twenty-seventh of Rajab, more than a month before Ramaḍān, while the earliest chapters show their connection with the beginning of the Call. The similar statements concerning a blessed night and the Night of Destiny also do not naturally mean only the beginning of revelation.

Al-Mizan argues instead that the use of inzāl permits two understandings. It may view a whole that comes gradually as a single collective entity, just as rain may be spoken of as sent down. More profoundly, it signifies that the Reality of the Book differs from its divided, articulated wording: the latter can be progressively revealed, while the former is one, indivisible, and non-gradual. Verses describing a Book whose verses were first confirmed and then made clear show that its division into parts came later. Other verses distinguish the Book’s later explanation from its final interpretation, implying that the real Book is that final interpretation which will become manifest on the Day of Judgement.

The Book that makes truth manifest was made into an Arabic Qur’an so people could understand it, but in its reality it is in the Source of the Book with God—elevated, full of wisdom, and without division. The honored Qur’an is also described as being in a Hidden Book, accessible only to the purified, and the same reality is called the Guarded Tablet. The Guarded Tablet cannot be the gradually revealed Qur’an, which includes abrogation and gradual completion, both forms of change. The Manifest or Hidden Book is therefore the foundation or Reality of the revealed Qur’an, which stands to it as clothing to its wearer, a metaphor to its meaning, or a proverb to its intended aim.

Accordingly, Al-Mizan interprets the Qur’an’s descent in Ramaḍān, on the blessed night, and on the Night of Destiny as the all-at-once descent of the Source of the Book, the Manifest Book, to the Messenger’s heart; the articulated Qur’an then descended to his heart gradually throughout his prophetic mission. Commands not to hasten with the Qur’an before its revelation was complete show that the Messenger had prior knowledge of what was being revealed. The gradually revealed Qur’an rests on a sublime Reality beyond common minds and untouched by imaginations defiled by lust, greed, and materialism; by its all-at-once descent, God taught the Prophet the Book’s true aim and meaning. Al-Mizan says that traditionalists, most theologians, and materialists who reject such a metaphysical reality are driven to reduce these descriptions to figurative language and thereby turn the Qur’an into poetic prose.

The commentary then rejects an unnamed writer’s account that the Call, first revelation, and command to warn all occurred on a night in Ramaḍān; that the Chapter of The Opening was taught after “Read in the name of Thy Lord …”; and that the command “Arise, and warn” followed the next morning. It regards these details as unsupported fabrications, established by neither clear Qur’anic verses nor reliable traditions. The writer also supplies no evidence for making the Prophet a prophet for one night before he became a messenger the next morning. His criticism that late Shīʿite collections cannot establish the beginning of the Call would equally discredit all Sunni and Shīʿite collections, since no collection was written before the end of the second Hijrī century or later; history supplies even less, and is equally exposed to charges of interpolation.

The earliest chapter, “Read in the name of Thy Lord …,” indicates that the Prophet was already praying before Meccans who forbade him and discussed the matter in their councils. It thus shows that he was already a prophet, upon guidance, enjoining piety, and worshipping before the alleged revelation of The Opening and before an open public call. The Chapter of The Opening was revealed later than the start of the Call: the suggested reason for its immediate revelation would not account for its form and final verses. Its description as the seven oft-repeated verses alongside the great Qur’an shows both its excellence and that it is one part of the Qur’an, not the whole Book. The later chapter that mentions it also commands the Messenger to declare openly what he is bidden, showing that he had earlier refrained from open warning. Similarly, whether the Chapter of al-Muddaththir descended all at once or in portions, “Arise, and warn” belongs to an early period after such a restraint, not necessarily to the first morning of prophethood.

Al-Mizan also rejects the writer’s dismissal of traditions concerning the Qur’an’s all-at-once descent to the Inhabited House. No clear Qur’anic verse contradicts them, and they do not state that the descent occurred before prophethood; the writer adds that claim himself. His assertion that the Guarded Tablet is the physical universe is deemed untenable, since the changing and perishable universe is neither guarded from alteration nor inaccessible to the unworthy. His interpretation finally reduces actual statements of descent to “as though” the Qur’an descended, a violation of language, usage, and context. If the writer can treat the revelation of The Opening, which contains the Qur’an’s principal knowledge, as revelation of the whole Qur’an, there is even less reason to deny that all its knowledge could have descended to the Messenger’s heart at once.

“A guidance for the people” refers to those of lesser intellectual capacity, who follow others and need a guide rather than being able to grasp abstract truths and distinguish right from wrong by proof. “Clear evidence of guidance and discrimination” concerns a more select group, complete in knowledge and action and prepared to receive divine light; for them the Qur’an provides proofs of guidance and distinguishes good from evil and truth from falsehood. The two descriptions therefore stand as general and particular.

“Witnessing the month” means being present when it arrives and knowing of its arrival, not merely sighting the new moon or not travelling; the verse provides no evidence for those restrictions. The repeated rule for the sick and traveller is not redundant: the preceding verses prepared minds for the law, while this verse actually promulgates it. They must break the fast because God desires ease rather than hardship, and must fast an equal number later so that the prescribed number is completed.

Finally, glorifying God and thanking Him state the purpose of the Ramaḍān fast in connection with the Qur’an’s descent as guidance and discrimination. Fasting glorifies God because even its outward form—abstaining in obedience—displays His greatness and the servant’s submission. It becomes true thanksgiving only when it has its inner spirit: sincerity toward God, purification from material involvement, and abstention from the heart’s greatest desires. This explains why glorification is expressed as a causal purpose, while thanksgiving is expressed with laʿalla, denoting hope: outward fasting necessarily manifests glorification, but may or may not attain the sincere gratitude that is its fuller aim.
verses.186:
Al-Mizan describes this verse as an exceptionally elegant and emphatic declaration of God’s response to prayer. Its repeated first-person singular language stresses the subject’s importance; “My servants” further dignifies it. God answers directly, without the intermediary phrase “say,” and “verily” reinforces the assurance. Calling Him “near,” rather than saying that He comes near, means that His nearness is abiding; and the aorist verb for answering signifies both present and continuing response. The phrase “when he calls on Me” is not an additional restriction on the promise, but intensifies that a real supplicant’s prayer is answered. The verse’s seven first-person singular pronouns are unique in the Qur’an and underline the importance of answering prayer.

Duʿāʾ and daʿwah mean directing the called one’s attention to the caller. Suʾāl, asking, is the purpose of such calling: placing one’s need before another in order to obtain a benefit. This includes every kind of request, such as seeking knowledge, reckoning, or beneficence. Likewise, ʿubūdiyyah, bondage, literally denotes being owned, and ʿabd is used for human or other intelligent beings.

God’s ownership of His servants is real, total, and unlike human ownership. People possess neither themselves, their attributes and acts, nor such connected things as family, wealth, honour, and rights independently of Him. Their natural possessions and their assumed social possessions belong to them only because God grants and sustains that relation. He gives them their selves, hearing, sight, and hearts; without His granting, they would be nonexistent. Therefore, He intervenes between a thing and itself and between it and all associated things, and is truly nearer to creatures than anything else: “And We are nearer to him than you, but you see [Us] not (56:85)”; “and We are nearer to him than his life vein (50:16)”; and “know that Allah intervenes between man and his heart (8:24).” Here, the heart means the rational soul or spirit.

Because creatures are truly His servants, God’s nearness gives Him unrestricted authority over them and authority to answer every need presented to Him; His ownership, power, and pervasiveness encompass every possible case. This refutes the claim ascribed to the Jews that, after creating things and decreeing their destinies, God’s work ended and His hands became folded, leaving no room for abrogation, change, or answered prayer. It also refutes the Qadariyyah’s denial of God’s power over creatures’ actions. A report accepted by both Sunnis and Shias calls the Qadariyyah “the Magians of this ummah.” In truth, all real ownership belongs to God: whatever He wills, grants, and permits to exist comes into being, while what He does not will cannot exist despite every effort to bring it about. “O people! You are they who are needy unto Allah, and Allah is He who is the Self-sufficient, the Most Praised One (35:15).”

Thus, the verse supplies the reason for the answering of prayer: servants belong to God; He is near to them; and, being near, He answers them without reservation. The apparent condition, “when he calls on Me,” shows that the promise concerns prayer in its reality, not a mere verbal formula. Just as one listens to a sincere adviser when he is truly sincere, the supplicant must truly be a supplicant: his heart must seek what his tongue requests in accordance with his innate and deeply rooted knowledge. Real supplication is the cry of the heart and the tongue of nature, not speech uttered heedlessly, whether true or false, serious or playful. For this reason, God speaks of requests made without spoken words: “And He gave you of all that you asked Him; and if you count Allah’s bounties, you will not be able to compute them; Verily, man is very unjust very ungrateful (14:34).” Human beings silently ask through their neediness, nature, and existence; indeed, “All those in the heavens and the earth do beseech Him; every day He is in a [new] splendor (55:29).”

Natural prayer addressed to God is therefore always answered. What seems unanswered lacks either genuine prayer or exclusive address to God. A person may ask for what is impossible without knowing it, or for something which he would not want if he knew its true reality. One who asks recovery for someone already dead, while lacking firm conviction sufficient to ask for resurrection, has not truly made the request which the situation requires. Or a person may verbally beseech God while inwardly relying on apparent causes or imagined beings as powers that fulfil needs. Such a request is not exclusively addressed to God, who has no partner in His affairs and does not operate as a partner alongside apparent or imaginary causes. In both cases the tongue may speak, but the heart is not sincere in prayer.

Human beings are created with an innate, silent request directed to their Lord. In ease, they become blinded by apparent causes, treat them as partners with God, and imagine that they do not beseech their Lord. Yet their inborn prayer remains directed only to Him. When hardship severs apparent causes from their expected effects and supposed partners and intercessors disappear, they return to their natural monotheism, turn wholly to the Beneficent Lord, and He removes their distress. Once prosperity returns, they often revert to polytheism and forgetfulness.

The verse “And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will answer you. Verily, those who are arrogant to My worship shall soon enter Hell, disgraced (40:60)” identifies prayer with worship. Its threat against those arrogant toward “My worship,” meaning prayer, could only be justified by abandoning worship itself, not merely one of its kinds. Prayer is consequently not simply an important form of worship but its foundation.

Other verses concerning prayer set out its essential manner. Above all, it must be exclusive to God: inward feeling must conform to spoken words, and the servant must abandon reliance on all apparent reasons besides Him and depend on Him alone. Its other elements include fear of God, hope in His answer, love and reverence, humility, perseverance, remembrance of God, good deeds, true faith, and presence of heart.

Finally, “So they should answer My call and believe in Me” follows from God’s nearness and care for His servants and their requests. Since nothing stands between Him and their prayer, they should accept His invitation, advance toward Him, and firmly believe that He is near and answers their call, so that they may be rightly guided in supplicating Him.
verses.187:
Al-Mizan explains that iḥlāl means allowing, its root ḥall being the opposite of tying. Rafath literally denotes openly saying words normally left unspoken, especially in sexual intercourse; the Qur’an employs it metaphorically for intercourse. Its other expressions for this act likewise are metaphors—such as mubāshirah, dukhūl, mass or lams, ityān, and qurb—rather than words originally coined for copulation. The preposition ilā after rafath is said to convey the sense of entering into.

The spouses’ being libās, apparel, for one another is a figurative expression: each restrains the other from unchastity, covers the other’s shame, preserves privacy, and protects society from debauchery. Just as clothing conceals one’s private parts from others but not from itself, spouses protect one another from relations with others while no such restriction exists between themselves.

The phrase that the Muslims had been “acting unfaithfully” to themselves indicates continuous and widespread secret sin after fasting had been prescribed. Although divine turning in mercy and forgiveness do not explicitly state that sin had preceded them, together they most plainly imply it. The verse therefore shows that intercourse on the nights of fasting had formerly been prohibited, and that this verse abrogated that prohibition. The wording, “It is made lawful,” the reference to their unfaithfulness and forgiveness, and “now be in contact with them” would otherwise be out of place; one would instead expect a mere declaration that there was no blame.

Al-Mizan considers, but finds inconclusive, the claim that no ruling was abrogated. On that account, Muslims had followed a Christian-like practice of abstaining from food, drink, and intercourse after the early part of the night; youths secretly had intercourse and elderly people suffered if sleep overtook them before eating. The verse would then only remove their mistaken belief that these acts were forbidden at night, while “as it was prescribed for those before you” would concern fasting in general rather than all its details. This view also argues that “made lawful” need not imply prior unlawfulness, that their unfaithfulness was only according to their own judgment because it was “to yourselves,” and that ikhtiyān may mean diminishing desires.

But the verse’s clearest implication remains a preceding prohibition, especially “now be in contact with them.” Nor does the absence of an explicit earlier Qur’anic prohibition disprove abrogation: the prior verse did not explicitly prohibit intercourse even in the daytime, since the Messenger of God had explained the rules of fasting. The verse may therefore abrogate a Prophetic rule, not another Qur’anic verse.

The apparel metaphor is not by itself the reason for the nocturnal permission, since it is equally true by day. Rather, the successive clauses—night of fasting, the spouses’ being apparel, and the continuing unfaithfulness—jointly explain the easing. Intercourse between spouses is beneficial in itself; yet fasting required abstention from food, drink, and sexual relations. Since abstaining from intercourse for the whole month proved difficult and the violation became common, God mercifully lightened the burden by permitting it at night. Thus apparel expresses the benefit of intercourse as such, while the fast restricts that general implication to the night. This combined reason did not exist under the former rule.

The command to be in contact, following a prohibition and preceded by the declaration of lawfulness, means permission. “Seek what Allah has written for you” means seek the children God has decreed for humankind. Sexual desire is a God-given means through which people seek that gift, even when they consciously seek only gratification, just as eating and drinking serve life, growth, and health even when one seeks only to satisfy hunger, thirst, or taste. Al-Mizan rejects the interpretation that what is written means merely what God has permitted, because the Qur’an does not use “writing” for permission.

There are two dawns. The false dawn, called the tail of the wolf, is a temporary vertical beam at the eastern horizon. It is followed by the true dawn, a horizontal light spread like a white thread across the horizon and connected with sunrise. The white thread in the verse is this true dawn, while the adjoining darkness is the black thread; “at dawn-break” clarifies the metaphor. The permission to eat, drink, and have intercourse ends precisely at the beginning of true dawn, before the advancing daylight causes both figurative threads to disappear.

“Complete the fast until night” gives the fast’s other boundary, its beginning having already been given as dawn. It also indicates that a day’s fast is one single act of worship. Completion (tamām) concerns the coming into being of such a single thing, whereas perfection (kamāl) concerns a thing composed of parts having distinct functions. Thus religion, consisting of such acts as prayer, fasting, and hajj, may be perfected, while God’s favor, being one without parts, is completed.

ʿUkūf and iʿtikāf mean remaining continuously at a place. Iʿtikāf is worship consisting in staying in a mosque, leaving only for a genuine need, and fasting is essential to it. The prohibition of intercourse while confined in mosques prevents the nocturnal permission from being mistakenly extended to the nights of iʿtikāf.

Finally, ḥadd means restraint or restriction; the ḥudūd allāh are God’s restrictive ordinances. Not approaching them figuratively means not committing the relevant sins: eating, drinking, or intercourse during their forbidden times, transgressing the prescribed limits, or neglecting the fast and the guarding against evil required in this particular worship.
verses.188:
Al-Mizan explains akl, “to eat” or “swallow up,” as a common metaphor for taking or using something, especially wealth: food is man’s first and most basic natural object of acquisition, and the expression is used similarly in all languages. Māl is desired possession, apparently related to mayl, inclination or desire; baynakum means the interval among two or more persons; and bāṭil, wrongful means, is the opposite of ḥaqq, that which is confirmed.

The phrase “among yourselves” indicates that wealth belongs to all people, although God has justly distributed it among them through laws founded on justice and equity that eradicate corruption and immorality. Transgressing those legal limits is invalid and wrongful; in this respect the verse explains, “He it is who created for you all that is in the earth (2:29).” The possessive expression “your property” confirms the right of ownership, a right recognized by human society throughout history. The Qur’an repeatedly recognizes it through such expressions as mulk, māl, the possessive l…, and istikhlāf, as well as through its regulations of sale and trade; authentic (mutawātir) traditions also support it.

Idlāʾ, rendered “to gain access,” literally denotes lowering a bucket (dalūʾ) into a well. Here it is an allegory for offering money or the like to authorities to obtain a favourable judgment: the sought judgment is the water in the well, and the bribe is the bucket used to draw it. Farīqan means a portion separated from a whole. On the apparent grammatical reading, the clause prohibits seeking such access in order to wrongfully consume part of people’s property, knowingly.

Alternatively, the conjunction w… may mean “with” (maʿ), with inna understood after it. The verse would then prohibit the collusion of giver and taker of a bribe: each knowingly shares in wrongful consumption of people’s property, the official taking the offered portion and the bribe-giver usurping the remainder.
verses.189:
Al-Mizan explains that ahillah is the plural of hilāl, the crescent at the beginning of the lunar month; the word derives from a root connected with raising one’s voice, because people hail the new moon when they see it. Mawāqit, here, means appointed times, not appointed places.

The plural “new moons” shows that the question was not about the moon’s essence, phases, or the single crescent’s reappearance. Rather, it concerned the benefit of successive crescents in marking lunar months. God’s answer concerns the months marked by them, which provide fixed times for human material and spiritual affairs. Human activities require time to be measured and divided, and the lunar month is the clearest and most universally accessible division: scholars and ordinary people, nomads and townspeople alike can observe its beginning and count its days. The lunar months therefore serve as prescribed times for people, especially for hajj, which is performed in known months; the mention of hajj introduces what follows.

Reports state that some pre-Islamic Arabs, once in iḥrām, avoided their houses’ doors and entered through holes made in the walls. The verse disapproves of this custom and directs them to use the doors. Without such reliable reports, the words could have been read metaphorically as requiring religious rites to be performed only in their prescribed manner and time—for example, hajj in its appointed months and fasting in Ramaḍān. But the traditions support the former explanation. Calling entry from the backs of houses “not righteousness” shows that the practice had never been approved by religion; it was a bad pre-Islamic custom. Righteousness instead lies in fearing God and guarding oneself against evil.

The wording “righteousness is the one who guards himself” emphasizes the practice of piety rather than piety as an abstraction, as in: It is not righteousness that you turn your faces towards the east and the west but righteousness is the one who believes in Allah … (2:177). Entering houses through their doors is guidance to the proper, customary, and rational way, not a compulsory command that every entry must be through a door. Yet entering otherwise while believing the custom to be religious is an unlawful innovation.

Al-Mizan says that taqwā gathers all ranks of faith and stages of perfection, but only its final stages, which remove every shade of polytheism and misguidance, bring spiritual success and happiness. This accounts for “so that you may be successful.” It is also possible that “fear Allah” here means obeying this particular direction and abandoning entry through the backs of houses.
verses.190: Al-Mizan commands fighting in the way of Allah against those who fight you, without exceeding the limits; Allah does not love those who exceed them.
verses.191: Al-Mizan commands killing and expelling them wherever they are found, as they expelled you, because mischief [disbelief] is more grievous than slaughter. Fighting at the Sacred Mosque is forbidden unless they fight there; if they do, slay them, such being the recompense of the unbelievers.
verses.192: If they desist, Allah is forgiving and merciful.
verses.193: Al-Mizan directs that they be fought until mischief [disbelief] ceases and religion is only for Allah; if they desist, hostility is due only to the oppressors.
verses.194: Al-Mizan permits reprisal in sacred matters: aggression may be answered only with like aggression. It commands fear of Allah and affirms that He is with those who guard against evil.
verses.195:
Al-Mizan holds that verses (2:190-195) were revealed together as one legislation: the first permission to fight the Meccan polytheists who were fighting the believers. Their shared subject is indicated by expulsion, disbelief, retaliation, the Sacred Mosque, and military spending; they should neither be treated as separately revealed nor as mutually abrogating. “Those who fight with you” is not a condition meaning fight only if they first fight, nor a restriction to men rather than women and children; it identifies the Meccan polytheists then engaged in fighting. The permission corresponds to the permission granted to oppressed believers expelled from their homes in (22:39-40). The verses establish fighting in Allah’s way, prohibit exceeding limits, define the pressure to be exerted, restrict combat at the Sacred Mosque, specify its duration, permit reciprocal action in sacred matters, and require financial preparation.

The commentary defines qitāl as attempting to kill one who is attempting to kill oneself. Fighting is “in the way of Allah” because it seeks to establish religion and raise monotheism, as worship seeking Allah’s favour rather than property or honour. Islamic war is basically defensive, protecting a natural human right; consequently it is limited. The prohibition of iʿtidāʾ is general: it includes fighting before calling the opponent to truth, beginning war, killing women and children, and refusing to desist when ordered.

In verse (2:191), thiqāfah means finding. Although fitnah can denote testing, hardship, punishment, or sins that entail punishment, here it means associating partners with Allah, disbelieving in His Messenger, and persecuting and oppressing the Messenger and believers, as the Meccan polytheists did before and after the Hijrah. The command is to put the utmost pressure on them, killing them wherever found until they are driven from their town as they drove out the believers. Their mischief is more grievous than killing, because killing ends worldly life, whereas disbelief destroys this world and the next. Combat at Masjid al-Ḥarām is prohibited so long as its sanctity is respected; “therein” refers to the Sacred Mosque.

The desisting in (2:192) means desisting from fighting near the Sacred Mosque, not accepting Islam and obeying all its commands. It therefore differs from the later desisting in (2:193). By mentioning Allah’s forgiveness and mercy in place of the result, the verse means that believers must likewise desist from fighting there when their opponents desist.

Verse (2:193) sets the duration of the fighting: fitnah here is the polytheism and idol worship that the Meccan polytheists both practised and imposed on others, as shown by “religion be only for Allah.” Fighting must be preceded by calling the adversaries to monotheism; if they accept, there is no fighting. Al-Mizan rejects the claim that this verse was abrogated by the command concerning the People of the Book in (9:29), because the two concern different subjects. This verse concerns Meccan idolaters and requires the abolition of idol worship and acceptance of Allah’s Oneness. Although the People of the Book are, in reality, described as unbelievers, Islam accepts their profession of monotheism and fights them for jizyah, thereby raising the true creed above theirs and making Islam victorious over religions, not in order to make them monotheists. If the Meccan polytheists desist from the disbelief in question, fighting must cease, since hostility belongs only against oppressors.

The sacred things, ḥurumāt, of (2:194) include the sacred month, the ḥaram of Mecca, and the Sacred Mosque. If the Meccan polytheists violate their sanctity by fighting—as when they prevented the Prophet and his companions from ʿumrah at Ḥudaybiyah and attacked them—believers may fight back in the sacred month, the ḥaram, or the Mosque. “The sacred month for the sacred month” is a particular instance; reprisal in all sacred matters is broader; and equal response to aggression is the most general rule. Retaliation must remain exactly proportionate. Because revenge invites excessive force and disregard for religious limits, believers are commanded to fear Allah and remember that He is with the God-fearing. Reciprocal action is not blameworthy aggression or transgression: it is defence against degradation, slavery, oppression, and injustice.

Verse (2:195) commands spending for war in Allah’s way, including one’s own and others’ preparation. “With your hands” may emphasize that hands symbolize power and strength, so that failure to spend wastes that strength; alternatively, it may mean casting oneself into perdition by one’s own means. In either reading, the command is general and forbids every excess or deficiency that causes ruin. Miserliness in preparing for war weakens Muslim fighters and exposes them to death, while extravagance produces poverty, misery, and social degradation. Doing good does not mean abandoning fighting or showing clemency where it emboldens the enemy. It means doing each act properly: fighting when required, restraining oneself when restraint is preferable, being strict where reason requires strictness, and forgiving where forgiveness does not strengthen the enemy. Repelling an oppressor by the most reasonable means protects humanity’s right and religion, while not exceeding limits in obtaining one’s due is also good. These verses begin by denying Allah’s love to those who exceed the limit and conclude by affirming His love for those who do good.

Al-Mizan explains that the Qur’an first ordered Muslims to endure persecution patiently and refrain from fighting. It then authorized fighting against the Meccan polytheists and their allies, apparently including defence at Badr; against the People of the Book until jizyah is paid; against polytheists generally, a category here excluding the People of the Book; and against unbelievers near the Muslims. Islam, as the religion of monotheism, is founded on true human nature and is responsible for humanity’s well-being. Establishing and preserving this religion is therefore humanity’s foremost right, and defending it is another natural right. Since monotheism survives only through defence against enemies, fighting in defence of Muslims, Islamic territory, or even fighting initiated for this purpose is, in reality, defence of humanity’s right to life; polytheism is humanity’s death and a corruption of nature.

The fighting specified in these verses removes manifest polytheism, namely idol worship, and raises the true creed above that of the People of the Book through jizyah. Yet the latter, though professing one Creator, retain hidden polytheism and are not true believers in Allah. The Qur’an gives no explicit command to compel them into Islam, but its promises that the Messenger’s religion will triumph over all religions, that the earth will belong to Allah’s righteous servants, and that believers will be made successors who worship without associating anything with Allah imply a final cleansing of the earth from every form of polytheism. The promise of making believers successors entails removing others from their place and thus implies war. The description of a people who will strive in Allah’s way in (5:54) supports the view that this promise follows a divinely commanded call and religious movement.

Against the charge that Islam is a religion of sword, blood, force, and compulsion unlike earlier prophetic movements, Al-Mizan argues that true nature requires individual and collective affairs to be governed by laws founded on belief in one God. This fundamental human right must be spread and protected from disorder by all possible means, though moderation remains essential. The sequence is first the Call and patient endurance of persecution, then defence of Muslim lives and territory, and finally war begun by the divine representative to defend humanity’s right and pure monotheism. Every kind of fighting must be preceded by a rational call to the right path, with wisdom, kindly exhortation, and the best discussion. When explanation and exhortation fail and a group’s refusal produces disorder, it may be compelled to accept the truth, just as states compel those who reject their laws after first calling them to obedience. This compulsion affects one generation; subsequent generations will be educated to accept the religion of nature and monotheism willingly. Al-Mizan therefore considers it unobjectionable to compel one generation if all later generations thereby follow the right path.

The assertion that earlier prophets used only verbal persuasion is rejected. Many lacked the opportunity or power to fight, as did Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, and Jesus during his mission; Jesus’ call spread only near the end of its validity, before Islam. Conversely, both the Old Testament and the Qur’an recount prophets who fought in Allah’s way, including the prophets accompanied by devoted fighters, Moses’ call to enter the holy land, the conflict of Saul and Goliath, and Solomon’s warning to the queen of Sheba after calling her to submission.

From a sociological perspective, Al-Mizan argues that every human and animal society is grounded in the natural urge for survival. Nature gives each species a right to use what preserves it and, necessarily, a right to defend that use. Human reason recognizes both rights. In society, however, the primary right of use is balanced by reciprocal claims: one must serve others as one expects them to serve oneself, according to the scale fixed by society. Fighting instead arises from the secondary right of defence, when someone believes a presumed right is threatened. Thus all wars are defensive in the mind of those who wage them: even rulers, or those seeking territory for population or economic reasons, suppose themselves entitled to what they pursue, however absurd their justification appears to others.

Defence is nonetheless secondary to use. The propriety of a defensive action depends on the importance and validity of the right defended and on whether its social damage cancels or exceeds its benefit. The Qur’an identifies belief in Allah’s Oneness and laws founded on revelation as the most important human right, alongside the right to live under laws that secure individual well-being. Defence of these rights consequently takes precedence over other considerations.
verses.196: Al-Mizan commands that ḥajj and ʿumrah be completed for Allah. One prevented from completing them must provide an available offering and not shave before it reaches its destination; sickness or an affliction of the head permits shaving with redemption by fasting, alms, or sacrifice. A secure pilgrim enjoying the interval after ʿumrah before ḥajj must offer what is available, or fast three days during ḥajj and seven after returning; this applies to one whose family does not dwell near the Sacred Mosque. Ḥajj falls in known months, and one who undertakes it must avoid sexual intercourse, bad language, and quarrelling, provide for the journey with piety as the best provision, and fear Allah, who knows every good deed.
verses.197: Al-Mizan commands that ḥajj and ʿumrah be completed for Allah. One prevented from completing them must provide an available offering and not shave before it reaches its destination; sickness or an affliction of the head permits shaving with redemption by fasting, alms, or sacrifice. A secure pilgrim enjoying the interval after ʿumrah before ḥajj must offer what is available, or fast three days during ḥajj and seven after returning; this applies to one whose family does not dwell near the Sacred Mosque. Ḥajj falls in known months, and one who undertakes it must avoid sexual intercourse, bad language, and quarrelling, provide for the journey with piety as the best provision, and fear Allah, who knows every good deed.
verses.198: Al-Mizan permits seeking bounty from Allah during the pilgrimage. On departing ʿArafāt, pilgrims should remember Allah near the Holy Monument and remember the guidance that brought them out of error.
verses.199: Al-Mizan commands pilgrims to march on as the people march on, seek Allah’s forgiveness, and trust in His forgiveness and mercy.
verses.200: Al-Mizan calls for remembrance of Allah after the rites with a devotion equal to, or more intense than, remembrance of one’s fathers. Whoever seeks only this world has no portion in the Hereafter.
verses.201: Al-Mizan presents the prayer for good in this world and the Hereafter, and for deliverance from the chastisement of the Fire.
verses.202: Al-Mizan says that they will receive their earned portion, while Allah is quick in reckoning.
verses.203:
Al-Mizan states: The introduction states that these verses were revealed during the Messenger of God’s last pilgrimage, ḥajjat al-widāʿ, and promulgated ḥajj al-tamattuʿ.

Al-Mizan distinguishes completion, tamām, from perfection, kamāl. Completion is the final constituent by which an assembled thing becomes whole and produces its intended effects; itmām is the adding of that final part. Perfection is a quality or condition that gives an already complete thing an effect it otherwise lacks. Although tamām can metaphorically denote an indispensable perfection, completing ḥajj and ʿumrah here has its literal sense: being prevented means being stopped from carrying the rites through to their end, not from perfecting them.

The commentary describes ḥajj as an enduring Islamic worship begun by Abraham, involving iḥrām, the stays at ʿArafāt and the Sacred Monument, sacrifice at Mina, stoning the three Stone-pillars, circumambulation, prayer, and the march between Ṣafā and Marwah, besides other duties. Its forms are ḥajj al-ifrād, ḥajju al-qirān, and ḥajj al-tamattuʿ, the last ordained near the end of the Messenger’s life. ʿUmrah likewise begins with iḥrām at an appointed place and includes circumambulation, prayer, the march between Ṣafā and Marwah, and cutting nails or hair. Both rites can be complete only when done for Allah.

Iḥṣār means obstruction after iḥrām, through illness, an enemy, or the like. The hady is the animal brought or led for sacrifice. A sickness permitting early shaving is one in which not shaving would cause suffering; an affliction of the head is a distinct hardship, such as vermin or lice. Either permits shaving, provided redemption is made by fasting, alms, or sacrifice. An unnamed tradition specifies three days’ fasting, feeding six poor persons, or sacrificing one goat.

When secure from hindrances, the pilgrim who enjoys by the ʿumrah for the ḥajj enjoys because completion of ʿumrah lifts the restrictions of iḥrām—including restrictions concerning women and perfume—until iḥrām for ḥajj begins. Thus the bi in bi al-ʿumrah is causative. The required offering is an independent rite, not compensation for failing to assume the iḥrām of ḥajj from a mīqāt outside Mecca. The claim that it compensates for a concession that lightens hardship is rejected: the enjoyment comes only after ʿumrah has ended, when its restrictions have already ceased, and before iḥrām for ḥajj begins. At most, the wording indicates that sacrifice follows the ordination of enjoyment by ʿumrah; it does not suggest compensation for bypassing the mīqāt.

The wording concerning enjoyment treats ḥajj al-tamattuʿ as an already prescribed rite and, on that basis, prescribes the offering; it does not initially legislate tamattuʿ. Its original promulgation is in the later clause, “this is for him whose family dwells not near the Sacred Mosque.” If the offering cannot be found, the three-day fast belongs within the time of ḥajj, from its iḥrām until return. Traditions from the imams of Ahl al-Bayt place it before the Day of Sacrifice, or, if that is missed, after the 13th of Dhu al-ḥijjah, and finally upon returning home. The seven-day fast is after reaching home, as indicated by “when you return,” rather than merely while returning. The change to the second-person pronoun also hints that the hearer is at home.

The three days and seven days are ten perfect days: the latter perfect the former but do not complete them. Each set consequently retains a separate identity and rule; the three-day fast is complete in itself, though perfected by the seven days. Tamattuʿ is for the non-resident, defined as one whose dependents dwell at least twelve miles from the Sacred Mosque. Describing the rule through his family both identifies those governed by it and explains its alleviation of the distant pilgrim’s hardship: after ʿumrah, he may enjoy the released restrictions until ḥajj and then enter its iḥrām from the Sacred Mosque without returning to a mīqāt. This is a general rule for all non-resident pilgrims, at every time and in every situation.

The severe closing warning indicates an anticipated refusal or hesitation. Arabs had practiced the inherited rites of ḥajj since Abraham and were accustomed to their established form; hence they resisted the change brought by tamattuʿ. Reports say that many objected, prompting the Messenger to declare that the authority belonged to God, who ordains as He wills, and that the rule was universal, exempting neither him nor the ummah.

For (2:197), ḥajj initially means the time of ḥajj. The sunnah identifies its known months as Shawwāl, Dhu al-qaʿdah, and Dhu al-ḥijjah, even though only part of the last month contains the rites. The three occurrences of ḥajj carry different senses—its time, the act determined, and its time and place—so repeating the noun is more concise than pronouns would have been. To determine ḥajj is to make it binding on oneself by beginning its rites; once begun, it must be completed. In this context, the sunnah explains rafath as sexual intercourse, fusūq as lying, and jidāl as swearing by God, such as “No, by God” or “Yes, by God.” Allah’s knowledge of every good deed calls for inwardly present devotion rather than merely external ritual. The shift from “Allah knows” to “fear Me” emphasizes piety and direct divine address to the pious; knowledge without practice has no value in Islam.

For (2:198), seeking Allah’s bounty means trading, as the Qur’anic pairing of leaving trade for remembrance and subsequently seeking Allah’s grace shows; trade during pilgrimage is therefore lawful. Ifāḍah is departure in a group, so the command concerns both the stay at ʿArafāt and the stay at the Sacred Monument, al-muzdalafah. Remembrance should be as intense as the guidance received from Allah, since before that guidance people were astray.

For (2:199), the command to march on from where the people march requires the immediate audience to follow the other pilgrims. It accords with reports that the Quraysh and their allies, the ḥums, claimed the sanctity of their territory as a reason not to leave it: they went directly to al-muzdalafah instead of staying at ʿArafāt. The verse requires them also to stay at ʿArafāt and depart from it with the rest. Its later placement and use of thumma are an istidrāk: the preceding rules stand, except that they must depart from ʿArafāt, not al-muzdalafah. They are then commanded to seek forgiveness from the Forgiving, Merciful Allah.

For (2:200), remembrance after the rites must equal remembrance of one’s fathers or, rather, exceed it in intensity. Allah’s grace of guidance outweighs the claims of forefathers. It has been said that pre-Islamic Arabs stayed at Mina after ḥajj to boast of their ancestors in speeches and poetry; the verse redirects this to Allah’s remembrance. Here aw means “rather,” and “more intense” concerns quality, not frequency. True remembrance belongs to heart and mind, while words merely display it; intensity is especially fitting after rites, when one may turn away and forget Allah.

The one who says, “Our Lord! give us in this world,” is not necessarily verbally asking; saying in both this and the following verse means inward desire manifested by one’s condition. The expression covers those whose concern is worldly glory and material greatness, with no concern for the Hereafter, as well as the believer who seeks Allah’s pleasure and accepts worldly gifts only as gifts Allah is pleased to give. The first class has no share in the Hereafter, whereas the second seeks what Allah is pleased to grant in both worlds and has its share there.

For (2:201), the believer asks specifically for ḥasanah, good, in this world and the Hereafter, and protection from the Fire. Unlike one whose desires alone make the whole world appear good, whether or not it is good before Allah, the believer recognizes that the Hereafter may be good or bad and seeks only its good.

For (2:202), the contrast between having no Hereafter portion and receiving a portion of what one has earned shows that the worldly group’s deeds, unlike the believers’, are void and forfeited. Sariʿ al-ḥisāb, “quick in reckoning,” is a divine name whose generality includes this world as well as the Hereafter: recompense for each good or evil deed is already being given. Together, the verses urge remembrance of Allah so that one seeks what He approves and receives a Hereafter share, rather than seeking only this world and being disappointed.

For (2:203), the counted days are the days of brightness, the 11th, 12th, and 13th of Dhu al-ḥijjah. Their position after the principal rites and the possibility of leaving in two days show that they are three days; traditions give the same interpretation. The unrestricted wording “there is no sin on him” negates the whole genus of sin. It therefore declares that a pilgrim who has performed the rites returns forgiven of all sins whether he departs after two days or stays; the verse’s purpose is not simply to state a choice between departure and delay.

“[This is] for him who guards [himself]” qualifies not forgiveness but eligibility for the choice, since it says “for him,” not “on him.” As the earlier phrase identifies those governed by tamattuʿ, this identifies those allowed to hasten or tarry: one who guarded against what Allah prohibited during iḥrām. If he did not, he must remain at Mina for all three days and remember Allah. Some traditions from the imams of Ahl al-Bayt give this meaning. The final command to fear Allah and remember that all will be gathered to Him makes recollection of the Day of Recompense necessary to complete piety and avoid sin. The term tuḥsharūn aptly closes the pilgrimage rules: the pilgrims’ gathering and march should recall the day when Allah gathers all people and leaves none behind.
verses.204: Al-Mizan describes a man whose speech in worldly life pleases you, who calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, yet is the most violent of adversaries.
verses.205: Al-Mizan describes one who, when he becomes ruler, strives on earth to cause mischief and destroy crop and progeny; Allah does not love mischief.
verses.206: Al-Mizan says that, when told to fear Allah, he is overcome by honor [pride] by sin; Hell is enough for him, and it is an evil abode.
verses.207:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as a classification of people by character—hypocrisy or sincere faith—following the preceding classification according to whether they seek this world or the Hereafter.

The commentary explains that worldly life requires reliance on outward appearances, while inner traits remain concealed. Thus a man's pleasing speech may seem devoted to truth, public good, religion, and the ummah, and his calling Allah to witness what is in his heart may seem to confirm his sincerity; nevertheless, he is in fact the truth's most violent enemy.

Tawallī may mean acquiring authority and power: when this hypocrite rules, he actively spreads mischief. It may alternatively mean turning away, so that his conduct when absent contradicts his public speech. Destroying crop and progeny describes this mischief because human survival depends on food, ultimately based on crops, and on procreation. The mischief Allah does not love is not the natural destruction and decay built into the divinely ordained order, where destruction is followed by construction, life by death, and existence by extinction. Rather, it is corruption in the shariah and legislation, whose laws were ordained to improve human action and character, keep society on moderation's straight path, and bring prosperity in this life and the Hereafter. The hypocrite pretends to reform while misinterpreting God's words, altering His laws, and manipulating religious teachings; this produces corrupt character and enduring religious and social conflict, negates religion, and destroys humanity. Al-Mizan points to the history of unauthorized rulers imposing themselves on the Muslim ummah and corrupting religious and state affairs as an illustration: religion, Muslims, and the ummah suffer evil results, decline, and internal strife. Some traditions accordingly interpret the destruction of crop and progeny as the destruction of religion and humanity.

When such a person is told to fear God, the honor that overcomes him is only an apparent honor earned through sin and hypocrisy. The phrase “by sin” qualifies honor, not “is overcome”: it neither says that pride leads him into sin or rejection of the admonition, nor that sin causes his pride. True honor comes from God and cannot be sinful; the honor of the verse is a deceptive, transient semblance, as is the self-exaltation attributed elsewhere to unbelievers.

Verse (2:207) contrasts this hypocrite with one who sells his self to God, seeks only His pleasure, desires nothing for himself, and derives honor and strength only from God. Through such a person, religious and worldly affairs regain their proper form, truth is revived, humanity attains a happy life, and Islam's good reaches all. Allah's affection for the servants is shown in making such people a mercy: without them, hypocrisy and mischief would ruin religion and righteousness. God's way is to repel falsehood through truth and to repair the harm caused by His enemies through His beloved, chosen servants. The decline inflicted by people devoted only to themselves can be removed only by the good that flows from those who have sold their souls to God and seek the world's virtue. This transaction is among those God praises (9:111).
verses.208: Al-Mizan commands believers to enter submission wholly, all together, and not follow Satan’s footsteps, for he is their open enemy.
verses.209: If you slip after clear signs have come, know that Allah is Mighty, Wise.
verses.210:
Al-Mizan presents these verses and the four following them as guidance for preserving religious unity. Unity requires complete submission to God, restricting oneself to God’s word and to the deeds whose way He has shown. It maintains that no people’s religious unity was broken, or their welfare in both worlds turned into misery and disaster, except through abandoning submission and manipulating God’s signs by altering or misplacing them. This occurred among the children of Israel and other peoples, will surely occur in this ummah as well, yet God ultimately promises help, and His help is near.

Silm, islām, and taslīm all mean submission. Kāffatan emphasizes both “all” and “wholly”: because believers are addressed, the command concerns every individual as well as Muslim society collectively, and calls for total submission after faith. Believers must submit all their affairs to God and His Messenger, neither independently deciding what benefits them nor choosing a path without divine and prophetic guidance. Al-Mizan says that peoples were destroyed through following their own opinions and desires and speaking without true knowledge, and forfeited life and happiness through disunity.

Following Satan’s footsteps does not mean accepting every falsehood to which he calls; rather, it concerns religion. Satan marks paths of untruth with the signs of truth, introducing into religion what does not belong to it and thereby deceiving believers. Such an interpolation may be recognized by asking whether God and His Messenger ever taught it as part of religion. Since footsteps occur on a trodden path, the image indicates satanic marks placed within the highway of true faith. Thus, wherever a believer proceeds without complete submission to God and His Messenger, he is following Satan’s footsteps. Unlike similar general warnings, this verse addresses the community as a whole; it therefore implies holding fast together to God’s cord rather than dividing, and following His single straight path rather than paths that scatter people from it. It also implies that Islam contains the laws and knowledge human beings need for their welfare and good.

Al-Mizan defines zallah as a slip or fall. The slip after clear signs have come is following Satan’s footsteps and failing to enter submission wholly. Allah’s might means that none can overcome His orders, and His wisdom means that He decides people’s affairs according to wisdom, enforces His decision, and cannot be hindered.

The third verse shifts from addressing believers directly to speaking of them in the third person and addressing the Messenger. Al-Mizan takes this to imply that those who slip and follow Satan’s footsteps are no longer worthy of God’s direct address. By their division and conduct, they appear to await a decree: God and the angels come amid cloud-canopies, the matter is settled while they are unaware or without pity for their plight, and there is no escape from God’s judgment and decree. The verse thus explains the threat implicit in the preceding warning that Allah is Mighty, Wise. It notes that ẓulal, the plural of ẓullah, means things used for shade, such as canopies, awnings, or tents, and that “the angels” apparently stands in conjunction with the divine name.

The commentary insists, on the basis of the Qur’an and the sunnah, that bodily and transient attributes—implying transience, need, deficiency, or want—cannot be ascribed to God. Clear, decisive verses affirming His incomparable self-sufficiency and creatorship govern the interpretation of ambiguous verses. Therefore, when “coming” is attributed to God, it must initially be understood in a manner befitting divine sublimity: as sending chastisement, surrounding people with divine power or wrath, and here specifically surrounding them with power in order to enforce the decree.

God sometimes attributes an action to Himself or to His command rather than to its apparent intermediate agents, to show that those agents are not independent of His order. Death, for example, is attributed in different places to Allah, the angel of death, and angels, while angels act only by His command. Likewise, the comparison with the verse that speaks of the angels coming or the order of the Lord coming shows that Allah’s coming here means the coming of His order. Al-Mizan says that wherever an action ascribed to God would be beneath His power and dignity, “order” or “command” is understood. This explanation, accepted by most commentators, is correct.

It then gives a deeper meaning. An attribute inseparable from deficiency cannot belong to God; but if its deficient, material aspect can be removed, it may be attributed to Him when suitable to His perfection. Material coming suggests a body moving and closing distance. Once material features are removed, what remains is nearness and the removal of obstruction. In that sense, God’s coming may be literal rather than metaphorical: no curtain remains between creatures and His judgment.

The threatened punishment may concern the Hereafter, as in the similar verse about the coming of angels or the Lord’s order; it may concern a worldly chastisement, for this world is a foretaste of the Hereafter in which its realities appear more perfectly; or it may concern both worlds together. The meaning of the cloud-canopies depends on where the punishment is to occur. Finally, the matter is decreed by God, though His name is omitted in the verse to display His greatness; all matters return to Him.
verses.211:
Al-Mizan reads (2:211-212) as reaffirming the preceding threat that God seizes sinners as the Mighty and Powerful. The Israelites, visible to the hearers, had received the Book, rule, prophethood, territory, good things, and excellence over other nations. Yet, after knowledge had come to them, they altered God’s words, followed self-invented things contrary to God, His Book, and His signs, and rebelled. Their punishment appeared in misguidance, division and mutual disagreement, unlawful consumption of one another’s property, loss of power and happiness, and humiliation and wretchedness in this world; the punishment of the Hereafter will be still more humiliating, without help for them. This illustrates God’s unchanging practice: whoever changes and misuses God’s favor is severely chastised. The verse therefore states a firm general decree, not merely a judgment on one people.

The commentary explains that worldly life’s alluring appearance is the principal cause of the Israelites’ and similar peoples’ deviation. Materialism directs a person toward lust and sensuous appetite, makes him forget truth and reality, and reduces his aim to worldly rank, dignity, wealth, beauty, and the like. He then uses everything, including religion, to obtain these ends. Religion is made a means to privilege and distinction: it honors leaders and bosses, gives them worldly prestige, and leads ordinary people to seek nearness to such figures and their favors rather than to God. Al-Mizan says this was seen among the Israelites and is also seen in the Muslim ummah.

Apparently, kufr here bears its literal sense of hiding, and thus includes both disbelief and concealing religious truth. Worldly life is made fair not only to outright disbelievers but also to those who hide religious truth or alter divine favors; such a person is likewise a kāfir and should expect severe punishment. Although these people mock believers, those who guard themselves against evil will stand above them on the Day of Resurrection, while God provides whom He pleases without measure. The change from “those who believe” to those who guard against evil stresses that īmān without taqwā—guarding oneself against evil, piety, and fear of God—is of no use.
verses.212:
