verses.213:
Al-Mizan explains verse (2:213) as an account of why religion was instituted, why human beings must follow it, and why differences arose both in worldly life and within religion. Humanity was initially one people. Differences then emerged over acquiring the necessities of life, and these could be settled only through laws that assign rights and require their observance. God therefore sent religion, with worship, laws, glad tidings for obedience, and warnings for wrongdoing, through prophets and messengers. A later and distinct difference concerned religious knowledge and mankind’s beginning and end. It disrupted religious unity and spread into other affairs, but it arose through the rebellion of those given the Book after religion’s foundations and proofs had been made clear. Thus the verse distinguishes natural differences over worldly interests from religious differences caused by revolt. God guided believers, by His will, to the truth disputed in both matters.

Divine religion is the sole means of human happiness and orderly life because it balances the various instincts and urges, preventing excess and deficiency, and thereby establishes the best order for material and spiritual life in this world and the Hereafter.

The commentary holds that the Qur’an presents mankind as a species directly created by God from the earth, beginning with a male and female from whom present humanity descends. The claim that species transformed into one another and that human beings developed from apes or aquatic animals is only a scientific hypothesis: it may function as an assumption for research, but is not a definite fact and has no greater value than this.

Human beings are composed of a material body and an immaterial soul or spirit. During worldly life they remain joined; at death the body dies while the living soul departs to its Creator. The Qur’anic descriptions of bodily development distinguish the later emergence of ‘another creation,’ and the angel of death’s taking people shows that the human reality is not merely the body: bodies disintegrate in the earth, but the souls themselves are not lost, dissolved, or dead.

God gave man hearing, sight, heart or wisdom, intelligence, and the power of thought. By them he knows present things, learns of the past, anticipates the future, and establishes relations with things in order to benefit from them directly or through instruments. This is part of the subjection of what is in heaven and earth to man. Intelligence and the ability to use things also produce practical knowledge: the discovery of new means by which things may be used to human advantage.

Knowledge divides into that which has no direct relation to human action, such as knowing external things and their properties, and that which directly governs action, such as judging acts good or evil, obligatory or permissible, or conceiving rule and subjection. The latter does not originate as an external object of perception. It is formed in the mind through instinct, thought, and feeling. Bodily systems such as nourishment and reproduction generate desires for what assists them and aversion to what hinders them; from this arise love, hatred, inclination, and desire, which in turn yield judgments concerning what should or should not be done. Such moral ideas are practical knowledge because, as mere ideas without action, they have no value.

God inspired these practical judgments in man so that he might act toward his preservation and perfection. The general guidance by which God gives each thing its creation and guides it to its end applies to every creature. In particular, the soul is inspired concerning its vices and piety. The judgments ‘should do’ and ‘should not do’ exist in the mind, as do such social aspects as prestige, wealth, progress, mastership, servitude, presidency, and possession; the underlying man or object exists externally, but these relations and valuations do not.

Man naturally uses material things, plants, animals, and finally other human beings to preserve himself and satisfy his needs. Yet each person finds others seeking to exploit him in the same way. This compels a reciprocal arrangement: people live together, cooperate, and safeguard one another’s rights against their duties. Social justice and human sociability therefore arise, in this account, not from an original altruistic urge, but from the unavoidable mutual tendency to exploit. When one obtains power, this compromised justice is readily forgotten: strong individuals, nations, and states disregard the weak. If social justice were the primary natural urge, justice would predominate; instead, history displays the rule of might, subjugation, and exploitation.

Differences of body, habitat, habit, character, and strength intensify this original drive. The powerful exploit the weak with little return; the weak resort to deception, await an opportunity, and retaliate severely when able. The result is disorder, disruption of the social system, and the loss of felicity. Although human beings share humanity and some common activities, their differing conditions, feelings, characters, ambitions, sins, and aims generate divergent acts and inevitable social conflict. This made comprehensive laws necessary to give each person his right and secure obedience to law.

The commentary criticizes two contemporary methods of enforcing law: coercive legislation that discards belief in God and makes morality follow social fashion, and moral training combined with force while excluding religion from education. Both, it says, are founded on ignorance of human reality. Man belongs to God, returns to Him, and continues eternally after death; the quality of his next life depends on his conduct, relation to his Creator, and acquired traits in this life. A life built on denying divinity destroys the self and ruins the Hereafter.

The passage compares worldly life to a caravan’s temporary stopping place. Those who settle disputes only by dividing present provisions, whether through punishment or through worldly moral ideals, forget that the caravan is travelling toward a distant home. The sensible course is to use provisions according to present need while preserving what is required for later stages and the final destination. Likewise, life in this world must be governed in view of the everlasting life to come.

For this reason God’s laws rest upon His oneness, true faith, noble character, and good deeds. They teach the whole reality of life, from its origin to its destination, and make worldly life preparation for the everlasting Hereafter. Divine law alone is based on knowledge. Sending prophets with glad tidings and warnings is joined to sending the Book containing laws in order to judge human differences. Denial of the Hereafter is presented as an attempt to evade the responsibilities it entails: worshipping the Creator and obeying His laws in worship, social dealings, and penalties. Those who make this world their ultimate concern follow conjecture and ignorance, whereas religion calls to knowledge, clear sight, wisdom, purification, and the life that God and the Messenger give.

Al-Mizan rejects the allegation that true religion rests upon blind faith or opposes learning. Some scientists, confined to natural and social sciences, failed to find a physical proof of metaphysical realities and treated absence of proof as proof of absence. They also encountered myths falsely imposed as religion and priestly demands for unquestioning acceptance. These factors led them to condemn religion as hostile to knowledge. But true religion neither encourages ignorance nor commands action without understanding; it comes with guidance and an illuminating Book.

Religion initially removed social and worldly differences; even apparently nonreligious laws ultimately rest on that original religious teaching. Afterwards, those who possessed the clear Book and knowledge of it created divisions in religion through rivalry, injustice, and rebellion. This was not a demand of nature, for divine religion is based on the unchanging nature in which God made mankind. Nature can coexist with forgetfulness and doubt, but not with conscious revolt and deliberate transgression. The verse therefore identifies the origin of religious differences as those given the Book, especially its learned possessors, after signs had been clarified. This does not mean that every person who has gone astray is a rebel: God may pardon those confused or unable to find the way, whereas the rebel has knowingly rejected clear signs.

After death man enters barzakh (intermediate life) and then the Hereafter. That life is individual, without social cooperation, mutual aid, partnership, exploitation, civilization, or practical knowledge of the worldly sort. Each person returns alone to his Lord, accompanied by his deeds and confronted with their good or evil results. Reality and the Great News disputed in this world become manifest; striving is no longer undertaken, but its results are seen and fully recompensed.

In the detailed exegesis, nās means men or mankind, while ummah means a group united by a single aim, goal, or ambition. This root meaning permits its use for one person, a group, a period, or, according to some commentators, religion. ‘Mankind was but one people’ refers to humanity’s beginning, when people had simple lives and thoughts and no conflict over livelihood or religion. The subsequent clause shows that worldly differences arose after this original unity, since prophets and the Book were sent to judge those differences. The later clause shows that religious disagreement began only after the Book’s revelation, with those who received it.

The commentary regards the primitive state of early humanity as consistent with this reading. As one goes back in human history, people appear less familiar with nature’s possibilities and possessed only simple means of obtaining food, shelter, and protection. Such people would not sustain major disagreements. As skills, knowledge, and means of mastery increased, stronger persons sought to reduce others to subjection and take more than they returned. Thus arose natural social differences. The same drive that helped produce society, through the need for mutual cooperation, also produced conflict. This is no contradiction: competing natural demands require a higher judge to balance them, just as reason regulates the conflict between hunger and digestion. God removed the social conflict by raising prophets and revealing the Book to judge human contentions.

Al-Mizan rejects several readings of the verse. It rejects the claim that all people were initially on the right path and differed only after the Book, because the verse contains two conflicts, and because sending prophets and a Book would otherwise lack justification. It rejects the claim that mankind’s original oneness meant universal error, because the verse attributes the later error and disagreement to the Book’s followers after its signs were clarified. It rejects restricting ‘mankind’ to Israelites merely because a similar phrase occurs concerning them elsewhere; a quality attributed in one verse to a people is not thereby exclusive to them. It rejects identifying mankind with Adam alone because the context does not bear it. Finally, it rejects reading kāna, ‘was,’ as simply a continuing present assertion that humanity is naturally social. Cooperation is not the primary urge but a compromise forced by reciprocal exploitation; the reading also requires an unstated conflict and, in any event, ignores the verse’s explicit distinction between the pre-Book universal conflict and the post-Book religious conflict of those given knowledge.

Baʿth literally means awakening, revival, or bringing to life, rather than merely sending. Its use suits the early period’s quietness and inactivity. Perhaps this also explains why the verse calls God’s representatives nabiyyīn rather than mursalīn: a nabī is one possessing news, and prophetic teaching awakens people to the truth that they are created by the one Lord, are returning to Him, will be resurrected, and are now in a transient station like sport or play. They must remember their origin, present condition, and destination in every act.

God alone sends the prophets, which establishes their protection from error in receiving and explaining revelation. They bring mercy, God’s pleasure, and Paradise as glad tidings to believers who guard against evil, and chastisement, divine displeasure, and Fire as warning to those who reject truth and sin. Glad tidings and warnings are the most effective means of directing ordinary people, though some of God’s righteous servants obey solely for their Lord’s sake, apart from hope of reward or fear of punishment.

Kitāb literally means what is written. Since writing confirms covenants and decrees, it can also denote binding commands and established, irrefutable truth; the Qur’an is called a Book in this sense. ‘The Book’ may mean the class of all divine books or a particular understood Book. On the latter reading it is Noah’s Book. Read with (42:13), the verse indicates that Noah received a written Book containing a Law; that his was the first divine Book containing a shariah; and that the original human unity preceded Noah’s mission and Book.

God guided the believers to the truth concerning both worldly and religious differences. This occurred ‘by His will’ because no one can impose guidance upon God. The concluding statement, ‘And Allah guides whom He pleases to the straight path,’ explains that guidance belongs to His discretion; He willed to guide believers to the straight path.

From the verse as a whole, Al-Mizan defines religion as a way of life that secures worldly good in a manner that perfects the real and everlasting life near God. Its shariah must therefore include the laws needed for livelihood in this world. Religion was first instituted to remove natural differences and later perfected to remove both those and the unnatural differences arising from religious scholars’ rebellion. Religion develops until its laws encompass every need and contingency of life; when it reaches such completeness, it is final and no subsequent religion follows. Hence a final religion must be comprehensive, every succeeding shariah was more complete than its predecessor, and the Book brought to Muḥammad is presented as final, explanatory of all things, and protected against falsehood.

The reason for prophetic mission is that human nature advances toward social cooperation and toward conflict at the same time. Since the source of the defect is nature itself, nature cannot repair it. Reform must come from the Creator, who completes every creature’s creation and guides it to its perfection. God’s unrestricted bounty aids every being according to its need; any limitation comes from man, not God. Prophethood, through revelation, is this divine intervention. It is called baʿth because its relation to ordinary human perception resembles wakefulness in relation to sleep. The prophet receives from the unseen the knowledge by which life’s differences can be removed; this received perception is revelation, and the condition of receiving it is prophethood.

Reason and experience, the commentary argues, confirm these points: human beings continue exploiting one another; reciprocal exploitation creates society; no society is free of conflict; conflict requires social laws; and human reason has not devised laws that eradicate its roots. The modern world’s wars, destruction, tyranny, national subjugation, degradation of human dignity, and seizure of life and property illustrate this despite claims of civilization and scientific progress. Religion can remove the conflict because it summons people to real knowledge, high character, and noble action; Islam is said to have demonstrated this during the period when it governed Muslim society.

The final religion shows that humanity has reached the final stage of its completion. Prophethood ends with Muḥammad, whose religion is never abrogated and whose shariah remains until the end of the world; there can be no situation without Islamic guidance. Material and physical sciences have advanced greatly since Islam’s advent, but morality has not advanced and may have declined. Humanity has strengthened the body while weakening the soul, so its development is one-sided. Islamic law therefore remains relevant.

Against the objection that laws must change as society advances, Al-Mizan replies that religion seeks not merely material or technological perfection but balanced bodily and spiritual perfection and both material and spiritual felicity. Materialist societies change with matter, but Islam does not seek a one-sided social development. Those who demand its abrogation must first produce a person or society uniting religious tenets with material progress and identify the deficiency that a new shariah would need to complete; without this, they have no ground for claiming that Islam should be abrogated.

The passage then argues that all prophets are maʿṣūm. ʿIṣmah, literally protection, here has three relevant forms: protection from error in receiving revelation, protection from error in communicating it, and protection from sins, meaning whatever violates God’s obligatory command and the requirements of human servitude to Him. It does not concern unrelated perceptual or practical mistakes, such as misjudging food or medicine.

God’s sending prophets with the true Book to guide people to true belief and deeds proves that revelation must be received and transmitted correctly, since God neither errs nor fails in His purposes. The revelation is guarded from its descent to its delivery, so that it does not decay or undergo alteration from Satan or any other source. Protection in delivery also entails protection from sin. Actions preach as words do: if a prophet did what he forbade, his action would declare the act lawful while his words prohibited it. He would then convey contradiction rather than truth. Thus truthful delivery depends on sinlessness.

Other Qur’anic arguments reinforce this conclusion. All prophets are guided by God, and one whom God guides cannot be led astray; since every sin is misguidance and obedience to Satan, prophets are free of sin as well as error in revelation. They are among those upon whom God bestowed favors, who are opposed to those under wrath or astray. They are described as guided, chosen, devout, humble, and unlike the later generation that neglected prayer and followed desires. Therefore they did not follow sensual desire or incur sin, even before their appointment.

Miracles confirming a prophet’s claim also confirm that he neither lies nor lacks the capacity faithfully to communicate God’s message. One who committed sins that undermined the project he preached would not be qualified to invite people to it; therefore divine authentication through miracles entails protection in receiving and delivering revelation and faithful obedience to God. It would be unfitting to compare God’s choice of prophets with human reliance on imperfect agents, since men tolerate inadequacy either because they accept deficient performance or require only limited service. Neither possibility applies to a divine purpose.

The fact that Muslim scholars may warn people despite not being sinless does not undermine this argument. Scholars are permitted to communicate what they have learned, but their words are not thereby divinely confirmed or made a proof against people. Such confirmation is distinctive to prophethood, not to mere warning.

A messenger must be obeyed by Allah’s permission in both words and actions. If he erred in revelation or committed sin, obedience to him would make God at once command and forbid, will and not will, approve and disapprove the same thing. This is not merely an order to do what is impossible; it is an impossible order in itself. Likewise, messengers leave people without an argument against God only if they themselves avoid every forbidden error and act. Otherwise people could justly cite the messenger’s sins or mistakes as an excuse, frustrating the purpose of sending him.

The objection that these proofs establish only that prophets did not sin, not that they possessed ʿiṣmah as an inner faculty, is answered in two stages. For the immediate argument, their not sinning or erring suffices. More fully, every event has a cause, and the prophet’s lifelong, unvarying correctness and obedience disclose a stable faculty in his soul that protects him from error and sin. His deeds remain voluntary, as all human acts are voluntary, but unlike ordinary people his knowledge and will are invariably sound and directed to serving God rather than pleasure and lust. This firmly rooted knowledge is a trait analogous to chastity, courage, or justice. To deny such a faculty while affirming constant obedience would imply that the prophet has no choice and that his acts arise directly from God rather than from his own knowledge and will. ʿIṣmah is from God, who creates in the prophet this causal faculty, while the prophet’s obedient acts proceed by his own will.

Finally, Al-Mizan discusses rasūl and nabī. Rasūl means one who brings a message, risālah, and has the distinction of mediating between God and His creatures. Nabī means one who brings news, nabaʾ, and has knowledge of God and from God. The common claim that every messenger is a prophet but not every prophet a messenger, because a prophet need not be commissioned to convey, is not fully supported by Qur’anic usage. Moses is called both messenger and prophet in a context where the descriptions rise in distinction, and another verse speaks of sending both messenger and prophet. Yet other verses show prophets sent to people with divine communication. The likely reconciliation is that both are sent: the prophet conveys knowledge of the unseen and what benefits people in this world and the Hereafter, while the messenger bears an additional special message that completes the proof, so rejection brings destruction and chastisement. Thus the difference is what their literal meanings indicate: mediation in the case of the messenger and divinely given knowledge in the case of the prophet.

The Qur’an mentions many prophets but not all. It names Adam, Noah, Idrīs, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Abraham, Lot, Ishmael, Alyasaʿ, Dhu al-Kifl, Ilyās, Jonah, Isaac, Jacob, Jethro, Moses, Aaron, David, Solomon, Zachariah, John, Ishmael (Ṣādiq al-waʿd), Jesus, and Muḥammad, and it alludes to others without naming them. The status of such figures as Moses’ servant, Dhu al-Qarnayn, Amram, and ʿUzayr is unclear. Reports of the total number of prophets are not mutawātir and differ; the best-known narration, reported from Abū Dharr, says that the Prophet spoke of one hundred and twenty-four thousand prophets, of whom three hundred and thirteen were messengers.

The chief prophets are the ulu al-ʿazm: Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muḥammad. Their ʿazm means that they firmly maintained the original covenant with God and did not forget it. Each brought a new law and a Book. Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muḥammad are explicitly associated with Books, while the present verse together with (42:13) establishes a Book for Noah; all these Books contained shariah. David received the Zabūr, and traditions report Books for Adam, Shīth, and Idrīs, but these did not contain a law or shariah. Revelation, a mode of God’s speech, is essential to prophethood; a fuller discussion of it is deferred to the Chapter of al-Shūra (Ch. 42).
verses.214:
Al-Mizan presents this verse as the conclusion of the preceding discussion. Religion is God’s guidance and grace, leading to human prosperity and happiness in this world and the hereafter. People must therefore submit to it rather than follow Satan, create divisions, or turn this divine remedy into a disease. By pursuing lusts and worldly adornment, they would turn God’s bounty into disbelief and ingratitude and incur His wrath, as the Israelites did when they perverted the bounty given to them. The trial continues: like earlier peoples, this community will be tested, and none attains the bliss of religion and nearness to God except through fortitude and complete submission to His commands.

The believers are again directly addressed here after the intervening verses had spoken of them in the third person. Although they were the audience throughout, the style changed in the verses concerning chastisement and punishment, then returned to direct address once that purpose had been served. The particle am, literally “or,” has the contextual sense of “but”: will they devote themselves to submission, faith, steadfastness on religion, unity, and cooperation, or instead imagine that they will enter the Garden without undergoing what befell earlier believers?

The commentary explains that mathal and mithl denote a likeness that forms an image in the hearer’s mind. Here mathal has the sense of an illustrative likeness, not an adjective, because the verse itself explains it through the afflictions suffered by former peoples. Baʾsāʾ is hardship affecting matters outside a person—such as property, prestige, family, or social order—whereas ḍarrʾ is hardship affecting the person, such as wounds, murder, or sickness. Zalzalah and zilzāl literally signify an earthquake; derived from a root meaning to slip or stumble, with repetition suggesting repeated stumbling, they are used metaphorically for agitation and disturbance, hence “were shaken violently.”

Al-Mizan holds that apparently both the Messenger and the believers said, “When will the help of Allah come?” There is no difficulty in the Messenger saying this: he may have sought the help God had promised His messengers, that they would be assisted (37:171-172) and that God and His messengers would prevail (58:21). The wording in (12:110) is even harsher than that of this verse. “Now, surely the help of Allah is nigh!” apparently answers their call. Thus, the verse establishes that testing and trial will continue in this community as they did among earlier ones, and that when the same actions and attitudes recur, the same consequences follow in religion as history repeats itself.
verses.215:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse both answers the question and deliberately redirects it. The phrases “Whatever of good you spend” and “whatever of good you do” indicate that what is spent is wealth, whatever its form or quantity, and that spending it upon deserving people is a good deed fully known to Allah. Yet the principal reply directs attention to the more worthwhile question: where, or for whom, wealth should be spent—parents, near kin, orphans, the poor, and the wayfarer. Thus, the view that the question was obvious and that the verse instead supplies the beneficiaries is basically sound, but incomplete because it overlooks this indirect answer concerning what is spent.

The commentary rejects attempts to make mā (“what”) mean “how,” whether on the ground that a logical question about quiddity would be unfit for eloquent speech, or because it was already known that wealth was to be spent. Mā is not a technical term restricted to seeking a definition by nearest genus and species; rather, it asks for features that distinguish a thing from others. Those features may be supplied through such a definition or through other recognizable qualities. It therefore cannot be shifted to “how” merely because the general nature of the thing is known. The question about the cow in (2:70-71), for example, correctly sought its distinguishing particulars, not its genus and species. Nor can the claim that the questioners asked both what to spend and where to spend it explain the verse; Al-Mizan dismisses this as nonsense.

The redirection is an instance of a recurrent Qur'anic style in which speech moves from one subject to another that deserves greater attention—such as from a parable to satire against idols, ultimate loss, multiplied reward, or the person who possesses a pure heart. The commentary calls this an exceptional beauty of the Qur'an.

Finally, changing “spending” into “doing good,” and referring to what is spent as “good,” yields two principles. Spending on the stated beneficiaries is highly recommended whether little or much is given, but what is given should be good, desirable, and loved, not inferior goods one would dislike receiving. It must also be given in a good manner, without reproachfully reminding the recipient of the gift or causing injury to his feelings.
verses.216: Al-Mizan states that fighting is prescribed despite its being disliked: people may dislike what benefits them and love what harms them, whereas Allah knows and they do not.
verses.217: Al-Mizan gives this answer to the question about fighting in the sacred month: such fighting is grave, but obstructing Allah’s way and denying it, barring people from the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people are still graver with Allah; mischief is graver than killing. The opponents will continue fighting believers, if they can, to turn them back from their religion. Whoever apostatizes and dies an unbeliever forfeits their deeds in this world and the hereafter and will abide among the inmates of the Fire.
verses.218:
Al-Mizan presents those who believe, flee their homes, and strive in Allah’s way as hoping for His mercy; Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.

It explains that kitābah, when used legislatively, denotes an obligatory command; fighting in God’s way is thus compulsory for believers, apart from exemptions established elsewhere, such as for the weak, sick, or those unable to provide the means while remaining sincere. The passive form kutiba avoids explicitly naming God in connection with a command disliked by its recipients, thereby preserving the sanctity of the divine name. Kurh is hardship felt within oneself, whether natural or otherwise, whereas karh is hardship imposed by an external agency.

The commentary records three explanations for believers’ dislike of fighting. First, fighting naturally brings death, injury, financial loss, scarcity, and social disorder; the community addressed included steadfast believers who would not dislike a divine command and a more numerous group of weak faith and crooked thought who would. This is judged the most fitting explanation, especially in light of the passive wording. Second, believers may have wanted to delay battle because their enemies were stronger and better equipped; the verse corrects their reliance on appearances by affirming God’s hidden purpose and superior knowledge. Third, some believers’ mercy toward God’s creatures may have made them prefer gentle invitation to fighting, lest opponents die in disbelief. The verse rejects this judgment because the call of truth would not affect those spiritually ruined people from whom true religion could expect no good.

In divine speech, “may be” does not express uncertainty in God; it directs the hearers to expect the stated possibility. Its repetition corrects two separate errors: dislike of fighting and love of peace and ease. The verse first makes them doubt the soundness of these preferences and then discloses the decisive reason: Allah knows the hidden realities of things, while people know only what He permits them to know. They must therefore leave such determinations to Him. Knowledge in its reality and totality belongs to God alone.

On fighting in the sacred month, Al-Mizan holds that the verse prohibits it. It says the context indicates an incident involving an unintentional killing, and that its indications confirm traditions concerning ʿAbdullāh b. Jaḥsh and his companions. “God’s way” means worship and virtuous deeds, especially hajj; apparently, the pronoun in “denying it” refers to this way and signifies practical denial rather than denial in belief. The Sacred Mosque is joined to God’s way, meaning hindrance from both. The commentary rejects the claim that the prohibition was abrogated by the command to slay idolaters.

The idolaters’ expulsion of the Messenger and the believers—who were truly the people of the Sacred Mosque—is graver than fighting in the sacred month. Their mischief in reproaching believers and attempting to return them to disbelief is graver than killing, so they cannot rightly condemn the believers for the killing. Here ḥatta signifies purpose: they will continue fighting believers so that they may turn them back from their religion. Apostasy is threatened with forfeiture of deeds in this world and the next and with abiding in the Fire.

Forfeiture, ḥabṭ, is the nullification of a deed and the loss of its effect. It concerns all actions by which a person seeks happiness in life, not merely acts of worship done before apostasy. Faith gives deeds life, making worldly life happy and actions illuminated; disbelief and apostasy render deeds ineffective in producing felicity in either world. One who comes to true faith after disbelief has deeds given a new life. One who apostatizes has deeds rendered dead and void; if he returns to Islam, it is hoped that they will revive, but if he dies an unbeliever, the forfeiture is confirmed.

Accordingly, the commentary dismisses the dispute over whether an apostate’s earlier deeds are forfeited at apostasy or only at death. One position preserves them until death unless he returns to faith, while the other regards apostasy as permanently nullifying them even if he returns; both overlook that deeds become ineffective through disbelief, while their forfeiture is confirmed at death. Recompense, punishment, forfeiture, and atonement are effects of deeds in the soul. Good and evil actions immediately produce qualities entitling a person to reward or punishment, yet these qualities remain alterable while the soul is joined to the body. At death, action and change cease, and the acquired qualities become fixed, except through God’s mercy or the intercession of His chosen servants. Thus entitlement begins with the act, but its irreversible confirmation comes at death; forfeiture begins with disbelief, applies to worldly as well as otherworldly deeds, and is confirmed at death.

Al-Mizan rejects iḥbāṭ, the theory that good and evil deeds cancel one another. This includes both the claim that each later good or evil act erases its predecessor and the claim that the lighter side is subtracted from the heavier. Good and evil deeds can remain together in a person’s account, and each is separately recompensed; only sins that sever the servant’s relation to the Master, such as disbelief and idolatry, forfeit all deeds. Takfīr, however, is affirmed: particular good deeds can expiate evil deeds, and repentance, faith, and good action can even change evil deeds into good ones.

The commentary then sets out further rules of recompense. Apostasy, disbelief in God’s signs, and enmity toward them may forfeit good deeds in both worlds, while submission to Islam and repentance may expiate evil deeds in both. Opposition to the Messenger and raising one’s voice over his may nullify some deeds; prayer, hajj, and avoidance of great sins may atone for particular sins. Some sins transfer good deeds from their doer to another: murder is one example, and traditions of the Prophet and the imams of Ahl al-Bayt identify backbiting and calumny among others. Some acts of obedience transfer evil deeds from their doer to another. Misleading others makes a person bear evil deeds like those of the people led astray, while some obedience brings a person good like that done by others. Sins may bring double punishment, while good deeds may bring doubled or multiplied reward. A good deed’s like may be granted to another without diminishing the doer’s reward; likewise, oppression of orphans may bring comparable oppression upon one’s children after death. The commentary also affirms exchanges in which good deeds transfer one person’s evils to another and the other’s good deeds to him, with a reverse exchange possible through evil deeds; it defers the detailed circumstances of this last rule.

The effects of deeds in happiness and misery differ from their physical effects. In the order of recompense, deeds may be changed, transferred, or given effects opposite to those expected in physical causation. This does not abolish reason: divine judgment, including at death, in Barzakh, and on the Day of Resurrection, proceeds with justice and intellectual proof. The Qur’an speaks in the language of mastership, servitude, command, warning, reward, and punishment so that people can understand what exceeds ordinary human thought; its account of recompense is therefore expressed through the practical wisdom of social law.

Changes and transfers in recompense do not violate the rule that no one bears another’s burden. The unjust killer bears the consequences of the slain person’s wrongs because, in this order, they are his own deed; a leader who misleads and a follower who accepts the misguidance are each responsible for his own participation; and whoever aids oppression shares in the oppressor’s acts to that degree. Every soul is repaid for what it has actually done according to God’s knowledge, not human reckoning. Statements that sinners lack knowledge mean that they do not act upon what they know in this world and cannot escape the effects of their own foolishness in the next, not that rational argument and awareness disappear altogether.

Imam al-Ghazālī’s reported explanation treats transfer as a metaphor for the transfer of reward or punishment: obedience creates light in the heart and sin darkness, so oppression extinguishes the oppressor’s light and produces light in the victim, while the victim’s darkness is removed and new darkness appears in the oppressor. Al-Mizan objects that this makes the rules of recompense a double metaphor. Since practical social wisdom treats them as realities, recompense too should be treated as real in that context, even though the material world may be regarded metaphorically from the spiritual world. Deeds are also preserved, written, and embodied for the Day of Resurrection.

Good and evil deeds further relate to outward events. Obedience opens blessings and felicity, while persistent disobedience, injustice, and corruption bring social disorder, conflict, destruction, and natural calamities. This applies to nations and individuals; people may also receive blessings linked to righteous forefathers or suffer effects linked to ancestral injustice. For the righteous, prosperity is both blessing and trial, and gratitude brings increase; for the wicked, prosperity may be a gradual leading toward ruin or a respite completing the proof against them. Hardship purifies and tests the righteous, whereas it punishes the wicked. Passages that speak of worldly luxury being given to disbelievers do not concern this subject; their purpose is to show the world’s lack of value before God.

The commentary does not deny physical and natural causes of calamities, nor treat deeds and natural causes as joint causes. Rather, it posits human good and evil deeds as a higher cause that moves the apparent causes, as a writer moves the hand and pen without negating their respective effects. Creation equips each species to resist harm and advance toward perfection; humanity likewise is guided toward its end through divine call, trial, and, where there is no hope of attainment, destruction. Because creation is purposeful and returns to God, this system of trial and retribution is invincible, although God pardons much.

Actions that cause happiness ultimately prevail over those that cause misery. Stability, permanence, peace, hope, and victory belong to the good, while instability, decline, fear, defeat, and destruction belong to the evil. People may fail to see this because they judge by their short present, whereas God governs the whole of time and may allow a brief disturbance or an individual tragedy for a lasting good. Spiritual victory also differs from material domination: coercive rule is temporary, but faith conquers hearts and forms people willing to sacrifice for the truth. Falsehood cannot endure against truth. A believer is therefore never truly vanquished: if victorious, he gains victory and reward; if forced by an enemy to do what God dislikes, he must comply to save his life and God is pleased with that outwardly irreligious conduct; and if killed in God’s way, he receives an everlasting life. Nature is leading humanity toward truth and felicity, so apparent victories of falsehood are only stages toward truth’s manifestation. Good is attributed to God as existence, while evil and wrong are forms of non-existence attributable to the human being; hence good words and deeds endure and benefit, whereas falsehood passes away.

Finally, Al-Mizan says that good words and deeds accord with reason, the faculty that distinguishes right from wrong and good from evil. Divine law rests on this faculty and forbids acts that derange or confuse it, including intoxicants, gambling, vain speech, sexual immorality, cheating, false speech, slander, false accusation, embezzlement, and murder. Personal and collective human ills arise from actions that disturb sound perception and judgment.
verses.219:
Al-Mizan explains that khamr is every liquid made to intoxicate. Its root signifies hiding, and it is so called because it conceals reason and prevents discrimination between right and wrong and good and bad. Although the Arabs had known intoxicating drinks chiefly from grapes, dates, and barley, later varieties with differing degrees of intoxication all remain khamr. Maysir means gambling, named from ease because it promises wealth without the labour of earning it. The term was especially used for an arrow-game in which ten participants divided a slaughtered camel: those allotted one of seven winning arrows received specified shares, while the three others received nothing and paid for the camel.

The commentary defines ithm, sin, as an evil condition in a thing or in reason that prevents a person from attaining good, bringing unhappiness and failure even into other affairs and disturbing the felicity of life. Intoxicants and gambling plainly have this character. Alcohol harms the body, while its addiction produces moral and social ruin: depravity, shamelessness, disclosure of secrets, slander, injury, crime, and murder. Above all, it damages reason itself, disarranging thought, feeling, and perception during intoxication and afterwards; this impairment of the faculty of perception and reason is its greatest disaster and the source of its other evils.

Al-Mizan holds that Islam founds its laws on true reason and emphatically prohibits actions that obstruct its proper functioning. Intoxicants, gambling, adultery, and falsehood belong to this class; drinking is particularly destructive among deeds and lying among words. Practices that nullify reason’s rule—and especially politics founded on alcohol and lies—endanger humanity and undermine happiness. Their apparent remedies only worsen the burden and end in failure. For the commentary, Islam’s grounding of its shariah in reason and its prohibition of what damages reason distinguishes it from humanly devised systems.

Because people readily pursue lusts, bad habits spread easily and are hard to leave, whereas chastity and piety do not spread in the same way. God therefore legislated gradually and sympathetically, leading people step by step to the intended end. The prohibition of alcohol illustrates this process. First, the Meccan verse prohibiting sin (7:33) already prohibited it, though alcohol was not yet identified explicitly as sin; this ambiguity was perhaps a compassionate temporary overlooking. The Meccan verse distinguishing intoxication from “goodly provision” (16:67) hinted indirectly at the same point without calling it bad provision. Then the Medinan command not to approach prayer while intoxicated (4:43) imposed a partial ban at the best time and place, prayer in the mosque. Reason and context show that this partial prohibition preceded the total prohibition, since a gradual law moves from the easier stage to the harder, not in reverse.

The present verse, revealed after (4:43), is therefore held to impose the total prohibition of intoxicants and gambling: it declares both to contain great sin, while the earlier verse (7:33) had categorically prohibited sin. Al-Mizan rejects the view that the verse was unclear because ithm merely means harm and because something partly harmful and partly beneficial might be permitted until the later command in al-Māʾidah. Ithm cannot be reduced to harm merely because profits are mentioned beside it; its Qur’anic uses show it to be sin. Nor does the verse make its legal command conditional on a person’s estimate of harms and benefits, leaving room for personal opinion. Even if its statement were treated as a reason for the ruling, the reason would be that the sin is greater than the profit, not simply that harm exists.

Moreover, even on the supposition that the verse did not itself explicitly announce prohibition, it unmistakably calls intoxicants and gambling great sins, while (7:33) had already prohibited sin. Taken together, the Meccan and Medinan verses leave no excuse for contrary personal judgment. The use of kabīr and akbar shows their sin to be among the greatest; the Qur’an applies “great sin” to no sins other than polytheism and these two. Thus, in Al-Mizan’s view, there is no doubt that the verse absolutely prohibits them. The later injunction, culminating in “Will you then desist?” (5:93-94), indicates that Muslims had nevertheless continued drinking after this verse and required a stronger admonition. Gambling likewise causes evident social evil and ruins the structure of life.

Kibr denotes greatness in magnitude, as kathrah denotes multiplicity in number; each is relative to comparison. What is greater than one thing may be smaller than another, and without comparison there is neither greater nor smaller, numerous nor few. Nafʿ, profit, is opposed to ḍarar, harm or loss: these describe things desired or disliked for the sake of something else, unlike good and bad, which are liked or disliked in themselves. The profits of intoxicants and gambling are monetary gain and the amusement and merriment sought through them. The verse uses the plural for profits but the singular when comparing sin with profit because the comparison concerns magnitude, not number.

Regarding spending, Al-Mizan takes ʿafw, “whatever can be spared,” to mean moderation in expenditure. The answer corresponds to the question in the manner of the earlier answer concerning what should be spent. The phrase fid-dunyā wa al-ākhirah does not mean that people will ponder while located in this world and the hereafter; it identifies the subject of their reflection. Believers are urged to consider the realities and affairs of both worlds: this world is the place in which they live and acquire what benefits them in their permanent home, where they return to their Lord for recompense. The command embraces inquiry into existence, the beginning and end, nature’s mysteries, social concepts, moral and ethical values, and the laws governing individuals and communities—in short, all knowledge and affairs that bear on human happiness and misery from man’s origin to his return to God.

Although the Qur’an requires unqualified obedience to God and His Messenger, the commentary says that it also wants people to reflect on the commands and their philosophy, grasp their realities, and follow their light rather than obey blindly. “Thus does Allah make clear” probably refers to explaining the philosophy behind the laws and commands and clarifying the fundamentals of faith and belief.

On orphans, Al-Mizan sees a clear indication that the verse lightens an earlier hardship. Its permission to mingle with orphans, followed by the statement that God could have made matters difficult, shows that prior rules of guardianship had caused Muslims anxiety. The verse apparently came after severe warnings against consuming orphans’ property or substituting inferior property for theirs (4:2) and (4:10). Iṣlāḥ, setting matters right, is a noun denoting real and sound management, not a mere appearance of reform, as is indicated by God’s knowledge of the mischief-maker and the well-doer.

The permission to mingle rests on the equality and brotherhood of believers. This principle abolishes the distinctions that produce injustice, rebellion, arrogance, and the treatment of others as inferior, establishing balance between the weak orphan and the powerful guardian, as between rich and poor. A guardian may therefore mix property and affairs with an orphan’s only as one brother deals with another, with equal obligations toward each other. If he takes something from the orphan’s property, he must give an equivalent in return and add it to the orphan’s property. This relaxes the prior rigour, but only where the guardian’s intention is genuinely to improve the orphan’s affairs and he acts as a brother. God will not reproach such mingling, but He knows and distinguishes the mischief-maker from the well-doer. The use of min after “knows” probably indicates that yaʿlamu here carries the sense of distinguishing; ʿanat means difficulty and hardship.

God will not reproach such mingling, but He knows and distinguishes the mischief-maker from the well-doer. The use of min after “knows” probably indicates that yaʿlamu here carries the sense of distinguishing; ʿanat means difficulty and hardship.
verses.221:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse forbids marrying idolatrous women, or giving believing women to idolatrous men, until they believe; it also declares a believing bondswoman or bondsman better than an alluring idolater. Al-Rāghib’s view that nikāḥ originally means ʿaqd, the marriage-tie, and was only later used metaphorically for intercourse is sound, provided that ʿaqd means the marital bond itself rather than merely the formulae of proposal and acceptance.

Mushrikāt is an active participle derived from ishrāk, ascribing a partner to God. Polytheism, belief, and unbelief have degrees. Its open form consists in affirming more than one god, worshipping idols, and treating them as intercessors. A less manifest form occurs among the people of the book through denial of Muḥammad’s prophethood and such beliefs as that ʿUzayr or Jesus is God’s son, or that they are God’s sons and beloved. More hidden is the belief that apparent causes independently produce their effects and reliance upon them; the most hidden form is forgetfulness of God and attention to other than Him, from which only God’s chosen servants with pure hearts escape.

Yet Al-Mizan distinguishes between applying a verb, adjective, or active participle literally and using it as a settled designation for a person. One who neglects an obligatory pilgrimage may be said to have “disbelieved,” as in (3:97), but is a sinner, not simply called an unbeliever; at most he may be called a disbeliever in pilgrimage. The same distinction governs such Qur’anic terms as righteous, thankful, purified, sinner, and unjust. Thus, not everyone who commits open or hidden polytheism may be named a polytheist.

The Qur’an’s designation “idolater” or “polytheist” is used for disbelievers other than the people of the book. Jews and Christians are instead given the distinct name “people of the book,” while kāfir is the broader term covering all outside Islam. The statements that Abraham was upright and not among the polytheists do not identify Jews and Christians as polytheists: “upright” indirectly contrasts Abraham with their deviation, while “not among the polytheists” alludes to idol-worshippers. Other verses may apply the active participle mushrik to people who associate others with God, such as those under Satan’s power; in that broad sense nearly all believers except God’s rare, truly righteous friends could fall under it. Nevertheless, such usage does not authorize making “polytheist” their nomenclature.

Accordingly, the apparent meaning of this verse concerns idol-worshipping men and women only, not marriage with the people of the book. There is therefore no basis for claiming that it abrogated verse (5:5), which concerns marriage with chaste women of the people of the book, or that verse (5:5) abrogated this verse. Nor do (2:221) and (60:10) together abrogate (5:5). Verse (60:10) concerns a man who becomes Muslim while his wife remains an unbeliever, forbidding him to retain that existing marriage; verse (5:5) concerns entering a new marriage with a woman from the people of the book. Their subjects differ, so abrogation does not arise.

Even if (2:221) and (60:10) were provisionally understood to forbid marriage with Jewish or Christian women, they could not abrogate (5:5). The latter is a relaxation described as God’s grace to believers, and relaxed rules take precedence over strict ones; if abrogation were supposed, (5:5) would abrogate the earlier restrictions, not the reverse. Chronology confirms this: al-Baqarah was revealed soon after the Hijrah, al-Mumtaḥanah before the conquest of Mecca in 8 A.H., and al-Māʾidah last. Although al-Māʾidah abrogated some earlier rules, no rule revealed in it was ever abrogated; earlier verses could not abrogate a verse not yet revealed.

The preference for a believing bondswoman over an idolatress reverses the social contempt then directed at slave-girls and the scorn attached to marrying one. By qualifying the bondswoman as believing while leaving the idolatress unrestricted, the verse teaches that faith outweighs even the noble birth, wealth, and beauty that attract men to an idolatress. The same applies to the believing bondsman and the idolater. The interpretation that amah and ʿabd here mean female and male servants of God—that is, simply believing women and men—is farfetched.

The prohibition is explained by the fact that idolaters follow falsehood and a wrong path until evil traits become rooted in them, disbelief and sin appear attractive, and they lose sight of truth. Their conduct and speech consequently invite believers to the fire. Believers, through true faith and righteous conduct, invite others by God’s leave to the garden and forgiveness. The verse names Allah rather than believers as the inviter in order to show that believers depend upon their Master in this invitation and in all their affairs. It may also mean that the law prohibiting marriage with polytheists is itself an invitation to the garden and forgiveness.
verses.222:
Al-Mizan explains that maḥīḍ and ḥayḍ denote the familiar periodic discharge of blood peculiar to women. The verse calls it adhā, meaning discomfort, distress, or the effect of something disagreeable, not simply ḍarar, harm or loss. The two terms have different opposites and usages, and Qur’anic usage distinguishes causing harm from causing distress. A condition may sometimes be both discomfort and harm, and those who interpret adhā here as harm cite physicians’ view that intercourse during this time disturbs the womb while it is cleansing itself and preparing for pregnancy. But the primary meaning intended is disagreeableness and distress.

The command to keep aloof and not go near women during menstruation means abstaining from sexual relations while the blood is flowing. It does not prescribe literal withdrawal from the woman in every respect. Al-Mizan contrasts the severe Jewish practice of isolating menstruating women, even in food, drink, household life, and sleep, with the Christians’ lack of restriction and the inconsistent customs of the pagan Arabs. The Qur’an takes a middle course. Its later phrase about going in to women after cleansing shows that the earlier expressions are metaphors for sexual relations: the prohibited act is intercourse in the front, while companionship in eating, drinking, sleeping, and other ordinary matters remains unrestricted. The repetition of maḥīḍ is meaningful: in the question it refers to menstruation itself, while in the answer it refers to its period.

The commentary then sets the immediate ruling within the wider Islamic ideas of ṭahārah and najāsah. Their pervasive legal use has made them al-ḥaqīqat al-sharʿiyyah, as though they were originally coined for religious meanings. In their basic human sense, cleanliness is the state in which a useful thing remains attractive and fit for use; uncleanliness arises when a change in such things, often of taste, smell, or colour, makes them repulsive. These are mutually exclusive qualities. Human beings first perceive them through the senses, then extend them to mental and spiritual matters, including parentage, character, belief, deed, and speech. Islam likewise applies cleanliness and uncleanliness to ideas, principles, and social laws as well as material things.

Al-Mizan distinguishes related words. Naẓāfah is sensible cleanliness after prior uncleanliness; nazāhah literally denotes distance and metaphorically being far from ugliness or uncleanliness; quds and subḥān are reserved for mental and spiritual matters. Qadhārah, used for filthiness, is metaphorically connected with putting a disliked thing apart, while rijs and rujz derive from fright and aversion and are likewise used figuratively for uncleanliness. Islamic law treats certain things as inherently unclean, including blood, urine, stool, semen of man and some animals, corpses, dogs, and pigs, and requires believers to avoid them in prayer, food, and drink. Ṭahārah is either from khabath, through removal of contact with such inherent impurities, or from ḥadath, through wuḍū or an obligatory bath.

This wider account has a theological order. Monotheism is the highest cleanliness before God; the other fundamentals of faith further purify the person, followed by ethical righteousness and the laws of the shariah that secure good in this world and the next. On this basis, Al-Mizan also relates the verse of purity concerning the People of the House to the same principle: Allah only desires to keep away the uncleanliness from you, O People of the House! and to purify you a [thorough] purifying (33:33).

In the present verse, “until they have become clean” means until the menstrual blood ceases, which begins the period of ṭuhr. “Then when they have cleansed themselves” means after an obligatory bath, or at least after washing the place from which the blood came. The subsequent command to go in to them follows a prohibition and therefore lifts the restriction; it permits sexual relations after cleanliness but does not make them obligatory. The expression is a euphemism, and “as Allah has commanded you” directs attention away from treating intercourse as mere amusement. The more apparent sense is a creative command: God has placed reproductive organs, power, and inclination in human beings for the survival of the species. The suggestion that it is instead a legislative command requiring a sufficient number of people to marry for human continuity is possible but far-fetched.

For the same reason, Al-Mizan rejects as the weakest argument the claim that “as Allah has commanded you” proves a prohibition concerning the posterior. The command following prohibition establishes permission, not a personal obligation whose omission would itself be an offence. Moreover, the command in view is creative rather than legislative. Even if it were taken legislatively, an obligation to ensure the continuation of humanity would rest only on a sufficient number of people, and disobeying an obligation is unlawful only where it is personally binding.

The ending that Allah loves those who turn much to Him and those who purify themselves applies to all the preceding rulings. Tawbah is return to God, and taṭahhur is cleansing oneself by turning away from dirtiness and returning to one’s original cleanliness. Obedience to God’s commands and avoidance of His prohibitions both remove the uncleanliness of disobedience and return the servant to his Lord. Since the statement is unrestricted, it covers every grade of repentance and purification: seeking forgiveness, obedience, and true faith, as well as washing, ablution, obligatory bathing, good deeds, and true spiritual knowledge. The emphatic forms tawwābīn and mutaṭahhirīn also convey both abundance in kind and repetition in number.

Turning to the next verse, Al-Mizan notes that ḥarth means tilling or cultivated land. Annā can mean “when” or “whenever,” and can sometimes mean “where”; under either possible reading, the phrase gives the couple a measure of freedom and cannot be a compulsory order. The repeated description of women as tillage nevertheless confines that freedom to the tillage itself: it concerns the place of intercourse or its time, not a licence to enter anywhere in the body. If the phrase means going to one’s tillage at any place one likes, it makes no statement about time and does not conflict with the menstrual prohibition. If it means at any time one likes, it is limited by the preceding verse to the period of purity from menstruation.

The verse of tillage cannot abrogate the prohibition during menstruation, whatever the order of revelation. The two grounds of the prohibition remain: menstruation remains a discomfort, and abstention preserves purity, which God loves and counts among His favours, as indicated by Allah does not desire to put on you any difficulty, but He intends to purify you and that He may complete His favor on you … (5:6). The procreative rationale of the tillage verse was already present when the menstrual prohibition was established; if it could not prevent that ruling, it cannot later repeal it. Moreover, the verse’s conclusion—doing good beforehand, fearing God, and knowing that one will meet Him—would be inappropriate if it merely granted a concession.

Women are compared to cultivated land because, as land preserves seed and produces food for continued life, the womb is the place in which a child develops from sperm into a human being and thus secures humanity’s continuation. God created between man and woman love, compassion, and attraction to lead to this end. Within the limits already established, the creative purpose does not require arbitrary confinement to one place or time where the purpose is served and no other obligatory work is hindered. This also explains the connection with the instruction to do good beforehand. Al-Mizan dismisses as patently absurd the interpretation that the verse permits withdrawal before ejaculation, and equally rejects the claim that doing good beforehand merely means saying bismiʾllāh before intercourse.

The final exhortations encourage marriage and reproduction, but human continuation is not an end in itself. It is wanted for the continuance of God’s religion, the dominance of monotheism, and worship through piety: And I did not create the jinn and the human beings except that they should worship Me (51:56). Thus, worldly commands are meant to facilitate worship, not to immerse people in sexual desire and worldly attractions. The apparent sense of doing good beforehand includes bringing new souls into the world and raising them as righteous servants of God and useful members of society, whose rewards may reach the forebears responsible for bringing them into existence. Its final sense, however, is to send good deeds ahead for the Day of Resurrection; righteous reproduction and upbringing are among such deeds.

Taqwā here requires approaching the tillage as God has commanded: neither exceeding His limits, neglecting His ordinance, nor committing unlawful acts. Knowing that one will meet God is effectively a warning to fear the meeting and its severe reckoning; “know” can carry the sense of being on guard. The conclusion gives good news to believers because good deeds and fear of the reckoning are the chief marks of faith.
