verses.224: Al-Mizan says: Do not make Allah a target of oaths against doing good, guarding against evil, or reconciling people; Allah is Hearing, Knowing.
verses.225: Al-Mizan says that Allah does not call you to account for vain oaths, but for what your hearts have earned; He is Forgiving, Forbearing.
verses.226: Al-Mizan says that those who swear to abstain from their wives must wait four months; if they return, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
verses.227:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Urḍah comes from al-ʿarḍ, displaying a thing as fit for its purpose; its use for a shooting target retains this sense, while its use for a hindrance is a later metaphor. al-Aymān, “oaths,” is the plural of al-yamīn, “right hand,” whose role in swearing, allegiance, and contracts led to the metaphorical naming of the act after its organ; the reverse naming also occurs.

The commentary, while adding “And God knows better!”, takes the most obvious meaning of (2:224) to be that one must not attach to God’s name oaths by which one refuses good, guarding against evil, or reconciliation, thereby making His name a means to abandon what He commands. On one grammatical analysis, antabarrū is actually anlatabarrū, with the negative omitted after an. On another, no word is omitted: “make not” governs “your doing good ...” and directly prohibits such oaths. On a third, al-ʿurḍah implies excessive swearing. Habitual swearing trivializes the oath, may encourage false oaths, and deprives its user of respect and credibility, making him a meanswearer whose words are not accepted (68:10). “God is Hearing, Knowing” is a threat under every reading.

Al-Mizan defines al-laghw as what has no effect. An oath can have effects as speech, emphasis, a vow, or through its breach or perjury; here, because the vain oath is contrasted with what hearts have earned, it means a formula having no effect on the speaker’s intention, such as “No, By God” or “Yes, By God” uttered without serious intent. al-kasb, originally material profit, extends to any good or evil acquired through action. Some distinguish al-iktisāb, earning benefit for oneself, from al-kasb, earning for oneself or another; in either case, al-kāsib and al-muktasib apply only to human beings. Therefore “your hearts” means the person—the spirit or soul—not merely the bodily organ: although ordinary speech assigns thought and feelings to the heart as it assigns sensation to bodily organs, only a person can earn.

The commentary traces this usage to the observation that perception may fail in epilepsy or lunacy while life, shown by heartbeat and pulse, continues. This led people to regard the heart as the first attachment of the life-spirit, distributing life through the body and wielding organs which each perform their own function. Physical research, it says, has not pinpointed the ruling source that controls the body, although its diverse organs form one unit under one controlling power. Though people have always recognized the mind, and use “head” for authority, “heart” came to mean the spirit attached to the body and thus to bear perceptions, sentiments, and action; the usage was then extended to the breast because it contains the heart. The commentary leaves open whether Qur’anic expressions support this common belief before it is clarified, and reports that Shaykh Abū ʿAlī b. Sīnā inclines to the view that the heart perceives and the brain is its tool.

Returning to (2:225), Al-Mizan calls the second clause a metaphor in a metaphor: instead of contrasting a vain oath with a firmly intended one, it names the sin resulting when that oath is broken. This shows that God looks only at the heart. “God is Forgiving, Forbearing” also indicates that vain oath-taking is undesirable for a believer.

In juristic usage, al-Ilāʾ is a husband’s oath, made in anger with the intention of harming his wife, that he will not approach her. The word “from” denotes distance and abstention, and the four-month period indicates that cohabitation becomes obligatory at its end. To “resolve on divorce” means both intending it and carrying it out, since God’s being Hearing applies to the spoken words of divorce, not to intention alone. The Forgiving and Forbearing description shows that a husband who returns to his wife escapes punishment in the hereafter, but he must still pay the worldly penalty of al-kaffārah, which is not forgiven (5:89). The Muslim Qāḍī gives him four months to return; if by then he pays the penalty and resumes relations, he incurs no punishment in the hereafter, while divorce is the other course. God is Hearing, Knowing.
verses.228:
Al-Mizan explains al-Ṭalāq as release from bonds, a term that came to denote release from marriage. The command that divorced women keep themselves in waiting establishes al-ʿiddah: they must refrain from attaching themselves to another man, so that the sperm of successive husbands is not mixed and lineage and consanguinity are not corrupted. This both legislates the rule and indicates its general social wisdom, which need not appear in every individual case. Its declarative form serves to emphasize an imperative.

The commentary holds that al-qurʾ, though used for both the period of cleanliness and menstruation, originally means the period of cleanliness. Its root signifies a gathering followed by dispersal: blood gathers in the womb during cleanliness and is discharged during menstruation. The same idea of gathering and then proclamation explains al-qarʾ in recitation and the name Qur’an. Al-Rāghib, cited from al-Mufradāt, reports that al-qurʾ begins with the menses following cleanliness and, because it combines both elements, is used for either separately.

Women may not conceal pregnancy or menstruation, lest they hasten the end of al-ʿiddah or deprive the husband of the opportunity to revoke divorce. Unlike the basic waiting rule, this prohibition is expressly tied to belief in Allah and the Last Day, showing that truthful compliance is an essential demand of faith.

The husbands who have a better right to take them back are only those in a revocable divorce, and the right exists during the waiting period. Revocation must seek reconciliation, not injury. The comparative expression means that the former husband has a greater claim than another proposer, a claim exercised by taking her back during al-ʿiddah. Thus the ruling concerns consummated marriages where the divorcee is of menstruating age and not pregnant; other cases are governed elsewhere.

Al-Mizan defines al-maʿrūf as what society, while following sound human nature, recognizes as just and good; it encompasses reason, religious law, noble character, and moral values. Social justice gives people rights corresponding to their obligations while recognizing their differing places and capacities. Islam accordingly gives women rights corresponding to their duties toward men, while preserving a degree of authority for men in the marital union.
verses.229:
Al-Mizan takes the two divorces in this verse to be revocable divorces; the third is dealt with separately. After either divorce, the husband must either retain the wife in fairness through a sincere attempt at reconciliation or release her with kindness by not revoking the divorce during al-ʿiddah. Retention intended to prolong distress through repeated divorce and revocation is cruel and contrary to the purpose of the law. Likewise, release cannot be accompanied by quarrelling, revenge, or recovery of her dowry. Fairness protects against harmful revocation, while the stronger expression of kindness prepares for the prohibition on taking back anything given to the wife and partly compensates for the loss of family life caused by divorce.

The exception applies when both spouses have an overriding belief that, because of opposed dispositions and prevailing hatred, they cannot remain within Allah’s commands and prohibitions. The change to the plural address, if you fear, shows that this must be a reasonable judgment recognized by people generally, not a suspicion arising from obsession, infatuation, or evil suggestion. In al-khulʿ, the wife may pay an agreed amount to obtain release, and neither she nor the husband is blameworthy: otherwise he could not lawfully take anything from her, and she could not lawfully give it as cooperation in sin.

The commentary concludes that these limits of Allah join social legislation to ethical teaching. Treating the rules as mere outward forms while disregarding their moral purpose defeats the aims of the sharīʿah and turns the good of life into misery. It characterizes Islam as a religion of action rather than empty words, and attributes Muslim retrogression to attending to the body of the law while forgetting its spirit.
verses.230:
Al-Mizan explains that after the two revocable divorces and returns, a third divorce makes the woman unlawful to her first husband until she has married another husband. Her prohibition includes both remarriage and cohabitation; correspondingly, marriage to the second husband implies marriage followed by cohabitation. If that second husband divorces her, she and the first husband may remarry only through a new marriage, reconciliation, and mutual consent, provided both think they can keep within Allah’s limits. This mutual return is distinct from the unilateral revocation available to the first husband after either of the first two divorces, and the final reference to Allah’s limits concerns limits other than those mentioned previously.

The commentary calls the verse a miracle of brevity: its fourteen closely placed pronouns refer to distinct subjects without ambiguity. Its metaphors clarify the legal rulings: what was given means dowry; fear means reasonable grounds to believe; what the wife gives up is the redemption in al-khulʿ; the divorce is the third divorce; being unlawful includes marriage and cohabitation; marrying another husband includes cohabitation; and returning means marrying again. The verse’s eloquence also appears in its contrast between retaining and releasing, and between fearing that the spouses cannot keep Allah’s limits and thinking that they can.
verses.231:
Al-Mizan interprets reaching the prescribed time as approaching the end of al-ʿiddah, since the husband can retain or release the wife only before it expires. He must then retain her in fairness or set her free in fairness, and may not retain her in order to harm her and transgress Allah’s limits. The earlier prohibition on recovering what was given to her remains in force, apart from al-khulʿ.

Marriage is presented as completing life’s felicity through the spouses’ mutual happiness and complementarity; divorce disrupts that harmony, and revocation is meant to repair it. Retaining a woman to injure her therefore contradicts revocation’s very purpose. Such a man wrongs himself by departing from the path of sound nature and makes Allah’s signs a mockery. The commentary stresses that divine law is not an empty set of external acts: its rules serve the common good and human felicity, are joined to moral cultivation and purification of the soul, and are interwoven with fundamental knowledge, including Allah’s Oneness and the mastership of the Prophet and the Imams.

Allah’s favor may mean the blessings of religion, including the harmonious life produced by obedience. On this reading, the Book is the body of the sharīʿah, its commands, and the Wisdom is its soul, its philosophy. Alternatively, the favor includes all divine creative and other graces, including the harmony established between husband and wife. In either reading, believers must heed both the commands and their purpose, fear Allah who knows all things, and not make their outward conformity to the law differ from their inward reality.
verses.232:
Al-Mizan holds that the apparent address, do not prevent them, is to guardians and other relatives who may obstruct a divorced woman from remarrying her former husband after her waiting period has ended. If the two agree lawfully to restore the marriage, relatives must not let their resentment of the man for having divorced her stand in the way.

The verse does not establish that a guardian’s permission is necessary for marriage. The command may address all relatives whose counsel or pressure could hinder the remarriage, and it is apparently advisory, drawing attention to the benefit and purity of reunion. The commentary rejects a reported interpretation that addresses the divorced husbands and prohibits concealing news of divorce in order to delay the waiting period. The wording refers to their former husbands and to women who have already completed their term; during the waiting period the husband could take them back, and after it the verse speaks of marrying, not returning.

The admonition is tied to belief in Allah and the Last Day because al-tawḥīd promotes unity and togetherness rather than division. The alternation between singular and plural address reflects revelation’s address to the Apostle and, through him, the community, while renewing the audience’s attention. Whether this refers to the relatives’ noninterference or to the remarriage itself, it is more profitable and purer because it replaces discord with harmony, restores a broken relationship, strengthens unity and religious virtue, augments women’s chastity and modesty, protects their shame, and diverts them from thoughts of other men while seeking another husband. Allah alone knows, and people know only through His teaching.
verses.233:
Al-Mizan notes that the verse deliberately says al-wālidāt, the women who gave birth, and mawlūdunlahu, the man to whom the child was born, rather than the more general terms for mother and father. The ruling thus concerns the biological mother, the child she bore, and the father. Since the child is socially attached to the father in most affairs, he bears its feeding, clothing, care, and upbringing, including the maintenance and clothing of the nursing mother. The mother in turn must not harm the father in matters concerning the child.

The commentary rejects the view that mothers are merely receptacles and children belong only to fathers, observing that the verse itself calls them the mothers’ children. In creation, the child belongs to both parents; social systems may attach it to either, and this verse confirms the patriarchal social arrangement. By referring to her child and his child, the wording recognizes both the shared creative relation and the father’s social responsibility.

Two complete years means two full years. Custody and nursing are rights of the divorced mother, left to her discretion: she may nurse for the full term or waive that right. The father must provide her maintenance and clothing according to al-maʿrūf and his means, for Allah imposes no duty beyond capacity. Neither parent may use the child to injure the other: the father may not deprive the mother of custody or access, and the mother may not prevent his access to the child. According to traditions narrated from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt, which the commentary says agree with the verse’s apparent meaning, the father’s heir assumes his duty to maintain and clothe the nursing mother if he dies.

Early weaning is permissible by the parents’ mutual consent and counsel. If the mother returns the child, declines to nurse, is ill, lacks milk, or for another reason cannot nurse, the father may employ a wet-nurse but must pay her promised due according to usage. The command to fear Allah and remember that He sees what is done requires fair implementation of these observable duties; concealed intentions are instead matters of Allah’s knowledge.
verses.234:
Al-Mizan explains that a widow must observe al-ʿiddah of death for four months and ten days. Once she has completed it, the statement that there is no blame for what she does properly concerning herself affirms her full authority over her affairs, including remarriage. Neither her relatives nor those of her deceased husband may prevent a lawful remarriage.

The commentary contrasts this ruling with customs that killed widows with their husbands, buried them alive, barred them from remarriage, confined them for a year or nine months, or imposed an unspecified restraint. It traces such practices to the view that marriage unites two lives in a love whose sanctity demands courtesy toward the deceased spouse, especially from the widow, who is expected to preserve modesty and chastity rather than appear as merchandise passed among successive admirers. Islam instead fixes a waiting period of nearly one third of a year and thereafter leaves her free.

Allah’s awareness of what people do is fitting because these laws regulate actions and rest on divine wisdom: He knows what should be required in waiting and what freedom should be granted afterward.
verses.235:
Al-Mizan explains al-taʿrīḍ as indirect speech whose apparent meaning remains valid while another intended meaning is understood. It differs from metaphor, where the literal meaning is displaced. Thus a man may indirectly indicate to a woman in al-ʿiddah that he wishes to marry her when she becomes free, and he may keep that wish concealed in his mind; al-iknān is this mental concealment, unlike al-kann, the physical covering or hiding of a thing.

Allah permits this because mentioning such women in connection with marriage is natural and Islam is founded on nature. But secret promises are forbidden unless the speech is proper, and no one may resolve upon the marriage-tie until the prescribed waiting period has ended.

Resolve is a firm determination of the heart, and the marriage-tie is likened to a knot joining two cords. The connection of marriage with inward resolve indicates that its reality depends on intention, faith, and the recognition conferred by society or religion; outside such common recognition, it has no existence. The prescribed term means the waiting rule imposed on women in al-ʿiddah, so the women in this passage are not women generally but that previously mentioned group. Allah’s knowledge, forgiveness, and forbearance warn believers that proposals, indirect speech, and secret promises during this period are perilous matters which Allah dislikes, even though He has permitted what He has permitted.
verses.236:
Al-Mizan explains that touching is an allegory for cohabitation and that appointing a prescribed duty means fixing the dowry. Divorce is not prevented by the absence of consummation or a fixed dowry. Where no dowry has been fixed, the divorcing husband must make a provision of usable wealth according to al-maʿrūf and his means, whether wealthy or straitened; the commentary says it should correspond to the dowry of women of her standing. It distinguishes the following verse as governing the pre-consummation case in which a dowry had already been fixed.

The description of this provision as a duty upon doers of good might apparently suggest a recommendation, since doing good is not itself obligatory. Clear traditions of Ahl al-Bayt, however, declare the provision compulsory. Al-Mizan tentatively reconciles this by linking doing good here to al-iḥsān in the earlier command to release wives with kindness: divorcers are thereby obliged to be doers of good, and the command directed to doers of good consequently obliges them to make the provision.
verses.237:
Al-Mizan explains that if divorce occurs before consummation after a dowry has been fixed, the wife is entitled to half of it. She or her guardian may remit that half. The husband may also be the one in whose hand is the marriage-tie; if he had paid the whole dowry and remits his claim, the wife need not return half to him.

Forgoing a lawful due is nearer to piety because one who relinquishes what is rightfully his will more readily avoid what is unlawful. Al-faḍl, generosity, denotes excellence in virtue and noble excess, unlike al-fuḍūl, unwarranted excess such as idle chatter. The verse therefore exhorts the separated spouses to generosity, each surrendering rights and giving the other more than is due, while remembering that Allah sees what they do.
verses.238: Al-Mizan explains that maintaining the prayers means preserving and attending to them, with special emphasis on the middle prayer, though the verse itself does not identify which prayer it is; traditions cited later explain it. Standing for Allah means undertaking and remaining engaged in worship solely for His pleasure, in obedient submission and surrender. The verse thus commands constant obedience to Allah with true submissiveness.
verses.239:
Al-Mizan reads the conjunction at the opening as implying the condition: maintain the prayer when not in danger. Prayer is never relaxed altogether. In danger, it is to be performed as best one can, on foot or riding; when security returns, it is performed in the usual manner and Allah is remembered.

The comparison in remembering Allah as He taught what was not known requires remembrance proportionate to His favor in teaching the obligatory prayer and the other rules of religion. The phrase what you did not know magnifies that favor by extending it beyond the prayer itself to all divine teaching.
verses.240:
Al-Mizan takes the definite expression the year to show that this verse preceded the rule fixing al-ʿiddah of death at four months and ten days. It addresses husbands who die and leave wives, directing them to bequeath enough property for their widows’ maintenance during the pre-Islamic year of waiting and to prevent their expulsion from the home. This maintenance and residence were the widow’s right, though she could waive it and leave; in that case, the heirs were not blameworthy for her proper conduct concerning herself.

The commentary regards the ruling as parallel to the general bequest command and holds that it was plainly abrogated by the verses prescribing the waiting period of death and inheritance.
verses.241: Al-Mizan takes the provision according to usage as applying to all divorced women. Because it is addressed to those who guard against evil, it is a recommendation rather than a compulsory obligation.
verses.242:
Al-Mizan derives al-ʿaql from tying or shackling: it is the faculty that holds fast percepts, the percept held in the mind, and the power that distinguishes truth from falsehood and good from evil. Its opposed conditions include insanity, idiocy, foolishness, and ignorance. The Qur’an employs many distinct terms for cognition. Al-yaqīn is certainty that excludes its opposite; al-ẓann is the preponderant side of a judgment, unlike evenly balanced al-shakk and the weaker al-wahm; and al-ḥisbān, literally reckoning, is used metaphorically for a supposition. Al-shuʿūr is fine perception, chiefly of material things; al-dhikr recalls or retains a mental image; and al-ʿirfān or al-maʿrifah recognizes a newly obtained image by its conformity with what is already stored.

Al-fahm is the formation in the mind of an image through an external influence; al-fiqh is its deep imprint; and al-dirāyah is a fuller comprehension that includes hidden and less-known aspects. Al-fikr reviews known matters to discover the unknown. Al-raʾy is a conclusion reached by thinking, usually concerning practical action, and is close to al-baṣīrah, al-iftāʾ, and the metaphorical use of al-qawl for an opinion. Al-zaʿm indicates a mental image whether certain or merely probable. Al-ʿilm excludes the contrary; al-ḥifẓ preserves knowledge against change; al-ḥikmah is confirmed, precise knowledge; al-khubrah grasps conclusions from their premises; and al-shahādah is direct apprehension through the external senses or inward perceptive powers.

The commentary says that the last five of these terms are free of implications of matter, movement, and change and may therefore be ascribed to Allah; the others generally are not. Al-ʿaql, according to its created function, first knows itself, then perceives through the senses and inner feelings, analyzes and rearranges what it perceives through generalization and particularization, forms theoretical judgments, and directs practical action.

Lust and anger may overpower the other faculties and make apparent reasoning deviate into moral excess or deficiency. A person then resembles a judge who reaches a judgment from false testimony: he appears to judge but does not truly judge. Likewise, a conclusion based on false premises is not genuine reason, because it violates sound nature and the right path. The commentary cites a tradition that reason is that by which the Beneficent is worshipped; what does not benefit a person in religion or lead to true knowledge and virtuous action is not reason, even if it distinguishes worldly advantage from harm.

Thus Qur’anic use of al-ʿaql concerns perception attained through a sound and perfected nature, whether acquired independently or through hearing from others. Allah’s clarification of His signs produces knowledge, and knowledge is the foundation of wisdom and understanding.
verses.243:
Al-Mizan explains that “Did you not see” means “Did you not know”: the matter is so evident that knowing it is like seeing it. Citing al-Zamakhsharī, it adds that the idiom also conveys wonder, as though asking, “Are you not surprised that ...?” ḥadhar al-mawt may mean either “for fear of death” or that they feared death with an intense fear.

Allah’s command, “Die,” is creative rather than legislative. It does not deny that they died a natural death; traditions say that the cause was plague. The imperative, instead of the wording “God gave them death and afterwards gave them life,” more forcefully displays the effectiveness of God’s command and His absolute power, just as varying style can add emphasis in legislative commands. Their subsequent life means that they were truly restored from death and lived for a time. Had their revival been only a brief warning, a completion of proof, or an illustration of another reality, the Qur’an would have indicated this, as it does in comparable accounts. The declaration that Allah is Gracious to people likewise indicates that their restored life was not momentary.

The repetition of “people,” rather than use of a pronoun, alludes to their low level of thought. In “Allah is Gracious to people,” the word denotes the particular people raised from the dead; in “most people thank Him not,” it denotes mankind generally. The verse is also connected with the following injunctions about jihād, for jihād can give renewed life to a nation that has become dead.

A commentator, however, takes the account as a parable of the ummah. He argues that it cannot describe a historical event among Israelites or another people, because the Qur’an would then have named the nation or prophet concerned, and because the Torah does not record it in the history of Hezekiel; he consequently treats the related traditions as Jewish mythology adopted by Muslims. He further argues from Qur’anic references to the first death and to two deaths and two lives that there can be only one death and one life in this world.

On this reading, a powerful enemy subjugated a nation, and its people—though thousands in number—fled their homes from fear of death instead of defending their freedom. God’s command that they die signifies the death of disgrace and ignorance, since ignorance and inertia are death while knowledge and self-respect are life. God then gave the nation life by inspiring it to resist its oppressors, defend its rights, expel them, and regain independence. Although the later generation was not numerically identical with the earlier, both belonged to one nation and are therefore described as one people that died and was revived. The commentator also argues that, without this parabolic sense, the verse would lack a connection with the following verses on fighting in God’s way.

Al-Mizan rejects this interpretation as resting on patently false premises. First, it presupposes rejection of miracles, or at least of resurrection of the dead, whereas miracles have been established and the Qur’an explicitly affirms such miracles. Even were they not demonstrable through intellectual argument, the Qur’an’s own affirmation remains decisive. Second, its claim that the Qur’an excludes a further life in this world is contradicted by the accounts of dead animals and persons restored to life in the stories of Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Ezra. A single worldly life does not become two lives merely because death occurs during it: ʿUzayr remained dead for a hundred years, yet when raised he was unaware of that death.

Third, the Qur’an need not identify every people or prophet when recounting a real event. Its manner varies with time, place, and context: sometimes it supplies details and sometimes merely alludes to a people without identifying them. Fourth, no connection need be sought between adjacent verses merely because they stand together, since the Qur’an was revealed gradually; such a connection is required only when verses plainly belong to one context and were evidently revealed together.

Al-Mizan concludes that the verse narrates a real event. A statement presented so that most hearers understand it as factual would lose its style, eloquence, and force if it were actually an unfounded parable. Moreover, the Qur’an consistently distinguishes similes and parables from ordinary narration by explicitly marking them as such.
verses.244: Fight in Allah’s way, knowing that Allah hears and knows.
verses.245: Al-Mizan asks who will lend Allah a goodly loan, which He will multiply manifold; Allah holds and extends, and to Him all return.
verses.246: Al-Mizan relates that the chiefs of the children of Israel, after Moses, asked their prophet to raise a king so that they might fight in Allah’s way. Though they cited their expulsion from homes and children and insisted they had no reason not to fight, when fighting was ordained most turned back. Allah knows the unjust.
verses.247: Al-Mizan states that the Israelites’ prophet announced Allah had raised Ṭālūt as their king. They objected that they had a greater claim to kingship and that he lacked wealth. The prophet answered that Allah had chosen him and endowed him abundantly with knowledge and physique; Allah grants His Kingdom to whom He pleases, and He is Ample-giving, Knowing.
verses.248: Al-Mizan relates that their prophet gave the coming of the Ark as the sign of Ṭālūt’s kingship. It would contain tranquillity from their Lord and relics left by the family of Moses and the family of Aaron, while angels bore it. This was a sign for believers.
verses.249: Al-Mizan relates that when Ṭālūt departed with the forces, he announced Allah’s test by a stream: whoever drank from it was not of him, while whoever did not taste it was of him, except one who took a handful. Apart from a few, they drank. After he and the believers with him crossed, some said they had no power against Goliath and his forces; those who thought they would meet their Lord replied that a small party had often vanquished a numerous host by Allah’s permission, and that Allah is with the patient ones.
verses.250: Al-Mizan recounts their prayer before Goliath’s forces: “Our Lord, pour down upon us patience, make our feet firm, and help us against the unbelieving people.”
verses.251: Al-Mizan states that they routed Goliath’s forces by Allah’s permission and David slew Goliath. Allah gave David kingship and wisdom and taught him what He pleased. Without Allah’s repelling some men by others, the earth would be in disorder; but Allah is Gracious to the creatures.
verses.252:
Al-Mizan treats these verses as a single revelation joining the obligation of fighting, the exhortation to lend to Allah, and the story of Ṭālūt, David, and Goliath. Their purpose is to show how fighting in Allah’s way strengthens collective life, how a nation advances in worldly and religious life, and what brings real happiness. Jihād is made obligatory, and believers are called to spend in Allah’s way to prepare for war and increase their power against enemies. Such spending is called lending to Allah because it is in His way, is returned by Him, and draws the spender near to Him.

The story supplies the lesson for those commanded to fight: kingdom and victory belong to faith and piety even when their adherents are few, while hypocrisy and sin lead to defeat and destruction even when their followers are many. The Israelites remained disgraced and enslaved while inert; when they rose to fight in Allah’s way and sought help through the word of truth, Allah gave them victory despite the truthfulness of only a few. The majority had turned back when fighting was prescribed, objected to Ṭālūt’s appointment, drank from the stream, and despaired of facing Goliath. Yet Allah enabled their victory, David killed Goliath, and sovereignty was restored to them. Their prayer for patience, firm feet, and help against the unbelieving people expresses the faith and piety through which victory came. Believers should follow the righteous of earlier nations, for they will have the upper hand if they are believers.

The command to fight makes fighting compulsory, but its constant qualification, “in the way of God,” excludes the idea that it was ordained for the Muslims’ worldly domination over other nations or to spread their own kingdom. Its aim is rather the domination of religion, through which people prosper in both worlds. Allah’s being Hearing and Knowing warns believers neither to speak against Allah’s and His apostle’s commands nor to dislike them inwardly, as hypocrites do. They must not resemble the Israelites who objected to Ṭālūt, declared themselves unable to face Goliath, withdrew when fighting was ordained, and drank from the stream after Ṭālūt forbade it.

Al-Mizan explains that what is spent in Allah’s way is called a loan both to urge people to spend and because it will surely be returned manifold. The shift from the preceding imperative to the question, “Who is it that will lend?”, refreshes the audience: an invitation and exhortation are received differently from an order. Allah’s holding and extending mean that He decreases or increases what He pleases; since all return to Him, no expenditure lent to Him is lost, and He will repay it abundantly.

The Israelites’ request for a king implies that Goliath had subjugated them so severely that they had lost the conditions of a free life, including their homes and children. After Moses and the end of his successors’ rule, hardship awakened their self-respect. Their elders asked a prophet for a king who would remove internal differences, unite their ineffective power, and lead them in fighting in Allah’s way. Yet appointing the king and ordaining the fighting belonged to Allah, not to the prophet. The prophet’s wording, that fighting might be “written” for them, indicates divine authority, for writing in the sense of ordaining belongs only to Allah. Though he knew by revelation that they would disobey, he asked them so that their emphatic professions would complete the proof against them.

Their claim that they had been turned out of homes and children means that, having been expelled from their ancestral abode, they could neither manage nor benefit from their homes; this also explains the expression’s connection with their children. Their later refusal to fight confirms the prophet’s question and reply. Allah’s knowledge of the unjust shows that the question rested on revelation that they would turn away.

The announcement that Allah had raised Ṭālūt corrects their mistaken assumption that the prophet himself could appoint a king. They protested first that they possessed a greater hereditary right to kingship: among them the houses of prophethood and kingship were honored, while Ṭālūt belonged to neither. Their objection rested on the belief that Allah could not alter His former arrangements. The answer is that precedence follows Allah’s choice; when He chooses another, that person has the greater right. Their second objection was Ṭālūt’s poverty. Al-Mizan explains that kingship exists to unite a people under one will, govern them justly, and enable every member to attain his deserved perfection. Thus a king needs knowledge of what benefits and harms his people and bodily strength to enforce what is good, not abundant wealth. Allah’s abundant endowment of Ṭālūt in knowledge and physique therefore answers their objection.

Allah alone owns the Kingdom, and no one has any claim upon it except what He grants. As the Real and Perfect cause, He has authority to do as He pleases, without need of supplementary causes; therefore no one may object to His transferring kingship from one family or giving it to one without wealth or a great lineage. This does not mean that His actions are random, purposeless, or devoid of benefit. Allah is not governed by an end or benefit as human beings are, because benefit itself is His creation; nevertheless, whatever He does is good and beautiful and beneficial to His creatures. Thus His unrestricted will and His giving Ṭālūt knowledge and strength are complementary, not contradictory. His being Ample-giving means that none can restrict His bestowal, and His being Knowing means that His actions proceed from unfailing true knowledge; He does whatever He pleases and does nothing but what is beneficial.

The Ark is a chest, and al-sakīnah is tranquillity of heart: stable judgment and firmness in decision rather than perturbation. It is a quality of the higher degree of faith and among Allah’s greatest gifts. Reasoning directed solely to real benefit and happiness is accompanied by calmness, whereas attachment to the world and lower desires confuses thought and weakens will, leaving one unable to undertake difficult and dangerous tasks. The believer relies on Allah, true knowledge, and divine command; knowing that affairs are not in his own hand, he is neither frightened by possible loss nor grieved by harm and can distinguish good from evil. The disbeliever, lacking such a guardian, wanders in confusion, uncertainty, unreal imaginings, and unhealthy feelings.

The Qur’anic contrasts between Allah’s guardianship of believers and the darkness, fear, deception, and satanic guardianship of unbelief show that faith brings a further life and a light by which the believer walks. It is associated with faith written into hearts and a spirit from Allah that strengthens them. Tranquillity corresponds to that spirit and to the increase of faith; references to Allah’s hosts further suggest the angels and the spirit. From this, Al-Mizan says, it may be inferred that al-sakīnah is a divine spirit, or accompanies one by divine command, producing tranquillity of heart, firm purpose, and peace of mind. Traditions concerning it should be interpreted accordingly, without forcing the word away from its real meaning. The family of Moses and Aaron includes them and their closest relatives. The angels’ bearing of the Ark describes its state, and the verse’s presentation of it as a sign indicates that the Israelites had sought proof of their prophet’s assertion that Allah had raised Ṭālūt.

When Ṭālūt departed with the forces, the plural term indicates that they were still numerous even after most had previously turned back. The narrative exposes how the Israelites fulfilled their covenant: the large body that demanded a king had already been reduced, and the remaining forces were further tested at the stream. The placement of the exception concerning one who takes a handful establishes three groups, not two. Those who drank were shown not to belong to Ṭālūt; those who did not even taste were shown to belong to him; those who took a handful were removed from the first group but were not thereby placed in the second. The latter two groups crossed with Ṭālūt, but differed greatly: the handful-takers were restless, cowardly, and hypocritical, while those who did not taste the water were patient and wholly confident in Allah. Thus those who despaired of Goliath were the handful-takers, while the reply about a small party often defeating a numerous host came from those who had not tasted the water. Their “thought” of meeting their Lord means certainty, though it may also portray their humility in not deeming themselves worthy of that meeting. Their appeal to what had often occurred presents an established fact, rather than a bare possibility, and so makes their answer more compelling.

Their prayer before Goliath asks Allah to pour patience upon them in proportion to their capacity, like liquid poured into a mould, to make their feet firm, and to help them against the unbelieving people. Firm feet signify determination and steadiness before the enemy, so that they do not flee.

Their routing of the enemy means driving them back. The disorder that Allah’s repelling some men by others prevents is principally disorder in human society; disorder on the earth’s surface is included only as a consequence of social disorder. Human felicity requires society, mutual assistance, and sufficient unity for many individuals to become like one body and soul. As the universe is held together by the action, reaction, and mutual resistance of its components, society also depends on repulsion and overpowering. Without a means by which individuals can restrain one another, each would pursue his own will even against others’ interests, unity would dissolve, and society would perish.

Al-Mizan identifies the basic factor beneath society as the human instinct to subjugate others for one’s own benefit; mutual assistance and civilization are secondary results of it. This instinct operates in war and peace, ease and hardship, and becomes conscious when a person’s will is opposed; war is one of its degrees. It appears when believers repel oppressors to defend lawful rights and when others protect unlawful gains. Believers and unbelievers share the same human nature, and without this faculty no one could defend either a lawful right or an unlawful possession. Through it society is founded, people preserve or recover what they have gained or lost, and truth may be revived and society maintained on the way to eternal felicity. Perhaps this comprehensive benefit is what the verse indicates, and Allah’s grace to the creatures supports that reading.

The commentary regards the interpretation that the verse means only believers repelling unbelievers as correct but incomplete: the good intended is a comprehensive and continuous good that preserves society, not merely a temporary benefit in a particular conflict. Another interpretation takes the verse to mean that Allah saves sinners from destruction because of the righteous. A report attributed to Jābir says that the goodness of a Muslim safeguards his descendants, household, and neighboring households, while a report attributed to Imam al-Ṣādiq says that those among the Shias who pray, pay zakāt, or perform hajj avert misfortune from those who neglect these duties. Al-Mizan holds that the cited verses do not themselves bear this meaning, although the reports may illustrate ways in which Allah repels some people by others. It dismisses as plainly absurd the claim that the verse means Allah repels oppressors by other oppressors.

Finally, the declaration that these are Allah’s signs recited with truth serves as the epilogue to the story. Its affirmation that the addressee is one of the apostles also links the passage clearly to the verse that follows.
verses.253:
Al-Mizan holds that these verses remain closely connected with the preceding commands to fight and spend in the way of God, and with the story of Ṭālūt; their contextual similarities indicate that they were sent down together. They answer the objection that apostleship, especially when supported by arguments and miracles, ought either to have united people and ended their fighting or to have made fighting needless, since faith cannot be produced by coercion. The reply is that fighting arose because the followers of the apostles themselves differed. Had they not differed, they would not have fought. God could have prevented their difference, severed the usual connection between difference and fighting, forbidden fighting legislatively, or withheld the command to fight; but He has willed a system in which effects follow their causes and people retain freedom of choice rather than being compelled.

The opening expression, “These apostles,” uses the remote demonstrative tilka to indicate their grandeur. All apostles share the basic excellence of apostleship, while some surpass others in rank. This God-given difference of rank is wholly unlike the difference among their followers: the former is called excellence and is attributed to God, while the latter is a human conflict between belief and denial. The description of the apostles is thus a prologue to the subject of fighting. Apostleship, with all its blessings, clear proofs, and miracles, does not by itself eradicate the divisions of belief and disbelief, because such divisions originate in people’s envy, rebellion, obstinacy, and worldly desire.

Clear proofs are sufficient to refute false beliefs and remove doubts, but they do not by themselves remove these moral defects. For that reason, Al-Mizan says, fighting in God’s way is necessary when required to support truth and improve humanity’s condition; arguments alone have often not been effective without the sword. God therefore commanded His apostles to fight when necessary, and made such fighting a criterion through which the impure are separated from the pure and believers become known from hypocrites. Thus conflict among the followers of apostles cannot be avoided so long as the possibility of envy and rebellion remains.

Al-Mizan suggests, while saying that God knows better, that the shift from “We have made some of them to excel others” to “some to whom Allah spoke” and “some of them He exalted” reflects two kinds of excellence. Clear evidence, miracles, and strengthening with the holy spirit are honorable in themselves. By contrast, being addressed or raised in rank gains its honor from the greatness of the one who does it; being spoken to by God or raised by Him is therefore especially exalted. The divine name is explicitly used for these latter favors, whereas the first-person pronoun returns for the intrinsically noble favors given to Jesus.

Regarding those “to whom Allah spoke,” commentators have proposed Moses, Muḥammad on the night of the ascension, or all prophets through revelation. Al-Mizan rejects the last interpretation because “some” indicates a distinction granted only to some apostles, whereas revelation belongs to all of them. It judges Moses the most appropriate referent, since God’s direct speech to Moses had already been clearly established before this verse was revealed. Regarding those whom God “exalted by degree,” some restrict the clause to Muḥammad, citing his universal mission, mercy to the worlds, final prophethood, Qur’an, and established religion; others apply it to various prophets, or restrict “these apostles” to figures mentioned in this sūrah or in the preceding story. Al-Mizan concludes that Muḥammad’s exalted rank is certainly included, but rejects every arbitrary restriction. “These apostles” means all the apostles sent by God, and the exaltation covers every apostle whom God elevated in any way. The claim that the verse concerns only Jews, Christians, and Muslims, and therefore names Moses, Jesus, and Muḥammad alone, is also rejected: the Qur’an presents the apostles generally as sent to mankind, and the verse addresses the general human pattern in which followers divide through rebellion, envy, and desire, making fighting necessary when human good depends on it.

Al-Mizan treats God’s speech as an actual occurrence, not an allegory or analogy. The realities reported by the prophets—revelation, divine speech, angels, spirits, great divine signs, Satan, jinn, the Tablet, and the Pen—must not be reduced to mental faculties, moral impulses, or material phenomena. Such reduction would ultimately empty prophetic teaching of all realities beyond matter. God’s speaking is real, even though its manner is particular to Him and unlike human speech. Revelation, speech from behind a veil, and speech through a messenger establish real divine communication rather than a merely figurative expression.

Human speech serves social life: people use sounds produced by bodily organs and conventions shared by speaker and hearer to convey hidden thoughts. God, however, has neither limbs nor organs, nor does He need conventional vocal signs. Nevertheless, the essential effect of speech is making the recipient understand the intended message. Divine speech is real in that effect, though its modality is unknown and bears no resemblance to human utterance. Just as an old name can truly be applied to a new instrument when the instrument preserves the original function despite a radically different form, “speech” truly applies to God because He conveys what He intends, even though His mode of communication differs entirely from ours.

Divine speech is therefore an attribute of action, like creating, giving life and death, sustaining, guiding, and forgiving, rather than an attribute of Person such as knowledge, power, and life. As an action, it may be connected with a particular time and place, as are God’s other acts. God’s “speech” and “speaking” are used for His address to human beings; “word” and “words” can instead denote a created being, a divine decree, or a kind of creation. “Saying” has a wider use, applying to His address to human beings, angels, Satan, and inanimate things.

In creation, God’s saying is His creating itself. When He says “Be” and a thing comes to exist, no separate word passes from Creator to creature: the existence of the created thing itself manifests the particular divine intention and is itself the divine “Be.” When God addresses a human being, He creates something that gives the person inner knowledge of the intended message. This may include a created voice, as in the tree in God’s speech to Moses, or the curtain of light in the case of Muḥammad, or another modality unknown to us. The same essential reality applies to angels and Satan, though they do not communicate through biological, social, vocal, and auditory mechanisms like human beings. Likewise, the Qur’anic saying and revelation associated with animals need not be understood as human-style speech.

Their distinct names depend on context: “speech” emphasizes conveying a message to the recipient and thus suits the mention of prophetic honor; “saying” emphasizes the intended meaning and is used for creative and legislative commands; and “revelation” emphasizes that the communication is hidden from others. Al-Mizan similarly insists that God’s exalting apostles in rank is a real spiritual perfection, not an honor existing only in people’s minds, like a man’s being called president. To treat prophetic exaltation as merely mental also turns its consequences—such as paradise, hell, questioning, and reckoning—into unreal relations, and improperly makes God subject to His own suppositions. This error leads some to deny the genuinely existing spiritual perfections which the Qur’an and traditions attribute to prophets and chosen servants.

Jesus is named because clear evidence and strengthening by the holy spirit, though in a sense common to all apostles, belonged to him in a special manner. His miracles—raising the dead, creating a bird by breathing into it, curing the blind and lepers, and disclosing unseen matters—have a distinctive relation to life and spirit. Jesus himself, born without a father, was a clear sign of God’s power; he and Mary together were a sign for the worlds. The return to the explicit divine name in the statement that, had Allah willed, later people would not have fought, emphasizes that no event escapes His power or authority. Difference in faith and denial is nonetheless attributed to people, because it arises from envy, rebellion, and evil desire, not from God. God could have deprived this difference of its causal power, but He willed that it should lead to fighting within the established order of cause and effect.

Finally, Al-Mizan understands the command to spend from what God has given before the day when there will be no bargaining, friendship, or intercession as plain in meaning. Its closing statement implies that refusing to spend in God’s way is unbelief and injustice.
verses.254:
Al-Mizan holds that these verses remain closely connected with the preceding commands to fight and spend in the way of God, and with the story of Ṭālūt; their contextual similarities indicate that they were sent down together. They answer the objection that apostleship, especially when supported by arguments and miracles, ought either to have united people and ended their fighting or to have made fighting needless, since faith cannot be produced by coercion. The reply is that fighting arose because the followers of the apostles themselves differed. Had they not differed, they would not have fought. God could have prevented their difference, severed the usual connection between difference and fighting, forbidden fighting legislatively, or withheld the command to fight; but He has willed a system in which effects follow their causes and people retain freedom of choice rather than being compelled.

The opening expression, “These apostles,” uses the remote demonstrative tilka to indicate their grandeur. All apostles share the basic excellence of apostleship, while some surpass others in rank. This God-given difference of rank is wholly unlike the difference among their followers: the former is called excellence and is attributed to God, while the latter is a human conflict between belief and denial. The description of the apostles is thus a prologue to the subject of fighting. Apostleship, with all its blessings, clear proofs, and miracles, does not by itself eradicate the divisions of belief and disbelief, because such divisions originate in people’s envy, rebellion, obstinacy, and worldly desire.

Clear proofs are sufficient to refute false beliefs and remove doubts, but they do not by themselves remove these moral defects. For that reason, Al-Mizan says, fighting in God’s way is necessary when required to support truth and improve humanity’s condition; arguments alone have often not been effective without the sword. God therefore commanded His apostles to fight when necessary, and made such fighting a criterion through which the impure are separated from the pure and believers become known from hypocrites. Thus conflict among the followers of apostles cannot be avoided so long as the possibility of envy and rebellion remains.

Al-Mizan suggests, while saying that God knows better, that the shift from “We have made some of them to excel others” to “some to whom Allah spoke” and “some of them He exalted” reflects two kinds of excellence. Clear evidence, miracles, and strengthening with the holy spirit are honorable in themselves. By contrast, being addressed or raised in rank gains its honor from the greatness of the one who does it; being spoken to by God or raised by Him is therefore especially exalted. The divine name is explicitly used for these latter favors, whereas the first-person pronoun returns for the intrinsically noble favors given to Jesus.

Regarding those “to whom Allah spoke,” commentators have proposed Moses, Muḥammad on the night of the ascension, or all prophets through revelation.
