verses.255:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as a compact demonstration that divinity, life, sustaining authority, ownership, causation, knowledge, and true greatness belong ultimately to God alone. The name “Allah” denotes the Being in whom every perfection is gathered, while “there is no god but He” denies real existence to the supposed deities worshipped beside Him. Calling Him the Ever-living does not merely ascribe life for an indefinite duration. Created life appears in different forms and degrees, is subject to weakness and death, and remains a gift dependent on God even in the hereafter. The life of this world is especially defective and transitory, whereas the hereafter is enduring because God makes it so. Yet life in the fullest sense must be incapable of non-existence, not merely promised freedom from death. Only God is life essentially; every other living being receives life from Him.

The title al-qayyūm, “the Self-subsisting by Whom all subsist,” intensifies the sense of standing: protecting, accomplishing, managing, nurturing, and exercising power over every affair. God gives and withholds with justice, granting each thing what it deserves, and every created existence, attribute, effect, and secondary source originates from Him. His sustaining activity is both exclusive and unceasing: no one sustains independently of Him, and He is never other than sustaining. For this reason al-qayyūm underlies the divine names of action, such as Creator, Sustainer, Originator, Resurrector, Bestower of life, Giver of death, Forgiver, and Compassionate.

“Slumber does not overtake Him nor sleep” removes every suggestion of weakness from that sustaining authority. The order from slumber to sleep is rhetorically appropriate because the context concerns what could impair His governance: first the lesser impediment is denied, then the stronger. Neither the beginning of unconsciousness nor its completed state can interrupt His power. This denial also corresponds to the verse’s conclusion that preserving the heavens and the earth does not tire Him.

His perfect sustaining authority entails real ownership of everything in the heavens and earth. Created things, together with their properties and operations, exist through Him, so nothing from their beginning to their end falls outside His sovereignty. The apparent difficulty posed by the world’s system of causes and effects is answered by the question of intercession. Causes have genuine intermediary effects, but only by God’s permission; they are causes because He made them so and their efficacy is an exercise of His decree, not an independent power alongside Him. Intercession therefore includes both creative intercession, in which causes mediate the coming-to-be of effects, and legislative intercession concerning recompense on the Day of Judgment. Neither kind compromises divine sovereignty, because every intermediary acts through the attributes, permission, and grace of God.

The statement that God knows what lies before and behind the intercessors shows that His permission never releases them from His encompassing control. He knows what is present to them and what is absent or still to come, while they comprehend only what He chooses to bestow. Angels, prophets, and all other intermediaries cannot descend, communicate, or act beyond His command. Rational pronouns can include even non-rational created causes here because the Qur’an speaks of all things as glorifying, responding, and serving their Creator. Their agency and knowledge are real but derivative reflections of divine power and knowledge.

The shift from God’s knowing to creatures’ inability to comprehend also establishes that knowledge itself belongs originally to God, just as power, honour, and life do. No creature possesses knowledge independently, and withholding knowledge of what comes next is part of perfect management: an intermediary who independently mastered the plan could attempt to escape or disrupt it. God instead encompasses both the causes and whatever knowledge and effectiveness they possess.

Finally, the “Chair” is not treated as a bodily seat but as the divine station of authority and knowledge by which the heavens and earth are possessed, maintained, managed, known, and preserved. Its extension signifies the all-encompassing reach of that governance. The closing names, the Most High and the Great, gather the argument together: creatures cannot reach or weaken Him, their multitude cannot overwhelm Him, and the magnitude of the heavens and earth cannot burden Him. Eminence and greatness, like every perfection, are truly His alone.
verses.256:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse denies compulsion in religion because religion is fundamentally belief and faith, a matter of conscience. al-Ikrāh is compelling a person to act unwillingly. Physical acts may be forced, but belief cannot: it arises only from reason and understanding. The verse also declares that Allah is the Guardian of believers, bringing them from darkness into light, while the rebels lead disbelievers from light into darkness, where they abide in the Fire.

al-Rushd means attaining the reality of a matter or reaching the right path, while al-Ghayy is its opposite. They are broader than al-hudā, finding the path to one’s destination, and al-ḍalāl, failing to find it. When al-rushd is used for right guidance, the general term is applied to a particular instance, because one who follows the right path reaches reality. Likewise, al-ḍalāl is deviation from the path while knowing and remembering the destination, whereas al-ghayy is deviation without remembering the goal or even knowing what one seeks.

“There is no compulsion in religion” may be phrased as information about creation or as legislation expressed in an informative form. The commentary holds the latter to be apparently more correct, because “truly the right way has become clearly distinct from error” supplies the reason for the rule. In either case, the prohibition rests on a creational fact: coercion affects outward action, not the heart and conscience. A wise person uses compulsion only when the truth of an order cannot be made understood; where advantages, disadvantages, reward, and punishment are clear, a person should choose whether to accept the path and its reward or reject it and bear its punishment. Divine revelation and prophetic explanation have fully clarified religion as truth and shown that deviation leads to perdition; therefore, there is no reason to compel anyone to embrace it.

The commentary regards this as evidence that Islam is not founded upon the sword or upon forcing people to accept Islam. Jihād was not legislated for material expansion or religious conversion by force, but to revive truth and defend the faith of monotheism. Where people accept monotheism, even while remaining Jews or Christians, Islam does not fight them. The contrary objection therefore results from confused thinking.

Nor is the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword. Its ruling is founded on the continued distinction of right from error, and a ruling based on a cause cannot be cancelled while that cause remains. Verses commanding fighting do not remove the clarity of truth and falsehood; consequently, they cannot abrogate the prohibition of compulsion.

al-Ṭāghūt denotes intensified rebellion and transgression. It includes false deities, idols, satans, jinn, wrongful human leaders, and, in short, everyone followed without Allah’s permission; the term applies without distinction of gender or number. The verse places disbelief in the rebels before belief in Allah because one must first discard what is unwanted before holding fast to what is desired. “He indeed has laid hold on the strongest handle” is an allegory: belief in Allah, after rejecting all false deities, is related to eternal, real bliss as a vessel’s handle is to the vessel and what it contains. One cannot securely hold the vessel except by its handle, nor hope for that bliss without such belief. “For which there is no break off” intensifies the strength and unbreakability of this handle; al-Infiṣām means being cut off or broken. Allah’s being Hearing and Knowing further indicates that belief and disbelief pertain to the tongue and the heart.
verses.257:
Al-Mizan explains that Allah is the Guardian of believers and brings them from darkness into light, whereas the rebels are the guardians of disbelievers and take them from light into darkness; the latter are the abiding inmates of the Fire. It distinguishes carefully between the reality of light and darkness and the figurative language of being brought out or taken out.

The commentary first recounts two interpretations. The first treats all such expressions as allegories for human beliefs and deeds: light is correct belief, which removes ignorance, doubt, and perplexity, and also good deeds whose connection to the right path and bliss is manifest; darkness is wrong belief, doubt, confusion, and evil deeds. On this view, God and the false deities do not truly perform an act of bringing out or taking out, nor are light and darkness effects distinct from those beliefs and deeds.

The second interpretation affirms that God truly performs such acts and that effects such as light, darkness, life, mercy, and the descent of angels exist, although intellect and sense cannot comprehend them; they are accepted because God has reported them. As characterized by the commentary, it nevertheless treats expressions such as light, darkness, and taking out metaphorically. It differs from the first view by making light and darkness unknowable things other than beliefs and deeds, rather than beliefs and deeds themselves.

Al-Mizan rejects both views: one falls short and the other goes beyond the truth. The things which God says He creates and does in connection with obedience and disobedience are real, not merely allegorical, and they are inseparably related to beliefs and deeds. Thus there are two separate questions. Light, darkness, and similar expressions refer to real things in this life; but the use of “light” for guidance is metaphorical. Likewise, “He brings them out of the darkness into the light” and “they take them out of the light into the darkness” are metaphors meaning that Allah guides and the rebels misguide.

A literal reading of these clauses would imply that every believer was initially in darkness and every disbeliever initially in light. That is difficult to reconcile with the great majority who are born into believing or disbelieving families and remain, respectively, in light or darkness. It would also imply that a child is in both conditions at once and that, upon reaching maturity, accepting faith removes him from darkness while disbelief removes him from light. It may, however, be said that every human being possesses the general light of natural faith, while remaining in darkness regarding detailed knowledge and good deeds. From these different perspectives, light and darkness may coexist: correct faith brings the believer into the light of knowledge and good deeds, while disbelief removes the disbeliever from natural light into the darkness of disbelief and evil deeds. In every case, the two clauses denote guidance and misguidance metaphorically.

The singular “the light” and plural “the darkness” indicate that truth is one and undifferentiated, whereas falsehood is multiple, diverse, and variable, without unity.
verses.258: Al-Mizan recounts Abraham’s dispute with one whom Allah had given kingdom: when he claimed to give life and cause death, Abraham challenged him to bring the sun from the west rather than the east. The disbeliever was confounded, for Allah does not guide the unjust people.
verses.259: Al-Mizan recounts that a man who passed a ruined town asked how Allah would restore it to life. Allah caused him to die for a hundred years and revived him; although he thought he had tarried only a day or part of one, he was shown his unchanged food and drink, his donkey, and bones reassembled and clothed with flesh. Made a sign to men, he declared that Allah has power over all things.
verses.260:
Al-Mizan treats these three verses as a connected exposition of the oneness and omnipotence of the Creator, possibly revealed with the preceding verses. They illustrate three ascending modes of divine guidance: argument, in Abraham’s dispute with the king; direct demonstration, in the revival of the passerby; and the highest mode, in which the fact is demonstrated together with its cause, in Abraham’s revival of the birds. It takes the or in the second story and the and in the third to join implied alternatives or commands to remember the stories. Their differing styles renew attention. The withholding of names, places, dates, and other particulars presents even the overwhelming raising of the dead as insignificant before divine power; Abraham alone is named because of the special honour accorded him.

Al-Mizan explains that the dispute was about Abraham’s Lord. Historical and traditional accounts identify the king as the Babylonian Namrūd. It argues that human nature always acknowledges a Creator and manager of the universe, even where this recognition has become weak or dormant. Primitive people, measuring the world by familiar causes and social functions, assigned particular deities to particular phenomena, often associating them with stars, the sun, and the moon; the Sabaeans held such beliefs. Images were then made for these lesser deities and worshipped as intercessors with them and, through them, with the Supreme God. Gradually, attachment to what was visible and near caused idols themselves to displace both the lesser deities and the Supreme God in popular devotion.

Powerful rulers exploited this tendency. Since their control over people’s affairs seemed more manifest than that of the imagined deities, they could claim divinity and finally supremacy over the other gods while still worshipping their nation’s idols. Al-Mizan understands Namrūd in this way: he believed in a Supreme God and lesser deities, yet claimed to be the highest god himself. His inability to answer the argument about the sun shows that he accepted a Lord of Lords who ultimately controlled it.

Abraham’s assertion that his Lord gives life and causes death refers primarily to the life and death of animals and human beings, not to cultivation, breeding, release from danger, or killing. Lifeless nature cannot give life, and a living thing cannot create or destroy itself, since its life is its existence and its death its extinction. Namrūd could not answer this literal argument, so he used a sophism: the commentary explains his claim as releasing one prisoner and killing another, treating metaphorical rescue and murder as giving life and causing death. His courtiers accepted the deception. Since they would not accept an exposure of its defect, Abraham moved to an argument that could not be twisted: if Namrūd were truly lord and manager of the universe, then, since Allah brings the sun from the east, he should bring it from the west. Namrūd could neither make the sun’s course an uncaused chance occurrence, deny the Supreme God whose lordship he acknowledged, nor claim power over its direction. Abraham’s use of the proper name Allah also prevented Namrūd from misappropriating the expression my Lord.

The statement that Allah gave him kingdom is deliberately ironical: divine generosity, which should have elicited gratitude, became the occasion of Namrūd’s rebellion. The very kingdom on which he based his claim to divinity was a gift from Allah; without it he was merely an ordinary man. His omission by name further displays his insignificance. Al-Mizan rejects the view that the pronoun refers instead to Abraham and his kingdom. The Qur’an attributes kingdoms, wealth, and other gifts even to tyrants, while all kingdom ultimately belongs to Allah; moreover, the context concerns Abraham’s monotheism, not a worldly kingdom possessed by Abraham. Authority is a divine bounty in respect of its good aspect: used rightly, it is blessing, but transgression turns it into ruin.

The commentary takes the people’s acceptance of Namrūd’s trick as evidence of their weakness in abstract and non-material understanding, notwithstanding any material civilization they possessed. Abraham therefore did not use with them his broader proof from the Originator of the heavens and the earth, which such minds could not properly grasp. The assertion that Allah does not guide the unjust apparently explains why Namrūd was confounded in the argument, rather than saying that the absence of guidance first made him an unbeliever. Injustice itself is the cause of such deprivation of guidance.

Al-Mizan expands this into a universal rule: good deeds lead to guidance and evil deeds to misguidance. Creative guidance is universal and unfailing: every created thing is directed to its proper goal through its proper causal path, and an effect does not fail to follow its cause. The same order extends to social life. A corrupt tutor, unlawful ruler, incompetent judge, or one who assumes an unsanctioned responsibility necessarily leaves harmful effects, even when outwardly concealing the evil. Falsehood, injustice, deception, and dishonesty may confuse people temporarily, but their corruption is eventually exposed; truth remains firm through its effects. Thus an unjust person cannot reach through injustice the end attained by virtue and piety, and the endeavours of the unjust ultimately fail.

Regarding the passerby, Al-Mizan rejects explanations that make the or merely redundant, a simple conjunction of words, or a continuation of Abraham’s challenge to Namrūd. It sees the story as the second of the three forms of guidance. The ruined town denotes its dead inhabitants, not merely a town that might later be repopulated. The passerby’s question expresses awe at the magnitude of restoring life after long decay, not disbelief in resurrection. The commentary holds that he was a prophet accustomed to divine speech, and therefore sinless and already certain of Allah’s omnipotence. His final words, I know that Allah has power over all things, confirm that prior knowledge rather than announce a new faith.

Allah truly caused him to die by taking his soul, kept him dead for a hundred years, and then returned his soul and life. Al-Mizan emphatically rejects the interpretation of death as a hundred-year coma. The Qur’anic word means death, not a loss of consciousness; analogy with the sleepers in the cave cannot alter its meaning; and the surrounding references to revival, the unchanged food and drink, the donkey, and the bones all confirm actual death and resurrection. The contrary reading rests on an unsupported assumption that revival from death in this world is impossible. His estimate of a day or part of a day indicates that his death and revival occurred at different times of day, so that he mistook a hundred years for the interval of sleep.

The question before him involved both the length of time after death and the disintegration of the body. His own death and return after a hundred years answer the first aspect. The unchanged food and drink show that preservation over such a period is possible, while the decayed donkey indicates the passage of time; together they remove any possible doubt arising from the unchanged state of the man himself. The reassembly and clothing with flesh of the donkey’s bones answer the second aspect by showing how dispersed bodily parts are restored. The time between death and resurrection, and the magnitude of bodily change, make no difference to Allah’s power: old and new, distant and near, are equal to Him. His experience also resembles the way the resurrected will regard a long interval as short.

The repeated commands to look have distinct functions. The phrase that Allah might make him a sign to men identifies a further purpose of his death and revival: it both demonstrated the matter to him and made him a sign for others. The subsequent vision of the bones specifically showed him the manner in which Allah gives life. Al-Mizan accordingly rejects the claim that the bones are those of a living body, cited merely as an analogy from growth. They are the donkey’s bones, and the whole account is a single answer to the passerby’s question, not a sequence containing needless repetition.

His concluding declaration does not mean that he had formerly doubted Allah’s all-encompassing power. He says I know, not now I know; as a prophet he could not have been ignorant of the divine attributes; and what he witnessed establishes Allah’s power to revive the dead, not by itself His power over all things. The demonstration reassured and confirmed a knowledge he already possessed, and Allah’s approval of the declaration confirms that it was not an unwarranted conclusion produced merely by shock.

Al-Mizan takes the opening of the final story as an implied command to remember Abraham’s request. Abraham asks for demonstration, not for a logical proof that resurrection is possible. His use of how shows that he already knew that Allah gives life to the dead and sought to see the manner of the divine act. The question could concern either how scattered material bodies receive life, which concerns the result, or how Allah Himself bestows life, which concerns the cause and divine action. The commentary adopts the latter. Abraham says how Thou givest life, not how the dead become alive; the event is made to occur through his own actions and call; and the ending, Allah is Mighty, Wise, is more fitting to the divine bestowal of life than to the body’s mere reception of it.

Al-Mizan rejects a reading that turns the birds into a similitude rather than an actual resurrection. That reading makes fa-ṣurhunna mean tame or incline the birds toward yourself, takes the commands as merely informative, and argues from the pronouns, the delay indicated by then, the impossibility of observing minute changes in scattered pieces, the incomprehensibility of divine will, and the ending Mighty, Wise. The commentary replies that show me, the command to place a part of them on each mountain, and the enactment through Abraham all require actual cutting and revival. In context, fa-ṣurhunna means cut them into pieces, while the preposition conveys the accompanying sense of inclination. The pronouns can still refer to the birds themselves because creative speech differs from ordinary speech: ordinary speech requires its addressee to exist, whereas creative speech addresses what does not yet exist and brings it into existence. Allah’s will in this respect is an attribute of action, inferred from creating and giving life; what cannot be comprehended is the divine Person. The successive commands also contain the required delay in cutting, mixing, dividing, and scattering the pieces. Moreover, Mighty, Wise suits the actual disclosure of life-giving, whereas a merely theoretical explanation would more naturally have ended with an attribute of power.

It also rejects the view that Abraham asked only how dead matter receives life, that the divine question merely dispelled a possible misunderstanding of disbelief, and that ease of heart means freedom from speculative wandering about bodily restoration. That view treats the story as parallel to the preceding account and even identifies the passerby as ʿUzayr. Al-Mizan replies that Abraham asked to see the cause, not the effect; otherwise any dead body brought to life before him would have answered the question, and there would have been no need for the event to occur through Abraham himself. Nor would reviving only four birds answer a question confined to the material condition of all dead bodies. The two stories therefore have different purposes, and the alleged comparison does not establish Abraham’s superiority over the passerby.

The added and in Allah’s question, and do you not believe?, shows that Abraham’s request was proper and was not to be linked with disbelief; without it, the question would have been a rebuke asking whether he made the request because he lacked faith. Abraham’s affirmative answer confirms that resurrection is inseparable from belief in Allah. His desire for tranquillity does not imply a defect in faith. Rational certainty may coexist with the disturbance caused by sense-bound imagination before realities beyond sense; such fancies may trouble the spirit without overturning its belief. Demonstration removes this distress, for seeing has an effect that abstract knowledge does not. Abraham thus sought complete certainty and calm concerning the divine act, not a sensory explanation of how material pieces happen to become alive.

The detailed commands concerning the four birds are integral to this answer. Abraham was to know the birds distinctly, kill them, cut and mix their pieces, divide the mixture, place portions on separate mountains, and call them. His call, by Allah’s command, became connected to the creative decree through which life is bestowed. The miracle was not produced by a hidden force in spoken letters or by the prophet’s mental images; it depended on the prophet’s spiritual connection with the divine omnipotence that truly creates. In this way Abraham witnessed, through his own call, the divine bestowal of life that he had sought to see.

The plural dead also matters. The mixing and scattering obliterate every recognizable bodily distinction, yet each bird returns separately and flies to Abraham. The call is addressed to the birds themselves, that is, to their spirits, not to inert pieces; the wording call them supports this, rather than a wording appropriate to shouting at distant portions. Al-Mizan concludes that the body follows the soul, not the soul the body. The creative decree first concerns the spirit, and the body is restored through the special bond Allah has established and preserves between each spirit and its body. Separate bodily identity therefore follows the identity of the soul without delay, as indicated by their coming flying. It further infers from the mountains that the event occurred after Abraham’s migration from Babylonia to Syria. Allah is Mighty because nothing that has ceased to exist is lost to Him, and Wise because He creates bodies through creating their souls, by the proper method.
verses.261: Al-Mizan compares wealth spent in Allah’s way to a grain that yields seven ears, each bearing a hundred grains: Allah multiplies for whom He pleases, for He is Ample-giving and All-knowing.
verses.262: Al-Mizan promises those who spend their wealth in Allah’s way without following it with reproach or injury a reward with their Lord, and freedom from fear and grief.
verses.263: Al-Mizan says kind words and forgiveness surpass harmful charity; Allah is Self-sufficient and Forbearing.
verses.264: Al-Mizan warns believers not to void charity with reproach and injury. Such giving resembles a display-seeker who disbelieves in Allah and the Last Day: like soil washed by heavy rain from a smooth rock, it leaves no gain, and Allah does not guide unbelieving people.
verses.265: Al-Mizan likens people who spend seeking Allah’s pleasure and keeping their souls firm to a garden on elevated ground: heavy rain yields double fruit, and even light rain suffices; Allah sees what they do.
verses.266: Al-Mizan asks whether anyone would want a fruit-filled garden of palms and vines, watered by streams, to be burned by a fiery whirlwind just when old age and weak offspring make it indispensable; Allah clarifies such signs for reflection.
verses.267: Al-Mizan commands believers to spend from their good earnings and produce, not from inferior things which they themselves would accept only by connivance; Allah is Self-sufficient and Praiseworthy.
verses.268: Al-Mizan contrasts Satan’s threat of poverty and command to abomination with Allah’s promise of forgiveness and abundance; Allah is Ample-giving and All-knowing.
verses.269: Al-Mizan says Allah grants wisdom as He pleases; whoever receives it receives great good, grasped only by those of understanding mind.
verses.270: Al-Mizan says Allah knows every alms and vow, while the oppressors will have no helpers.
verses.271: Al-Mizan says open alms are good, but hidden gifts to the poor are better, expiating some sins; Allah is aware of all you do.
verses.272: Al-Mizan tells the Prophet that making people follow the right way is not his duty; Allah guides whom He pleases. Good spending, done only to seek Allah’s pleasure, benefits its giver and will be repaid in full without wrong. Charity is for constrained poor in Allah’s way, unable to travel for livelihood: their restraint makes the uninformed think them rich, though their condition can be recognized by their countenance and they do not beg importunately; Allah knows every good thing spent.
verses.273: Al-Mizan tells the Prophet that making people follow the right way is not his duty; Allah guides whom He pleases. Good spending, done only to seek Allah’s pleasure, benefits its giver and will be repaid in full without wrong. Charity is for constrained poor in Allah’s way, unable to travel for livelihood: their restraint makes the uninformed think them rich, though their condition can be recognized by their countenance and they do not beg importunately; Allah knows every good thing spent.
verses.274:
Al-Mizan treats the verses on spending as a single revealed unit. They establish that wealth spent in Allah’s way increases manifold—pictured first as a grain producing seven ears of a hundred grains each—and that the increase of sincere spending cannot fail, while ostentatious spending bears no fruit. They prohibit following charity with reproach or injury, require that what is given be good and lawful rather than worthless or unlawful, direct charity toward poor people besieged in Allah’s way, and repeatedly promise the spender a reward in this world and the next.

The commentary presents spending for people’s welfare as central to Islam’s concern for the rights of people. Its obligatory and recommended channels include zakāt, khums, expiatory payments, redemptions, obligatory maintenance, voluntary alms, endowments, life and residence settlements, wills, and gifts. Their purpose is to raise those unable to meet their needs nearer to those with means. Correspondingly, the wealthy may live reasonably and honourably but are forbidden extravagance, lavish display, and squandering beyond the reach of ordinary people. The intended society has relatively close standards of living, unity and cooperation instead of antagonism, and a good life whose members share its blessings equally or nearly equally. Since this requires meeting needs and reforming social conditions, wealth must be contributed from what people earn; believers are brothers, while land, property, and wealth belong to Allah.

Al-Mizan maintains that the Prophet demonstrated this system when he possessed authority, producing a stable and fruitful society. It invokes a sermon attributed to the Leader of the faithful, ʿAlī, lamenting an age in which virtue recedes, evil advances, the poor suffer, the rich answer Allah’s favour with ingratitude, and misers violate Allah’s right to enlarge their wealth. The commentary argues that later dominance of western culture concentrated wealth among a small class, deprived the majority, and generated class conflict, enmity, the World Wars, and Communism. It identifies closing the gate of spending and opening the doors of interest as a major source of this disorder, and treats the Qur’anic warning that interest leads to corruption as a fulfilled prophecy, invoked through (30:30-43).

For the first parable, Al-Mizan defines the way of Allah without restriction as every religious purpose leading to His pleasure, not merely fighting. Some scholars supply an unstated sower and take the growing grain as the likeness of the wealth rather than of the spenders. The commentary finds this linguistically sound but not wholly in accord with the Qur’an’s usual parabolic style: its parables often mention only the essential element of resemblance and omit the rest of the story for brevity, force, and an unexpected mental image. A parable may be imagined as well as externally found; moreover, ears containing a hundred grains and seeds yielding seven hundred are in fact often found.

Allah’s multiplication is not capped at seven hundred. Reading the clause as merely limiting the stated seven-hundredfold return would make it an explanatory cause that should have been introduced differently; Allah’s unrestricted multiplication is instead compatible with increase beyond that amount. The promised increase applies to this world as well as the Hereafter. Humanity resembles a single body: when one part supplies what restores another, the whole benefits far beyond the small expenditure, and the contributor shares in that social improvement. Helping the poor removes poverty’s harms, strengthens their work and goodwill, and particularly benefits society when directed to education and training. But spending for self-regarding motives—such as protecting oneself from the poor or making one’s own environment more comfortable—subjugates the recipient and may accumulate resentment into riot and revolution. Spending solely for Allah’s pleasure is free of these defects and necessarily produces good and blessing.

Reproach means reminding the recipient of what was given in a manner that makes charity burdensome, while injury is an immediate harm. Thus those who spend without either have their reward with their Lord and neither fear, the expectation of harm, nor grief, the distress of a real or nearly real misfortune. A kind word is due when a requester must be turned away without having spoken offensively; forgiveness is due when the requester has spoken unpleasantly. Both are better than fulfilling the need and then wounding the recipient. Such injury shows that the giver regards his gift as enormous and resents requests. A believer should instead take on the moral pattern indicated by Allah’s names: He is Self-sufficient, so no bounty is great to Him, and Forbearing, so He does not hasten to punish His creatures’ follies.

The commentary holds that reproach and injury specifically forfeit a charity, but rejects the broader inference that every later sin, especially every grave one, nullifies prior good deeds. It compares the giver who later reproaches or injures with one who spends merely to be seen by people. The latter charity is void from the outset, whereas the former begins validly and is subsequently annulled. Since the address is to believers, it prohibits reproach and injury rather than display: a deed performed merely for people is not a believer’s act in the first place. The display-seeker’s disbelief does not necessarily mean total denial of Allah; it is disbelief, with respect to that deed, in Allah’s summons to spend, His promised reward, and the Last Day. Had he believed in these, he would have sought Allah’s pleasure rather than people’s notice.

The soil on a smooth rock is washed away by a heavy rain and leaves a bare surface unable to hold water or nourish seed. Soil and rain ordinarily produce life, but the rock prevents their effect without any defect in either. Likewise, even an outwardly effective act such as spending earns no reward when the heart cannot receive divine mercy through a sincere intention to seek Allah’s pleasure. Allah’s refusal to guide unbelieving people therefore explains the forfeiture. Al-Mizan also notes a report transmitted by Sunnis and Shias from the Prophet that deeds are according to intentions.

Seeking Allah’s pleasure means obeying what He commands, after which He turns to the obedient servant with pleasure and mercy. Concerning keeping firm their souls, Al-Mizan rejects as linguistically strained readings that make it simply certainty, care in choosing the recipient, scrutiny of the manner of spending, steadfast obedience in general, or the strengthening of faith through habitual spending. It proposes, with God knows best, that sincere spenders first purify their purpose from display and every aim other than Allah, then keep their souls firm upon that original intention and do not later corrupt the act through deeds that nullify it. Grammatically, their souls are understood as making their souls firm.

The elevated garden shows that spending connected with Allah through this enduring purity cannot fail to yield its effect. Divine care makes it flourish, though the yield varies with the purity of intention and firmness of soul, just as rain varies in amount. Heavy rain produces abundant, doubled fruit, yet even a light drizzle is enough for such good soil. Allah sees every deed and never confuses one person’s recompense with another’s.

The garden destroyed by a fiery whirlwind depicts the spender whose valid charity is later annulled by reproach and injury. Its owner’s old age and weak offspring make the garden his indispensable means of livelihood: he cannot regain his strength to restore it, his children cannot restore it, and the burnt garden cannot recover its fruit. This heightens the image of an irretrievably forfeited deed. Love of wealth and honour, pride, and avarice cause such conduct by preventing reflection on benefit and harm, good and evil.

What is spent must come from good earnings and what Allah brings forth from the earth, not from bad property which the giver himself would accept only by connivance. Such a gift is not generosity but disposal of something unwanted; it neither cultivates generosity nor brings spiritual perfection. Allah’s being Self-sufficient and Praiseworthy may mean that He needs nothing yet appreciates good spending, or that nothing unworthy should be offered to His great sanctity.

The reluctance to give good property rests on fear that its loss will impoverish the giver. Al-Mizan calls this Satan’s threat, for Allah alone enriches and grants abundance; property itself has no power to make anyone rich. Spending good wealth for Allah is a profitable transaction. Satan’s further command to abomination works through miserliness and niggardliness: they lead people to disobey or reject commands affecting wealth, and they plunge the needy into poverty, deprivation, despair, loss of life and honour, and crime. There is no third position between truth from Allah and falsehood from Satan. Allah’s contrasting promise of forgiveness and abundance shows that these follow good spending, not niggardliness or disposal of inferior goods; His promise is certain because He is Ample-giving and All-knowing.

Al-Ḥikmah, wisdom, is precise and perfect true knowledge not liable to falsehood or error. The commentary says the preceding teaching on spending, its causes, and its social effects rests on such wisdom: it discloses realities concerning the origin and end of the world and humankind, and the natural principles relevant to human felicity on which religious law rests. Wisdom itself brings great good; the passive wording emphasizes this rather than merely saying that it is good because Allah gives it, since not every thing given by Allah necessarily reaches a good end. Calling it great good also indicates that every matter requires Allah’s care if its end is to be truly good. Wisdom depends on mindful reflection, moving from conclusions to premises and from premises to conclusions, and this in turn depends on understanding; hence only people of understanding mind take heed.

Allah knows every alms and every vow, rewarding obedience and threatening the oppressor with having no helpers. Al-Mizan takes the oppression here specifically as withholding the financial rights of needy people, not injustice generally. Other sins may have helpers in the form of repentance, expiation, avoidance of grave sins, or intercession regarding Allah’s rights, which also explains the plural helpers. By contrast, neglect of the poor’s due is a grave and mortal sin: it is not expiated, and repentance does not avail until the rights are restored to their owners; nor does intercession avail its perpetrator. Such an oppressor is not among those whose religion Allah approves, and withholding aid when needy people are present is treated as akin in some cases to associating partners with Allah and denying the Hereafter. The reference to zakāt in a Meccan passage is therefore understood as general alms, not the later specific poor-rate.

Ṣadaqāt denotes spending in Allah’s way and includes obligatory and voluntary giving. Open alms are good because they practically enjoin generosity, encourage others to give, assure the poor that society sympathizes with them and has wealth reserved for their need, remove their pessimism, renew their energy, and create social solidarity. Secret alms are also good: they are further from display, reproach, and injury, and preserve the poor from public shame. Open giving has greater social effects, but hidden giving is purer in intention; because purity of intention is religion’s foundation, hidden gifts to the poor are comparatively better and remove some sins. Allah knows the exact quality of every deed.

The statement that guiding them is not the Prophet’s responsibility is parenthetic consolation addressed to him. He was distressed by believers’ differing states in spending—some sincere, others reproachful or reluctant to give good property. Their existing guidance and its degrees belong to Allah; the Prophet cannot create or preserve it and need not be disheartened by its weakness or by the severe warnings addressed to them. When the discourse returns to the believers, it makes clear that the gain from spending is theirs alone, provided they spend only for Allah’s pleasure. Its recompense in this world and the Hereafter is an actual reality, fully repaid without reduction or loss. The passive expression of repayment underscores that the Giver has nothing to gain from calling them to spend.

The best recipients are poor people constrained in Allah’s way by circumstances beyond their control, such as an enemy’s obstruction, sickness that bars earning, or an activity such as acquiring knowledge that leaves no time to earn. Al-Mizan notes that al-ḥaṣr denotes constraint and cites al-Rāghib’s distinction between it and al-iḥṣār, which can cover both manifest and hidden hindrances. These poor preserve their dignity so thoroughly that the uninformed take them for wealthy; only signs that cannot be concealed, such as their faces or worn clothes, disclose their condition. One interpretation takes their not begging importunately to mean that they never beg at all. The commentary finds it more probable that the verse forbids importunity, not discreet requests: explaining one’s need in extreme hardship may be permissible or even necessary, whereas exceeding what is needed to state it is condemned. The singular address about discerning them by their countenance preserves their honour, for their poverty is not publicly notorious even though the Messenger may know their state.

Finally, spending by night and day, secretly and openly, encompasses every time and manner of giving. It reveals the spenders’ eagerness for reward and their deep desire for Allah’s pleasure. In response, Allah turns to them with mercy and promises their reward with their Lord, with no fear and no grief.
verses.275: Al-Mizan states that those who take interest manage their lives like one confounded by Satan’s touch, because they equate trade with interest although Allah permits trade and forbids interest. Whoever desists after receiving the Lord’s admonition retains what has passed and is left to Allah; whoever returns is an abiding inmate of the Fire.
verses.276: Al-Mizan says Allah effaces interest, causes charities to grow, and loves no ungrateful sinner.
verses.277: Al-Mizan says believers who do good, establish prayer, and pay the poor-rate have their Lord’s reward, with no fear or grief.
verses.278: Al-Mizan commands believers to fear Allah and forgo outstanding interest, if they are believers.
verses.279: Al-Mizan warns that refusal brings war from Allah and His Apostle. Repentance entitles one only to one’s capital, so neither party is wronged.
verses.280: Al-Mizan commands respite for a debtor in straitened circumstances until ease, and says that remitting the debt as alms is better.
verses.281:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as an exceptionally forceful reaffirmation and enforcement of an already established prohibition of interest, not as its original legislation. It considers the earlier prohibition most probably to be (3:130), while (30:39) had condemned interest even before the hijrah. The demand that believers relinquish outstanding interest shows that some still took it after its prohibition; the passage therefore orders them to desist and waive accrued claims. The commentary also notes that Judaism had forbidden interest, and that the Qur’an confirmed the Jewish book without abrogating this law. It takes the verses’ sequence and style as evidence that they came after the third chapter’s prohibition.

The commentary connects interest with the preceding injunctions to spend in Allah’s way. Interest takes without giving an equivalent, whereas charity gives without taking; their social effects are opposite. Charity cultivates mercy, mutual love, the strength of the poor, wealth, order, and peace. Interest produces their opposites. Al-Mizan says that no act is condemned in comparably harsh terms except befriending the enemies of religion. Other grave sins chiefly damage particular persons and traits, whereas these two evils uproot religion, destroy social order, and overpower human nature. It portrays the subservience of Muslim countries to the enemies of Islam as yielding plunder, loss of self-determination, wealth, honour, identity, religion, and virtue. It likewise holds that interest concentrates the earth’s wealth in a few houses, gives their owners power over the less fortunate, was the real cause of world wars, and divides humanity into affluent and destitute camps, threatening universal destruction. It treats this carnage as the fulfillment of the Qur’an’s forecast.

On (2:275), Al-Mizan explains al-khabṭ as uneven, disoriented walking. Human life normally follows a straight path: sound ideas guide actions in a balanced way, through the innate faculty that distinguishes good from evil and benefit from harm. The confounded person does not merely forget these distinctions or consistently invert them; rather, he mistakes evil for virtue and applies judgments without order, so that normal and abnormal are alike and he follows whatever desire confronts him. This is the condition ascribed to the interest-taker.

Interest is giving something and later recovering its like plus an increment. Trade, by contrast, exchanges a person’s surplus for property needed from another and accords with human nature. Interest destroys this balance: the debtor’s property is added to the lender’s, while the debtor bears an expenditure for which he receives nothing. His need then drives him to borrow more both to live and to pay the escalating interest, until his livelihood is ruined. Interest thus transfers and accumulates wealth on one side, diminishes it on the other, and opposes the social equilibrium established by Divine Creation. The interest-taker therefore fails to distinguish trade from interest and, when directed to leave the latter, treats trade as having no superiority over it.

“Standing” means managing one’s life and livelihood, not rising from sitting or from the grave. Nor does the verse compare the voluntary, confused conduct of the interest-taker to the involuntary convulsions of epilepsy. It describes his management of life as that of one confounded by Satan’s touch. The phrase nevertheless indicates that Satanic touch may be involved in some cases of lunacy; it does not say that every case is so caused, nor that Iblīs himself is the agent, since Satan can designate evil beings among jinn and human beings. The commentary holds that jinn are instrumental in some, perhaps all, cases of madness.

Al-Mizan rejects the claim that this is merely a simile using an erroneous popular belief about jinn without affirming it. The Qur’an, it argues, does not insert an unmarked falsehood into its decisive speech. Nor does divine justice preclude God from allowing mental disturbance through Satanic or natural agencies, provided the afflicted person is relieved of the responsibilities of sanity. Injustice would arise if impaired judgment carried sane responsibility, or if Satan made a sane person see truth and virtue as their opposites while he remained accountable as sane. Natural disorders are proximate causes of madness, while Satan may be a more remote cause; attributing events to metaphysical agencies adds a further link in the causal chain and does not displace physical causes.

It also rejects the interpretation that the verse describes interest-takers rising from their graves on the Day of Resurrection like epileptics. The context gives no indication that “standing” means resurrection, and reports about their condition on that Day do not themselves interpret this similitude. Al-Manār, following Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, correctly locates the simile in worldly life and observes that reports offered for the resurrection reading are defective or do not expound the verse. But Al-Mizan rejects al-Manār’s further explanation that money-obsession causes the interest-taker’s bodily movements to become disordered like those of a lunatic. Such loss of composure can result from any immersion in worldly pleasure and forgetfulness of God, even without interest; more decisively, the verse proves the confoundedness by their equation of trade and interest, not by their movements.

The wording “trade is only like interest,” rather than “interest is like trade,” reveals the depth of their disorder. It expresses their condition, not necessarily words they uttered. One who said that interest was like trade would at least recognize trade as good and mistakenly extend that status to interest; he would be a mistaken rejector of the law, not one who regards good and evil alike. By making trade secondary to interest, their state shows that they acknowledge no superiority in the lawful over the unlawful. For this reason, explanations that treat the reversal as rhetorical exaltation of interest, or as a preference for its allegedly certain profit, miss the point.

“And Allah has allowed trade and forbidden interest” is, in Al-Mizan’s reading, an independent statement, not a grammatical clause qualifying their saying. It recalls a prior law and leads into the ruling concerning those who desist; it is not the original enactment of the prohibition. Although the differing legal status of trade and interest would itself refute their equation, the commentary says that this is not the statement’s syntactical function. It also rejects the view that the difference rests solely on an arbitrary divine command with no connection to benefit or cause. Qur’anic laws have reasons and benefits: trade conforms to the natural path of life, while interest is a deviation from it, incompatible with belief in God and an injustice.

The admonition that comes from one’s Lord means that knowledge of the divinely ordained law reaches a person, and desisting means repentance and abandonment of the forbidden act. The principle is general, despite its occurrence in a discussion of interest: one who receives the admonition and desists is forgiven what preceded it, whether the violation concerned Allah’s rights or people’s rights. The law is not imposed retrospectively merely because the person previously acted in ignorance, but “his affair rests with Allah” means that repentance does not automatically remove every remaining consequence. Allah may require restitution, expiation, making up neglected obligations, or the prescribed penalty, according to the sin; or He may forgive without such further requirement. The rule embraces believers and unbelievers at the Prophet’s time and afterward.

“Whoever returns” contrasts with desisting and means one who continues in the sin without accepting Allah’s command. Such persistence, without shame or submission, uncovers hidden unbelief or apostasy and warrants abiding in the Fire. Thus eternal punishment here is conditional not simply on committing even a major sin, but on continuing in it as a rejection of the divine command. Al-Mizan consequently rejects the Muʿtazilite inference that every perpetrator of a major sin remains in the Fire forever.

On (2:276), the commentary defines al-maḥq as gradual decrease and deterioration ending in extinction, and al-irbāʾ as causing growth. Both the effacement of interest and the growth of charity belong to this world and the hereafter. Charity necessarily generates love, mercy, concord, mutual help, security, and protection from resentment; it closes many paths by which property deteriorates and makes wealth grow. Interest spreads hardness, cruelty, enmity, distrust, insecurity, and the desire of the deprived to retaliate; it opens paths to the destruction of wealth and often leaves its takers with ruined property and frustrated efforts.

These effects particularly concern the poor. Kindness that seeks no return awakens their goodwill and brotherhood, while greedy treatment that imperils their property, honour, and life provokes resistance. Al-Mizan qualifies the causal claim by distinguishing social from complete physical causes: social factors produce their effects in most cases, not without exception, and the Qur’an may state a recurrent effect as an ever-recurring one. It likewise treats society as having a life, death, actions, and effects distinct from those of an individual. An individual’s vice may bring quick consequences, while the same vice, once normalized socially, may take much longer to reveal its deeper results.

Accordingly, an individual interest-taker is almost always destroyed, though mitigating factors may occasionally spare him. In a society built on interest, some immediate effects can be obscured because the practice is accepted, but its intrinsic results—concentrated wealth, pervasive need, and confrontation between those who have and those who lack—must emerge over society’s longer lifespan. The Qur’an, the commentary says, safeguards the felicity of individuals, societies, and humanity in both present and future. Thus interest is ultimately effaced even though al-ribā literally means growth, while charity grows even though it bears no such name.

Al-Mizan rejects a reading that limits effacement to the interest-taker’s inability to enjoy his wealth, and another that confines it to the next life through the nullification of worship performed with unlawful wealth. The latter gives examples of effacement but not its full scope. The description of the interest-taker as al-Kaffār is emphatic: he is inveterately ungrateful or obstinately unbelieving. By obstructing natural dealings, using unlawful wealth in consumption and commerce, invalidating worship and transactions, usurping others’ property, and cultivating greed, hard-heartedness, and coercion against debtors, he becomes athīm, one in whom sin is ingrained. Allah does not love such ingrained ingratitude, sin, and unbelief.

The promise in (2:277) is a general rule: those who believe and obey divine law have their reward with their Lord and will neither fear nor grieve. It applies aptly to those who give charity and abstain from the interest Allah has forbidden. In (2:278), the address to believers and the closing condition “if you are believers” show that abandoning interest is inseparable from faith. The verse indicates that believers still had unpaid interest owed by debtors when it was revealed, and commands them to relinquish it under the ensuing threat of war.

Regarding (2:279), Al-Mizan notes that faʾdhanu means “be apprised” or “know,” while another recitation, faʾādhinu, means “announce.” The preposition in “war” conveys certainty: they must be sure of a great war, or of various kinds of war, from Allah and His Apostle. It is attributed to both because it concerns a law from Allah promulgated by His Apostle, who has no independent authority. Allah and His Apostle may fight a disobedient Muslim to compel his return to divine authority. Allah may also defend His law through the agency of nature, arousing the masses against persistent offenders and bringing devastation upon them.

The command to give respite to a debtor in straitened circumstances applies generally to every debt, although it includes interest-bearing loans. It requires a moratorium until the debtor is able to pay, and forbids the former practice of extending time in exchange for further interest. Remitting the debt as alms is better because it transforms what was meant to grow through interest, and was therefore destined for effacement, into charity, which is destined to multiply.

Al-Mizan treats (2:281) as the epilogue to the interest verses. It recalls the return to Allah, complete repayment of every soul for what it earned, and the absence of injustice, thereby urging fear of Allah and abandonment of forbidden acts, especially violations of people’s rights, on which the structure of life rests. It postpones explanation of the return to Allah and this full repayment to its discussion of the sixth chapter. It also notes, without affirming it as its own conclusion, the report that this was the last verse revealed to the Apostle.

In its first broader discourse, Al-Mizan argues that human work aims at fulfilling the material needs through which life reaches its perfection. A person is entitled to the effects of his work, broadly understood to include actions, reactions, and socially recognized relationships that produce effects. Since no one can fulfil every need alone, people cooperate and exchange their surplus products for what they need from others. The diversity, rarity, and unequal demand of goods made barter difficult, so gold and later other media came to serve as a standard of value, alongside measures of length, volume, and weight. Money enabled the value of disparate goods to be compared and commerce to develop, including the exchange of currencies.

Trade rests on exchanging something for something different, whether another commodity or its price, because the parties need different things or seek a profit through exchange. A loan of the same commodity without increase can be reasonable and may correct social imbalance and meet the poor’s needs. But receiving the same commodity with an increase—whether ten dirhams lent for twelve, or an item sold on credit for a higher delayed payment—is interest. The debtor borrows because his needs exceed his income; interest consumes part of that income, forces additional borrowing, and eventually consumes all he earns. Meanwhile, the lender receives both his own wealth and the debtor’s, so wealth accumulates on one side and disappears on the other.

This, Al-Mizan says, destroys the poor, makes the wealthy arrogant and dominant over people’s property, honour, and lives, and provokes the deprived to resist by every available means. The resulting confrontation brings disorder, violence, and the decay of civilization, quite apart from the recurring loss of capital when debtors cannot or will not repay. Commercial interest through banks may conceal the process, but it enlarges powerful firms beyond their true capacity; they compete, absorb weaker traders, increase the needy population, and concentrate wealth in a few houses. The commentary asserts that this excessive concentration gave rise to communism and the spread of socialism. It depicts the wealthy minority as insincerely invoking civilization, justice, freedom, equality, and human rights to preserve exploitation, until those claims rebounded against them. It also condemns the idleness created by interest: the rich can live in luxury on inactive hoards, while the poor remain idle because they lack employment, though human nature requires work for livelihood.

Al-Mizan then reports al-Ghazālī’s account of the dirham and dinar. Al-Ghazālī treats them as divinely given intermediaries and judges among unlike goods: because they circulate and permit goods to be valued against a common measure, one who owns them can obtain all necessities. He holds that using them contrary to this function is ingratitude. On this basis, he explains the prohibition of hoarding gold and silver as imprisoning the social judge, the prohibition of gold and silver vessels as turning the means of exchange into an end, and the prohibition of interest in the two metals as an unjust and ungrateful misuse of what was created for other things.

The commentary rejects both al-Ghazālī’s principle and its legal deductions. If gold and silver were not wanted in themselves, they could not measure the wantedness or value of other things; yet al-Ghazālī also calls them precious in themselves, and his account cannot explain their differing worth. Hoarding is prohibited because it withholds the poor’s dues and interrupts the cycle of work, payment, and exchange, not because it treats money as an end. His reasoning would also forbid gold and silver ornaments and money-changing, which the sharīʿah does not prohibit, while failing to cover interest in measured or weighed goods other than gold and silver. It therefore neither includes all cases of interest nor excludes transactions that are not interest.

For Al-Mizan, the Qur’anic reason is that interest takes an excess without any exchange. It grows by adding portions of other people’s property to itself, just as a seed grows by drawing from the earth, until those properties are depleted. The ruling that a repentant creditor may keep only the capital confirms that interest is injustice against people: neither may the creditor deal unjustly by taking the increment, nor may he be dealt with unjustly by losing his principal.
verses.282:
Al-Mizan explains that these two verses lay down nearly twenty basic rules concerning loans, pledges, evidence, and related transactions; the many transmitted details belong in books of jurisprudence. A fixed-term loan should be written by a just scribe, who must not refuse to write as Allah has taught him. The debtor is to dictate truthfully, fearing Allah and diminishing nothing. The repeated phrase “he who owes the debt,” rather than a pronoun, prevents its being mistaken for the scribe.

If the debtor lacks understanding or is weak in body or mind, his guardian has complete authority to dictate, since the debtor cannot manage his own affairs. But where the debtor is otherwise unable to dictate himself, the explicit huwa gives debtor and guardian joint authority: the debtor does what he can, and the guardian what he cannot. Testimony requires two men, or, if they are unavailable, one man and two approved women, so that if either woman errs, the other—specifically the one who has not erred—may remind her. The first “one of the two” is indefinite between them, whereas the second identifies the other woman.

Debts, whether small or large, should be recorded with their term, because this is more equitable before Allah, more accurate for testimony, and less liable to later doubt. Immediate hand-to-hand merchandise need not be written, though witnesses should be present in trade. Scribes and witnesses must neither refuse their duties nor be harmed; harming them is transgression. When travelling without a scribe, a security may be taken into possession. Where one party trusts another, the trusted person must deliver the trust and fear Allah; testimony must not be concealed, for the concealer’s heart is sinful, and Allah knows what people do.

Al-Mizan holds that “and fear Allah” commands obedience to the verse’s orders and prohibitions, while “and Allah teaches you” is an independent statement of divine grace: Allah has taught believers religious rules and their permissions and prohibitions. It compares this with the inheritance verse, where Allah makes matters clear lest people err (4:176). Although the general principle that fearing God brings divine teaching is true and supported elsewhere in the Qur’an and traditions, the commentary rejects treating this verse as an expression of that causal principle. The conjunction “and,” the context, and the otherwise irrelevant ending oppose it; were that meaning intended, the wording would have been “and fear God, He will teach you.” The repeated divine name likewise shows that the clauses are separate: it is required in “fear God,” repeated because “and God teaches you” is independent, and used in “and God knows all things” as the proof that He knows all things because He is God.

verses.284:
Al-Mizan explains that God’s ownership of everything in the heavens and earth prepares for the declaration that He will call people to account for what they disclose or conceal within themselves. Human beings, their actions, and what their souls have earned all belong to God; He encompasses them and preserves their deeds, so manifest and hidden acts are alike before Him. It also reports an explanation linking the heavens with mental faculties, psychological traits, and spiritual characteristics: what is in minds belongs to God as part of what is in the heavens, while traits expressed through bodily acts belong to Him as part of what is in the earth. In either case, God will decide concerning them after calling people to account.

The commentary defines al-Ibdāʾ as manifesting and al-ikhfāʾ as hiding. “What is in your souls” means what is settled in the mind: good and evil traits such as belief or disbelief, love or hate, and strength or weakness of will. Such traits can become manifest through bodily acts, which reveal the motives fixed in their doers; or they can remain hidden when no act demonstrates them. The phrase does not mean only ineradicable, deeply rooted dispositions, but the real presence of traits or psychological states from which actions may proceed.

Accordingly, the verse does not concern involuntary, passing notions that enter the mind without intention, such as imagining a sin while having neither the intention nor inclination to commit it. Such notions are not settled in the mind and no action proceeds from them. Rather, the verse concerns settled mental states that underlie both obedience and disobedience, for which people will be called to account. Al-Mizan supports this by passages concerning what hearts have earned, sinful hearts, and the questioning of hearing, sight, and heart (2:225), (2:283), (17:36). It also cites the punishment of those who love that scandal should circulate among believers (24:19), since love itself is a state of mind.

This is the verse’s clear meaning: a person will be called to account for what is settled in the mind, whether it is concealed or displayed. The verse does not determine whether punishment is the same or different when such a state is manifested or hidden, acted upon or not acted upon, or when an intended transgression succeeds or fails.

Al-Mizan holds that most commentators erred by treating the verse as an accounting for fleeting, uncontrollable thoughts. Such a reading creates the problem of imposing a duty beyond one’s ability. Some accepted that God may impose such a burden; others claimed that the verse did impose it but was abrogated by the next verse, “Allah does not impose upon any soul a duty but to the extent of its ability.” The commentary rejects this entire argument because passing thoughts are not included in the first place. Moreover, imposing a duty beyond capacity is irrational from the outset and cannot be attributed to God even temporarily; He has declared that He did not lay hardship upon people in religion (22:78).

It likewise rejects the restriction of the verse to concealing testimony, because that contradicts its general wording, and rejects the restriction to unbelievers’ fleeting fantasies for the same reason. Another interpretation says that manifesting inner evil means committing sin openly, while hiding it means committing sin secretly, so that the accounting is for acts rather than ideas. Al-Mizan judges this wholly contrary to the verse’s evident meaning. It also rejects the interpretation that “what is in your souls” includes every idea but that “calling to account” merely means informing people on the Day of Resurrection about those ideas; this too contradicts the plain sense, which is accounting for reward or punishment.

Finally, the alternatives of forgiveness and chastisement indicate that “what is in your souls” especially concerns evil thoughts and traits. Although “forgiveness” is rarely used in the Qur’an where no sin is involved, diverting it to that unusual meaning would require a strong reason and clear contextual association. God’s power over all things supplies the reason for His forgiving and chastising, or possibly for the whole statement.
verses.285:
Al-Mizan presents these final verses as the chapter’s summary and as a mirror of its opening. The chapter’s central purpose is that worship of God requires belief in everything He has sent through His apostles, without distinguishing among them. Its accounts of the Israelites’ abundant gifts—the Book, prophethood, and kingdom—and of their disobedience, covenant-breaking, unbelief, hostility to apostles and angels, and discrimination among books and apostles are reflected in the believers’ contrasting response: “We hear and obey,” followed by prayer for forgiveness, protection, mercy, and help.

The opening of the chapter had described the God-fearing as believers in the unseen, maintainers of prayer, spenders from God’s provision, believers in revelation to the Apostle and earlier apostles, and certain of the hereafter; it then contrasted them with unbelievers and hypocrites. The later discussion of the people of the Book, especially the Jews, showed how they answered divine favour with arrogance and ingratitude, bringing upon themselves such burdens as the command to kill their own people, transformation into apes, and lightning and plague. The Apostle and his followers instead submit, believe in God, His angels, His books, and all His apostles, and recognize both their own weakness and God’s all-encompassing power. Although they accept the call without condition, they fear that weakness, ignorance, forgetfulness, error, or failure in worship may bring them disgrace as it did earlier peoples; hence their prayers.

Al-Mizan therefore rejects claims that these verses merely follow the preceding statement about being called to account for what is hidden in souls; that the preceding verse imposed an impossible duty; that the companions accepted such a duty; or that the second verse abrogated it. A reported reason of revelation—that this was the first chapter revealed at Medina—accords with this reading: the Helpers (anṣār) supported the Apostle with their property and lives, while the Emigrants (muhājirūn) left their property, homes, families, and children for Islam. The prayer for help against unbelievers further indicates a time when Islam had begun to advance and faced danger of attack. The verses unite general statement with specification and brevity with amplification, teaching the complete manner of submission and servitude and containing the bases of perfection and felicity.

The commentary explains that the Apostle is named separately before the believers in order to preserve his dignity, as is customary in the Qur’an. What was revealed to him entails belief in God and acceptance of the truth of His angels, books, and apostles. “We make no difference between any of His apostles” is quoted without “They said” because it depicts the believers’ inward, shared state of faith, not a collective verbal declaration; even if uttered, it would have been said individually in their hearts. By contrast, “We hear and obey” is introduced as speech because it was actually uttered. Belief is attributed to every believer individually, while the subsequent plural language suits matters shared collectively: the people of the Book collectively distinguished among apostles, divided into groups, received collective chastisement and burdens, and are met by the collective prayer for help.

“We hear and obey” is a declaration of submission, not bare information. Hearing allegorically means accepting and believing with the heart, and obeying means carrying out the command with the body; together they express perfect belief and the whole duty owed to God, namely worship. In return for this duty, God has decreed forgiveness for His servants, a grace needed by everyone, from apostles and prophets to ordinary believers, and promised to those who obey and worship Him from the time the shariah was first given to Adam. Having unconditionally fulfilled their side through faith and obedience, the believers ask for this promised grace: al-maghfirah and al-ghufrān, “forgiveness,” literally mean covering, by which due punishment is averted and shortcomings concealed. They mention their return to God because this grace is bestowed when the servant reaches his Lord.
verses.286:
Al-Mizan explains al-Wusʿ as ability and power. The term originally denoted the dimensions or capacity of a place or receptacle, and then came to denote human power as the capacity from which actions issue. A task within a person’s power is as though accommodated by that capacity, whereas an impossible task exceeds it.

The duty owed to God is to hear and obey. One can only “hear” what one can understand and only “obey” what one can perform through one’s faculties, organs, or available means; an order concerning what cannot be done is not an order to be obeyed. Thus the believers’ response, “We hear and obey,” means that the religious call concerns what lies within their ability. It is through this ability that they obey or disobey and earn either benefit or harm. “Allah does not impose upon any soul a duty but to the extent of its ability” therefore describes God’s established system: He neither commands belief in what cannot be understood nor imposes a duty that cannot be performed. It is the same reality expressed in the believers’ declaration of hearing and obedience.

This principle also explains the prayers that follow. Their request not to be punished for forgetfulness or error, not to be burdened as earlier peoples were, and not to be subjected to what they cannot bear is not a request concerning impossible religious duties. Such afflictions may be hard to endure, but when imposed on a people beyond their strength they are punishments for transgression and rebellion, not duties. Forgetfulness and error are in themselves beyond human control, yet people commonly prepare their causes and can avoid them by abandoning those causes, especially where error follows a wrong choice. Likewise, burdens placed upon previous peoples were hard rules substituted for easy ones after those peoples opposed the easy rules; they were consequences of their own choice and were not unjust legal obligations beyond ability.

After declaring unconditional surrender, the believers recognize their inherent weakness and imperfection and remember the fate of earlier nations. They consequently seek mercy, knowing that there is no power or strength except from God and no refuge from His displeasure except His mercy. The Apostle’s inclusion in this prayer does not conflict with his sinlessness and protection from error and forgetfulness, because that protection itself was God’s grace; he properly asks with the believers for a grace he knows comes from his Lord.

Al-Mizan takes al-Iṣr, “burden,” also to mean forcibly detaining or confining something, which is closely related to its heaviness. “Those before us” means the people of the Book, particularly the Jews. The request not to be imposed upon beyond their strength does not concern unbearable rules of the shariah, since reason and the preceding declaration both show that God’s commands are intelligible and practicable. Rather, it concerns severe punishments suffered by previous peoples: retaliatory hard rules, grievous chastisements, and transformation into animals or insects.

The pleas for pardon, forgiveness, and mercy proceed from branch to root and from particular to general. al-ʿAfw erases the trace of sin by removing its due punishment; al-maghfirah covers and conceals it so that all concerned forget it; and al-raḥmah is mercy that covers the sin and makes the servant worthy of grace. These requests concern sins possibly committed through forgetfulness or error. They are therefore distinct from the preceding, unrestricted request for forgiveness, which followed the believers’ unrestricted acceptance of the call; the two prayers are not repetitions. Repeating “Lord” four times invokes divine mercy while expressing the supplicant’s servitude and complete dependence.

“Thou art our Guardian, so help us against the unbelieving people” is an independent prayer. al-Mawlā is not merely any helper, but one who takes charge of the helped person’s affairs; its root, al-wilāyah, means governing, ruling, or taking charge. Since God rules the believers, He is their Guardian in all their affairs. The prayer shows that, once they had resolved to hear and obey the fundamental religion, their foremost aim was the general call of all humankind to the true religion: spreading faith, fighting in God’s way to establish the word of truth, enjoining good, forbidding evil, and employing every means of religious propagation. The call to monotheism seeks to remove the root of discord from the human species. And God knows better.
